docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 16 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Vāstu–Śilpa: Architecture and Sculpture. It surveys the architecture of the Indian subcontinent: the vāstu texts; the stūpas and rock-cut monasteries of the Buddhist, Jain and Hindu traditions, which come first because they are the oldest surviving religious monuments; the temples of every region; the mosques, tombs, shrines and gardens of the Sultanates and the Mughals; palaces and the buildings of the colonial and modern periods; and, in three thematic chapters, the planning of towns, the building of tanks, stepwells and dams, and the houses of India’s regions. Its second part deals with the theory and practice of image-making, iconography, the regional schools of sculpture and the traditions of painting. Maps of the principal sites and drawn plans, sections and diagrams accompany the text.

The volume is an edited and corrected version of an earlier draft. In the course of revision every quoted verse was checked; passages that could not be verified as genuine, with a correct reference, were removed rather than repaired, and the many invented “quotations” of the earlier draft no longer appear. The prescriptions of the vāstu and śilpa texts are reported as what those texts say, with their approximate dates and regions, and not as statements of scientific fact; the modern claims made for them are examined in Chapter 2. Widely repeated myths about particular monuments, such as the shadowless tower and the monolithic capstone of the Bṛhadīśvara temple, are examined in their place. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such.

The book draws throughout on the work of modern scholars of Indian architecture and art, among them Stella Kramrisch, Bruno Dagens, Michael Meister, M. A. Dhaky, Adam Hardy, George Michell, Susan Huntington, Vidya Dehejia, Catherine Asher and Ebba Koch, whose works are cited in the text and collected in the select bibliography. It also tries to give a fair account of the social history of building: of the craft communities who built the monuments, of the place of caste in the vāstu texts, and of the many patrons, Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Muslim, men and women, who paid for them. A glossary of the principal technical terms is provided at the end.

No survey of this size can be exhaustive. Readers should treat it as an introduction, and turn to the editions, translations and studies cited for the texts and monuments themselves.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Architecture and Sculpture in the Indian Tradition
1.1 Building, Image and Text
docs.text:
Figure 1.1. The Great Stūpa (Stūpa 1) at Sāñcī, Madhya Pradesh. The hemispherical dome (aṇḍa), crowned by a square railing (harmikā) and a triple umbrella (chattra), goes back to a Mauryan brick stūpa of the 3rd century BCE, perhaps built under Aśoka, that was enlarged and cased in stone in the 2nd century BCE. The carved gateways (toraṇa), one of which is seen here, were added around the turn of the Common Era. Photo: PranjalG431, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The buildings and images of the Indian subcontinent form one of the longest continuous records of architecture and sculpture anywhere in the world. Planned brick cities of the Harappan civilisation, the polished stone pillars of Aśoka, the Buddhist stūpas (Figure 1.1) and rock-cut monasteries of the Deccan, the Hindu and Jain temples of every region, the mosques, tombs and gardens of the Sultanates and the Mughals, the stepwells of Gujarat and the timber houses of Kerala all belong to this record. So do the bronze and stone images made for worship, and the painted walls and manuscripts that accompanied them.

Alongside the monuments there is a body of technical literature in Sanskrit and, later, in regional languages. Its two most familiar names are vāstuśāstra, the science of building and site (from vāstu, “site, dwelling”, from the root vas, “to dwell”), and śilpaśāstra, the science of the crafts and especially of image-making. These texts describe how to choose and prepare a site, lay out a plan on a grid of squares, proportion a building or an image, and perform the rituals that accompany each stage of work. They are practical manuals, but they are also religious texts: they assume that a properly made temple or image is a fit dwelling for a deity, and that a house built according to rule brings good fortune to its occupants.

This volume treats both the texts and the buildings, and keeps the two distinct. The texts tell us what their authors thought ought to be done; standing buildings tell us what was actually done, and the two do not always agree. Throughout the book, prescriptions are reported as what a given text says, with its approximate date and region, not as statements of physical fact. The modern claims that vāstu works through “cosmic energy” or magnetism are examined, once and for the whole volume, in Chapter 2 (Section 2.15).

docs.title: 1.2 Regions and Materials
docs.text:
The geography of the subcontinent shaped its architecture. The great river plains of the Indus and the Gaṅgā have little building stone, and from the Harappan cities to the Mughal and colonial periods their monumental buildings were largely of baked brick, faced with plaster or carved terracotta, with stone brought from the hills for special purposes. The sandstone belts of central India and Rajasthan, the basalt of the Deccan plateau, the granites and gneisses of the southern peninsula, the marble of Rajasthan and Gujarat and the schists of Karnataka each favoured particular techniques and styles (Chapter 4). Timber, abundant in the Himalaya, the Western Ghats, Kerala and the North-east, was the principal material of early architecture everywhere, and remains so in those regions; bamboo, earth and thatch were, and are, the materials of most village houses. Climate imposed its own demands: heavy monsoon rains in the south-west and north-east favoured steep roofs and raised floors; the hot, dry north-west favoured thick walls, courtyards and screens; the cold mountains favoured compact, sun-facing houses. The architecture described in this volume should always be read against this background of regional diversity (Table 1.1; the principal sites are shown in Figure 1.2).

Figure 1.2. Principal temple sites, rock-cut sites, stūpas and monasteries discussed in this volume. Sites north of the frame, such as Mārtaṇḍ in Kashmir and Taxila, are not shown. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude and are approximate where several places share one symbol; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no rivers or political boundaries are shown. docs.title: 1.3 The Textual Tradition
docs.text: The surviving literature on architecture and image-making is large, uneven and, for the most part, difficult to date. Few texts have critical editions, many survive in more than one recension, and attributions to divine or legendary authors (Maya, Viśvakarman, Mānasāra) tell us nothing about historical authorship. The dates below follow current scholarship and are approximate; they are summarised in Table 1.2.

docs.title: 1.3.1 The Principal Texts
docs.text:
Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira (6th century CE) An encyclopaedic work on astral science and omens from Ujjain. Several of its chapters concern building and images: chapter 53 on vāstuvidyā (house sites, the 81- and 64-square grids, the deities of the grid, and the effects of doors), chapter 54 on finding underground water, chapter 56 on temples (prāsāda), listing twenty named temple types, chapter 57 on a cement or glue (vajralepa), and chapter 58 on the proportions of images (Bhat 1981). It is one of the few early texts that can be dated with reasonable confidence, and it is the oldest systematic account of the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala. Mayamata (c. 9th–12th century CE) A South Indian treatise on settlements, houses, temples and images, attributed to Maya. Bruno Dagens, its editor and translator, places it between the 9th and the 12th century and in the Tamil country, and shows that it is closely related to the architectural chapters of the Śaiva āgamas (Dagens 1994). Mānasāra (probably later than the Mayamata) A long South Indian text in seventy chapters covering measurement, site, villages and towns, houses, temples, gateways, furniture, vehicles and images. P. K. Acharya, who edited and translated it, dated it to c. 500–700 CE (Acharya 1934). Later scholars, among them Bruno Dagens in the introduction to his edition of the Mayamata, have generally regarded it as later than that text and as probably of the late medieval period (Dagens 1994), though no firm date can be given. Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra of Bhoja (11th century CE) An encyclopaedic work in 83 chapters attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja of Dhārā (r. c. 1010–1055). It covers town planning, houses, palaces and temples (especially the northern types, including the bhūmija form associated with Paramāra territory), and has a well-known chapter on mechanical devices (yantra) (Gaṇapati Śāstrī 1924). Its chapters on temple design can be compared with the unfinished Paramāra temple at Bhojpur and the architectural drawings engraved around it (Chapter 4) (Hardy 2015). Aparājitapṛcchā of Bhuvanadeva (c. 12th–13th century CE) A western Indian (Gujarat) text in the tradition of the Māru-Gurjara builders, important for northern temple types, iconography and the classification of temples (Mankad 1950). Prāsādamaṇḍana and Rājavallabha of Maṇḍana (15th century CE) Works by the master builder (sūtradhāra) Maṇḍana, who worked at the court of Rāṇā Kumbhā of Mewar; they are still used by the Sompurā temple builders of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Śilpaprakāśa of Rāmacandra Kaulācāra (Odisha; date disputed) An Odishan text on temple architecture with a strong Tantric orientation, edited and translated by Alice Boner and Sadāśiva Rath Śarmā (Boner and Rath Śarmā 1966). Śilparatna of Śrīkumāra (Kerala, 16th century CE) A compendium of architecture, sculpture and painting from Kerala; together with the Tantrasamuccaya (15th century) and the Manuṣyālayacandrikā (on houses, 16th century), both in Sanskrit, it represents the Kerala tradition. Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa, book 3, the Citrasūtra (c. 5th–8th century CE; proposed dates vary) The best-known Sanskrit text on painting, which also treats image-making and dance; see Chapter 14 (Sivaramamurti 1978).

To these must be added the āgamas and saṃhitās of the Śaiva (e.g. Kāmikāgama) and Vaiṣṇava (Vaikhānasa and Pāñcarātra) traditions, which contain chapters on temple building, image-making and consecration and which still govern ritual in many South Indian temples; the architectural sections of some Purāṇas (notably the Matsya and Agni Purāṇas); and the Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE; the traditional attribution to Kauṭilya, minister of Candragupta Maurya, places it c. 300 BCE), which describes fortified towns (Chapter 8) (Olivelle 2013).

North India; painting and images Mayamata c. 9th–12th c. Tamil country; settlements, houses, temples, images Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra 11th c. Mālwā (Bhoja); towns, palaces, temples, machines Aparājitapṛcchā c. 12th–13th c. Gujarat; northern temple types, iconography Mānasāra medieval (disputed) South India; comprehensive Prāsādamaṇḍana 15th c. Mewar; temples (Māru-Gurjara) Śilparatna 16th c. Kerala; architecture, sculpture, painting

Scholarly Note: Texts and Buildings

Art historians have long debated how far the surviving texts actually guided builders. Many of the great temples were built before the texts that are now most often cited, and some texts describe forms that do not survive, or survive only in regions far from where the text was written. Adam Hardy and Michael Meister have shown that the most useful approach is to read the texts alongside the buildings: the texts preserve a technical vocabulary and some of the design procedures of the builders, but the buildings themselves are the primary evidence for the history of architecture (Hardy 2007; Meister et al. 1983).

docs.title: 1.4 Ideas Behind the Buildings
docs.text: Several ideas run through the texts and help to explain the forms of Indian religious architecture. They are ideas held by the authors of the texts and by the communities who built and used the buildings; they are not claims about physics.

docs.title: 1.4.1 The Grid and the Square
docs.text: The texts prescribe that every building, from a house to a town, be laid out on a square grid, the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala, whose squares are assigned to deities, with Brahmā at the centre. The myth of the vāstupuruṣa, the being pinned to the ground by the gods, explains why the site must be propitiated before building (Chapter 2). Stella Kramrisch made this diagram the key to her influential interpretation of the Hindu temple (Kramrisch 1946).

docs.title: 1.4.2 The Temple as Mountain, House and Body
docs.text: The temple is described in the texts as the house (prāsāda, devagṛha) of a god who is present in the image. Its superstructure is often compared to a mountain, especially Meru, and its parts carry the names of the parts of a body: in the northern texts the lowest moulding of the base is the “hoof” (khura), the wall the “shank” (jaṅghā), the top of the tower the “shoulder” (skandha), above which come the “neck” (grīvā) and the “head” (śiras); in the southern texts the wall and pillar zone is the “foot” (pāda). These comparisons are found in the texts themselves; more elaborate correspondences between temple and human body found in modern books are often the authors’ own.

docs.title: 1.4.3 The Image as a Dwelling of the Deity
docs.text: Images made for worship are consecrated in a ritual of installation (pratiṣṭhā), which in many traditions includes the “establishment of breath” (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and the opening of the eyes. The proportions, gestures and attributes prescribed by the texts were intended to make an image fit to receive the deity. This explains the importance of iconographic rules (Chapters 11 and 12); it does not mean that every image actually followed them (Davis 1997).

docs.title: 1.4.4 Buddhist and Jain Architecture
docs.text: The ideas just described are those of the Brahmanical texts. Buddhist and Jain communities built on different premises. The Buddhist stūpa is a monument over relics; the monastery (vihāra) and the hall of worship (caitya) answer to the needs of a monastic community; and Jain temples are designed for the worship of the tīrthaṅkaras, often in multiple shrines and in sacred “temple cities” on hills such as Śatruñjaya and Girnār. Many builders worked for patrons of all religions, and Buddhist, Jain and Hindu buildings share techniques and ornament, but they should not be read as variants of a single “Hindu” scheme.

docs.title: 1.5 Architecture, Sculpture and the Other Arts
docs.text: The Indian arts were closely connected, a point made in a well-known passage of the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa on the dependence of image-making on painting, dance and music (Chapter 14, Section 14.3). Temples were built for music and dance as well as worship, with halls and pavilions for performance, and their sculpture draws on the stances and gestures of dance (Chapter 13). Poets described palaces, temples and cities in elaborate verse, and inscriptions on buildings are often fine Sanskrit or Tamil poems; Persian poetry was inscribed on Mughal monuments. Painting, textiles, metalwork and woodwork shared motifs with architecture. A building in India was rarely the work of a single art: the Tāj Mahal combines architecture, gardens, calligraphy, inlay and carving; a South Indian temple combines architecture, sculpture, painting, bronze-casting, music, dance and ritual.

docs.title: 1.6.1 Architects, Masons and Sculptors
docs.text: The texts use several terms for the master builder: sthapati (master architect), sūtradhāra or sūtragrāhin (“holder of the cord”, the surveyor who lays out the plan), takṣaka (carver) and vardhaki (carpenter or builder). The Mayamata and Mānasāra describe the qualities of each and how they should work together. Inscriptions sometimes name the architects and sculptors of particular buildings; the Bṛhadīśvara temple at Thanjavur, for example, records the name of its chief architect (Chapter 5), and Jain temples in western India record the names of their sūtradhāras (Chapter 4, Section 4.14).

docs.title: 1.6.2 Craft Communities and Caste
docs.text: In most periods architecture and image-making were hereditary occupations of particular communities. In South India the artisan groups known in Tamil as Kammāḷar (in Karnataka and Andhra as Viśvakarma or Pāñcāla) include smiths, carpenters, stone-carvers and bronze-casters and claim descent from Viśvakarman, the divine craftsman of the Ṛgveda; in western India the Sompurā Brahmins are the hereditary temple architects, and the Sūtār and Salāṭ communities are carpenters and stone-workers. These identities gave the crafts continuity, but they also expressed the hierarchy of caste. The dharmaśāstra literature ranks most craft work low, and the vāstu texts themselves allot sites, house sizes and even soil colours according to varṇa: the Bṛhatsaṃhitā and the Mayamata, for example, prescribe different house dimensions for brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras, assign soils of different colours to them (Chapter 2), and, like the Arthaśāstra, place those regarded as impure at the edges of a settlement (Chapter 8). How these prescriptions corresponded to the real layout of villages is discussed in Chapter 10 (Section 10.3). Artisan communities in turn contested their status; from the medieval period Viśvakarma groups in the south claimed brāhmaṇa rank. An honest account of the tradition must keep both facts in view: the extraordinary skill transmitted within these communities, and the social order that restricted who could do what, and where people could live.

docs.title: 1.6.3 Transmission
docs.text: Skills were passed on largely within families and workshops, through apprenticeship rather than through the study of texts. Texts were known to some master builders, and some families preserved manuscripts, but much of the working knowledge of proportion and construction was carried in drawings, templates, measuring rods and memory. The modern continuity of the tradition is real: the Sompurā families still build temples in the Māru-Gurjara manner, and in Tamil Nadu V. Ganapati Sthapati (1927–2011), who headed the Government College of Architecture and Sculpture at Mamallapuram, trained a generation of sculptors and architects in the Drāviḍa tradition (Ganapati Sthapati 2002). But modern practice has also been reshaped by printed editions, government schools of architecture and sculpture, and the expectations of modern patrons.

docs.text:
Table 1.3 gives an outline of the periods discussed in this volume; a fuller chronology is given at the end of the book.

Colonial and Indo-Saracenic buildings; New Delhi; modern Indian architecture; continuing temple building

docs.title: 1.7.1 The Harappan Cities
docs.text: The cities of the Harappan or Indus civilisation, at their height c. 2600–1900 BCE, are the earliest planned towns in South Asia, with streets on roughly cardinal alignments, houses of standardised baked brick, covered drains and, at Dholāvīrā, an elaborate system of reservoirs (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002). Their plans, and the open question of how much of their practice passed into later Indian building, are discussed in Chapter 8. The Harappan script is undeciphered, so the planners’ own ideas are unknown.

docs.title: 1.7.2 Vedic Altars and the Śulbasūtras
docs.text: No Vedic buildings survive; houses and halls were built of timber, bamboo and thatch. The Śulbasūtras (“rules of the cord”), appendices to the ritual manuals of the Vedic schools (Baudhāyana, Āpastamba, Kātyāyana, Mānava; c. 8th–2nd centuries BCE, the earliest perhaps c. 800–500 BCE), give geometrical instructions for laying out brick fire altars of prescribed shapes and areas, including the great bird-shaped altar of the agnicayana, built of five layers of bricks (Sen and Bag 1983; Staal 1983). They contain the earliest Indian statement of the relation between the sides and the diagonal of a rectangle (the theorem now named after Pythagoras), constructions for squares of a given area, the conversion of a square into a circle of approximately equal area, and a good approximation to \(\sqrt{2}\) (Plofker 2009). The Śulbasūtras are texts on ritual geometry, not on architecture (their mathematics is treated in Volume 11, Gaṇita); but they show that the cord-and-peg methods later used to lay out buildings had a long history.

docs.title: 1.7.3 Mauryan Stone and the Buddhist Monuments
docs.text: Monumental stone architecture and sculpture appear in the Maurya period. The polished sandstone pillars of Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE), with bell-shaped capitals and animal crowns, and the caves of the Barābar and Nāgārjunī hills near Gayā, cut for the Ājīvika ascetics under Aśoka and his grandson Daśaratha, are the earliest surviving examples. Over the following centuries Buddhist and Jain communities, with merchants, guilds, monks and nuns as donors, built stūpas, monasteries and rock-cut halls whose inscriptions record thousands of individual gifts. The stūpas of Bhārhut and Sāñcī and the caitya halls of the Western Ghats are discussed in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 1.7.4 Temples
docs.text: The earliest surviving free-standing stone temples date from the Gupta period, in the 5th and early 6th centuries CE: small flat-roofed shrines such as temple 17 at Sāñcī, and the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogaṛh, which had a tower. From the 7th century the northern (Nāgara) and southern (Drāviḍa) temple forms were fully established, and the next six centuries saw the great regional traditions surveyed in Chapters 4 and 5.

docs.title: 1.7.5 Indo-Islamic Architecture
docs.text: From the 1190s the Delhi Sultanate, and later the regional sultanates and the Mughal empire, introduced the mosque, the tomb, the madrasa and the walled garden, together with the true arch, the dome and new uses of lime mortar, glazed tile and inlay. These buildings were made by Indian masons and craftsmen working alongside architects from Iran and Central Asia, and they combined imported forms with local techniques and ornament. They are an integral part of the history of Indian architecture, and are discussed in Chapter 6; stepwells and gardens of the period appear in Chapter 9, and Mughal and Rajput cities in Chapter 8.

docs.title: 1.7.6 Colonial and Modern Architecture
docs.text: Under British rule, European classical and Gothic buildings were joined in the late 19th century by the “Indo-Saracenic” style, which combined Mughal and Rajput forms with modern construction, and in the 20th century by the new imperial capital of New Delhi (Metcalf 1989). After independence, Le Corbusier at Chandigarh and Indian architects such as B. V. Doshi, Charles Correa and Laurie Baker sought ways of building that responded to Indian climate, materials and ways of life. Both periods are described in Chapter 7. Temple building in the traditional manner, meanwhile, has continued and expanded, in India and in the diaspora (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 1.8 Buildings as Historical Evidence
docs.text: Buildings are documents. Their inscriptions record dates, rulers, donors, architects, endowments and disputes; their sculpture and painting show dress, ornament, musical instruments, weapons, ships, houses and the activities of daily life; their construction reveals technology, the organisation of labour and the movement of materials; and their alteration over time, by repair, enlargement, conversion and destruction, records the history of the communities that used them. Temple inscriptions are among the principal sources for the economic and social history of medieval South India, and the donative inscriptions of the early Buddhist sites are a principal source for the social history of the period. Conversely, buildings have also been used as evidence for claims about the past that the evidence does not support, as in some of the myths discussed in this volume. Reading buildings well requires both an understanding of how they were made and attention to the documents they carry.

docs.title: 1.9 Patronage
docs.text:
Monumental building required sustained funding. Inscriptions show several kinds of patron:

  • Kings and queens, for whom temple building was an act of merit and a statement of power: the Chola king Rājarāja I at Thanjavur, the Cālukya queen Lokamahādevī at Paṭṭadakal, the Gaṅga king Narasiṃha I at Konārak.

  • Ministers and merchants, especially in western India: the Jain ministers Vimala, and Vastupāla and Tejapāla, who built the Dilwārā temples at Mount Abu, and the merchant Dharaṇa Śāh at Raṇakpur.

  • Monks, nuns, lay donors and guilds, who paid for individual pillars, railings and caves at Buddhist sites; the inscriptions at Sāñcī and Kārlā record many such gifts.

  • Local communities and temple institutions, which maintained tanks, irrigation works and rest-houses, often from endowments of land recorded in inscriptions.

Under the Sultanates and the Mughals, mosques, tombs, caravanserais, stepwells and gardens were built by rulers, nobles and, notably, by royal women, such as Bega Begum (Ḥājī Begum), traditionally credited with Humāyūn’s tomb, Nūr Jahān, who built her father’s tomb at Agra, and Jahānārā; and charitable endowments (waqf) supported their upkeep.

docs.title: 1.10 Indian Architecture beyond India
docs.text: Buddhist and Hindu architecture and sculpture travelled with religious and commercial networks. In Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam (Champa) and Indonesia, local builders developed temples and stūpas that drew on Indian models while remaining distinctively their own: Borobudur in Java (late 8th–early 9th century), a stepped Buddhist monument with some 2,670 relief panels and over 500 Buddha images; Prambanan in Java (9th century); and Angkor Wat in Cambodia (early 12th century), the largest of the Khmer temples. Nepal and Tibet developed their own traditions of temple and monastery building in close contact with India. These buildings are best understood as independent regional traditions in dialogue with India, not as Indian buildings abroad.

docs.title: 1.11 The Modern Study of Indian Architecture
docs.text:
The systematic study of Indian architecture by modern methods began in the early 19th century. Ram Raz, a South Indian official, published Essay on the Architecture of the Hindus (1834), the first attempt to explain the southern building texts with measured drawings, made with the help of traditional builders (Ram Raz 1834). The Scottish merchant James Fergusson travelled widely in India in the 1830s and 1840s and wrote the first general history, History of Indian and Eastern Architecture (1876) (Fergusson 1876). His classification of buildings by religion and race (“Buddhist”, “Jaina”, “Dravidian”, “Indo-Aryan”) and his view that Indian architecture had declined after an early high point were influential and long contested.

The Archaeological Survey of India was founded in 1861 under Alexander Cunningham, who surveyed hundreds of sites in northern India and identified many places mentioned by the Chinese pilgrims. James Burgess documented the caves and temples of western and southern India. Under John Marshall (Director-General 1902–1928) the Survey excavated Taxila, Sāñcī, Mohenjo-daro and Harappā, and began a programme of conservation under the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act of 1904.

European writers of the 19th century often judged Indian sculpture and architecture harshly, measuring them against Greek and Renaissance models; Partha Mitter has traced how these prejudices formed (Mitter 1977). In the early 20th century E. B. Havell and Ananda Coomaraswamy reacted against them, insisting on the religious and aesthetic values of Indian art (Havell 1913); Coomaraswamy’s History of Indian and Indonesian Art (1927) remains a classic (Coomaraswamy 1927). Stella Kramrisch’s The Hindu Temple (1946) read the temple through the texts as a symbolic form (Kramrisch 1946), and Percy Brown’s two volumes on Buddhist and Hindu and on Islamic architecture became standard surveys (Brown 1942a, 1942b).

Since the 1960s, scholars such as M. A. Dhaky, Krishna Deva, Michael Meister, George Michell, Adam Hardy and Bruno Dagens have combined close study of buildings with the reading of texts and inscriptions, producing the regional volumes of the Encyclopaedia of Indian Temple Architecture and detailed studies of particular traditions (Meister et al. 1983; Hardy 2007; Michell 1977). Historians of Indo-Islamic architecture, among them Catherine Asher, Ebba Koch and Finbarr Barry Flood, have transformed the understanding of Sultanate and Mughal building (Asher 1992; Koch 1991; Flood 2009). Archaeologists working on the Harappan and early historic cities have provided a firmer chronology for the early periods. This volume relies on their work throughout.

docs.title: 1.12 Heritage and Conservation
docs.text:
India’s architectural heritage is protected by law at national and state levels. The Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act of 1958 empowers the Archaeological Survey of India to protect several thousand monuments of national importance, and state departments protect many more. India has more than forty sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List, including Ajaṇṭā, Ellora, Elephanta, Khajuraho, Konārak, Māmallapuram, Paṭṭadakal, Hampi, the Great Living Chola Temples, the Qutb complex, Humāyūn’s tomb, Fatehpur Sīkrī, the Agra Fort, the Tāj Mahal, the Rāṇī kī Vāv, Dholāvīrā and the Rāmappa temple (Table 1.4).

Table 1.4. Some UNESCO World Heritage cultural sites in India discussed in this volume, with the year of inscription Site Year Site Year Ajaṇṭā caves 1983 Sāñcī Buddhist monuments 1989 Ellora caves 1983 Humāyūn’s tomb, Delhi 1993 Agra Fort 1983 Qutb Mīnār and its monuments 1993 Tāj Mahal 1983 Mahābodhi temple, Bodh Gayā 2002 Sun temple, Konārak 1984 Champaner-Pavagadh 2004 Monuments at Māmallapuram 1984 Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus 2004 Churches and convents of Goa 1986 Red Fort complex, Delhi 2007 Fatehpur Sīkrī 1986 Jantar Mantar, Jaipur 2010 Hampi 1986 Hill forts of Rajasthan 2013 Khajuraho 1986 Rāṇī kī Vāv, Pāṭaṇ 2014 Elephanta caves 1987 Nālandā 2016 Great Living Chola Temples 1987, 2004 Historic city of Ahmadābād 2017 Paṭṭadakal 1987 Jaipur city 2019 Dholāvīrā 2021 Rāmappa temple 2021 Hoysaḷa temples 2023 Santiniketan 2023

Conservation in India faces particular problems. Many great temples are “living” monuments, in continuous worship, whose communities expect them to be renovated, painted, extended and reconsecrated; the traditional practice of renewal (jīrṇoddhāra) can conflict with the conservationist’s aim of preserving historic fabric, as debates over the sandblasting, replastering and rebuilding of old temples show. Many monuments are threatened by urban growth, pollution, encroachment and neglect, and unprotected vernacular buildings are disappearing rapidly. Since 1984 the Indian National Trust for Art and Cultural Heritage (INTACH), a non-governmental body, has listed unprotected historic buildings in many towns, pressed for heritage regulations in cities and promoted the repair of old buildings with traditional materials such as lime; and the demolition of notable modern buildings has extended the debate to the architecture of the 20th century (Chapter 7).

Theft has removed many images from their temples. Bronzes and stone sculptures stolen from Indian temples have been sold through the international art market; in recent years several have been identified in museum collections abroad and returned, among them a Chola bronze Naṭarāja returned from the National Gallery of Australia in 2014. Photographic archives, such as that of the French Institute of Pondicherry, have been important in identifying stolen images.

Monuments have also been at the centre of political and religious conflict. Medieval rulers of every religion destroyed or appropriated the shrines of their enemies, and the memory of such acts has been mobilised in modern politics. The most consequential modern case was the demolition in 1992 of the Babri Masjid at Ayodhya, a 16th-century mosque claimed to stand on the birthplace of Rāma, which led to widespread violence; after decades of litigation, the Supreme Court of India in 2019 awarded the site for the building of a temple and directed that land be given elsewhere for a mosque. Historians and archaeologists have an important responsibility in such disputes: to state clearly what the evidence shows and does not show, and to resist the use of the past as a weapon in present conflicts.

docs.title: 1.13 Measurement
docs.text: The texts measure buildings and images in units based on the human body. The basic unit is the aṅgula (“finger”), defined as eight yava (barley grains); 12 aṅgulas make a vitasti (span), 24 a hasta or kiṣku (forearm, cubit) and four hastas a daṇḍa (rod). The texts also allow cubits of 25, 26 and 27 aṅgulas for different kinds of work, and the absolute value of the aṅgula varied between periods and regions. For images, a unit relative to the image itself is used (Chapter 11). The equivalences of these units in centimetres given in modern books are approximations.

docs.title: 1.14 Plan of this Volume
docs.text: The first part of the book deals with architecture, beginning with the texts and then following the buildings roughly in historical order. Chapter 2 explains the principles set out in the vāstu texts and examines the modern claims made for them. Chapter 3 covers the oldest surviving religious monuments, the stūpas, monasteries and rock-cut halls of the Buddhists, Jains, Ājīvikas and Hindus. Chapter 4 describes the main temple forms, and Chapter 5 studies a selection of great temples, Hindu and Jain, region by region. Chapter 6 is devoted to the mosques, tombs and shrines of the Sultanates and the Mughals, and Chapter 7 to palaces and to the architecture of the colonial and modern periods. Three thematic chapters follow: towns and cities from the Harappan period to Jaipur and the modern capitals (Chapter 8), tanks, stepwells, dams and gardens (Chapter 9), and houses and vernacular architecture (Chapter 10). The second part deals with images and painting: the principles of image-making (Chapter 11), iconography (Chapter 12), the regional schools of sculpture (Chapter 13) and painting (Chapter 14). Maps of the principal sites are given in Figures 1.2, 6.1 and 13.1.

docs.title: A Note on Transliteration
docs.text: Sanskrit, Pali and Prakrit terms and the titles of texts are given in IAST. Tamil and Malayalam words follow the conventions of the Tamil Lexicon used in most scholarly writing: ē and ō mark the long vowels, which these languages distinguish from short e and o; ḻ is the retroflex approximant (as in kiḻakkini), ḷ the retroflex lateral, ṟ the alveolar r and ṉ the alveolar n (as in Peruntaccaṉ). Hindi, Gujarati, Bengali and Odia words are given in IAST, usually without the final -a that is not pronounced (havelī, bāolī, deuḷ). Persian and Arabic words follow a simplified form of the usual scholarly system: a macron marks a long vowel, ʿ the consonant ʿayn and ʾ the glottal stop, a dot below distinguishes consonants that English does not (ḥ, ṣ, ẓ, ṭ), q is the uvular stop, and the Persian connecting vowel is written -i (Dīwān-i Khāṣṣ). Well-known place names (Delhi, Agra, Thanjavur), dynastic names in common English use (Chola, Mughal) and the names of modern persons are given in their usual English spelling; the names of temples, minor sites and pre-modern persons carry diacritics where these help pronunciation. A glossary of the principal terms is at the end of the volume.

docs.title: Chapter 2: Vāstuśāstra: The Principles of the Texts
2.1 What the Texts Mean by Vāstu
docs.text:
The word vāstu (from the root vas, “to dwell”) means a site or a dwelling. In the technical literature it has a wide meaning. The Mayamata and the Mānasāra distinguish four kinds of vāstu: the ground (bhūmi), which is the principal one, and the things built or placed on it: buildings (harmya), vehicles (yāna) and seats or beds (śayana) (Dagens 1994; Acharya 1934). Vāstuśāstra or vāstuvidyā is therefore the knowledge of how to choose, prepare and lay out a site and how to build on it, from a village or town to a temple, a house, a gateway or a piece of furniture.

The oldest systematic account is chapter 53 of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (6th century CE), which deals with house sites (Bhat 1981); chapter numbers in this volume follow Bhat’s edition, and some editions number these chapters one lower. The Mayamata, the Mānasāra, Bhoja’s Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra and the architectural chapters of the āgamas and Purāṇas develop the same themes at much greater length. The texts share a common core, but they differ in detail, in technical terms and in the forms of building they describe, and they were written over a period of a thousand years in different regions (Chapter 1). What follows describes that common core and notes the main variations.

docs.title: 2.1.1 The Contents of a Vāstu Chapter: the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, Chapter 53
docs.text: Varāhamihira’s chapter on vāstuvidyā gives a good idea of what a vāstu text contains (Bhat 1981). After a brief statement that the knowledge has come down from Brahmā through a succession of sages, it gives the dimensions of houses for kings, princes, ministers, officials and the four varṇas, and the proportions of their halls; it then tells the myth of the vāstupuruṣa, describes the 81- and 64-square grids and the deities who occupy them, and warns against injuring the vulnerable points of the grid. It discusses the effects of doors in different positions and of obstructions in front of them; the trees that may or may not grow near a house, milky and thorny trees being generally inauspicious; the shape and slope of sites, and the signs and tests of good soil; the auspicious times for beginning construction; and omens observed during the work. The chapter combines in a single sequence social rules, practical advice, astrology and omen-lore, and it was this combination that later texts expanded.

docs.title: 2.1.2 The Larger Treatises
docs.text:
The Mayamata, in thirty-six chapters, and the Mānasāra, in seventy, follow a similar plan, moving from the general to the particular (Dagens 1994; Acharya 1934). They begin with the qualifications of the architect and the system of measurement; proceed to the examination of the site, the determination of the directions, the laying out of the grid and the offerings to its deities; then describe settlements of different kinds, from villages to royal capitals; then houses, temples of one to twelve storeys and their parts (bases, pillars, entablatures, superstructures), gateways, halls and enclosures; and finally furniture, vehicles, liṅgas and images. Large parts of both texts consist of lists of named variants, each defined by its proportions or its ornaments. They are working references rather than continuous expositions, and they presuppose a reader who already knew the craft.

How to Read the Vāstu Texts

The vāstu texts mix several kinds of instruction: practical surveying and construction; rules of proportion; ritual; and astrological and omen-based predictions of good or bad fortune. They do not distinguish between these, and modern readers should not assume that a rule which makes practical sense (raise a house above flood level) and one which is astrological (the remainder of a calculation determines the owner’s luck) rest on the same kind of evidence. In this book the prescriptions are reported as what the texts say.

docs.title: 2.2.1 The Myth
docs.text:
The Bṛhatsaṃhitā (53.2–3) tells briefly that a certain being once arose whose body blocked heaven and earth. The gods seized it and threw it face downwards onto the ground, and each god remained in the place where he had held it down; the Creator then made this being, filled with the gods, the “man of the site” (vāstunara, vāstupuruṣa). Other texts give longer versions. In the Matsya Purāṇa (ch. 252), for example, the being is born from a drop of Śiva’s sweat during his battle with the demon Andhaka, devours everything until the gods pin it down, and is granted by the gods the right to be worshipped, and fed with offerings, whenever a building is begun.

The myth explains two features of practice. First, a site is never neutral: it is occupied, and must be propitiated by an offering (vāstubali) and rites of pacification (vāstuśānti) before work begins and when a building is first occupied. Second, the gods who hold the being down each have a place on the site, so that the site can be drawn as a diagram of the being’s body and the gods who occupy it: the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala.

docs.title: 2.2.2 The Grid
docs.text:
The maṇḍala is a square divided into a grid of smaller squares (pada). The Mayamata and the Mānasāra name thirty-two grids, beginning with a single square and increasing by one row and one column at a time; the first ten are shown in Table 2.1 (Dagens 1994; Acharya 1946). Most of the theory concerns two grids, the 64-square maṇḍūka (also called caṇḍita) and the 81-square paramaśāyika. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā describes both, and several texts prefer the 64-square grid for temples and the 81-square grid for houses and settlements, although usage is not uniform.

Table 2.1. The first ten grids of the vāstumaṇḍala (after the Mayamata and Mānasāra) Name Grid Number of squares sakala 1 \(\times\) 1 1 pecaka 2 \(\times\) 2 4 pīṭha 3 \(\times\) 3 9 mahāpīṭha 4 \(\times\) 4 16 upapīṭha 5 \(\times\) 5 25 ugrapīṭha 6 \(\times\) 6 36 sthaṇḍila 7 \(\times\) 7 49 maṇḍūka (caṇḍita) 8 \(\times\) 8 64 paramaśāyika 9 \(\times\) 9 81 āsana 10 \(\times\) 10 100

docs.title: 2.2.3 The Forty-Five Deities
docs.text:
In both the 64- and 81-square grids the texts place forty-five deities. Brahmā occupies the centre: nine squares in the 81-square grid and four in the 64-square grid. Around him are four principal deities: Aryaman to the east, Vivasvat to the south, Mitra to the west and Pṛthvīdhara to the north. In the corners of this inner zone are eight lesser deities in pairs (in the commonest list, Āpa and Āpavatsa in the north-east, Savitṛ and Sāvitra in the south-east, Indra and Jaya in the south-west, Rudra and Rājayakṣman in the north-west). The outer ring of thirty-two squares is occupied by thirty-two deities, eight to each side, beginning with Īśa (Śikhin) in the north-east corner and proceeding clockwise through the east, where Mahendra (in some lists called Indra) occupies the fourth square, and then the south, west and north (Figure 2.1) (Bhat 1981; Kramrisch 1946). The names, and sometimes the positions, differ slightly from text to text.

Figure 2.1. The 81-square paramaśāyika grid with its forty-five deities, drawn with east at the top as in many Indian diagrams (after the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, ch. 53). Brahmā occupies the central nine squares; the four principal deities six squares each; the eight lesser deities of the inner corners two squares each; and the thirty-two deities of the outer ring one square each. The fourth deity of the outer eastern row is named Mahendra in the Mayamata and many other lists, and Indra in some; it is distinct from the Indra of the inner south-western pair (Indra and Jaya). Names and positions vary slightly between texts.

The vāstupuruṣa himself is imagined lying across the grid with his head in the north-east and his feet in the south-west; the deities are said to rest on parts of his body. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā accordingly warns that an injury to the owner will follow if the corresponding part of the vāstupuruṣa is “struck” by a post, a wall or a nail.

docs.title: 2.2.4 Zones of the Grid
docs.text:
The Mayamata and Mānasāra also divide the grid into concentric zones, which they use when placing buildings in a village, a temple enclosure or a large house: the central squares of Brahmā (brahmapada); around them the zone of the gods (daivika); then the zone of men (mānuṣa); and at the edge the zone of the piśācas, or goblins (paiśāca). The principal shrine or the central courtyard is placed in or near the centre; dwellings in the middle zones; and service buildings, and the shrines of lesser and protective deities, towards the edge (Dagens 1994). See Figure 2.2.

Figure 2.2. Schematic view of the concentric zones of the 81-square grid as described in the Mayamata and Mānasāra. The exact widths of the zones vary with the size of the grid.

docs.title: 2.3.1 The Guardians of the Directions
docs.text:
The eight directions are each ruled by a guardian (dikpāla). The list is standard across the Brahmanical texts, although the north is assigned to Kubera in some and to Soma in others (Table 2.2).

Table 2.2. The guardians of the eight directions (aṣṭadikpāla) Direction Sanskrit name Guardian East pūrva, prācī Indra South-east āgneya Agni South dakṣiṇa Yama South-west nairṛta Nirṛti West paścima Varuṇa North-west vāyavya Vāyu North uttara Kubera (or Soma) North-east aiśānya Īśāna

docs.title: 2.3.2 What the Texts Prescribe
docs.text:
The texts attach good and bad consequences to directions. East is generally the most favoured direction for the entrance of a temple, since the deity faces the rising sun, and for many houses; north is also favoured. The south, ruled by Yama, the god of death, is generally avoided for main entrances, although temples of some deities, and houses in particular situations, may face south or west. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā goes further: it assigns a specific result to a door placed in each of the thirty-two squares of the outer ring, so that a door in some squares brings wealth or favour, and in others fire, quarrels or loss (Bhat 1981). Rooms and activities are assigned to directions in house plans, though the assignments differ between texts and regions (Chapter 10).

These are rules of auspiciousness. Some of them coincide with good practice in a hot climate (an east-facing entrance catches morning light; a house closed to the south-west is shaded from the hot afternoon sun), and modern writers often explain them in these terms. But the texts themselves give no climatic reasons, and the same rules were applied, with little change, from the Himalaya to the far south.

docs.title: 2.3.3 The Five Elements in Modern Vāstu
docs.text: Many modern books on vāstu associate the five elements (pañcamahābhūta) with particular directions: water with the north-east, fire with the south-east, earth with the south-west, air with the north-west and space with the centre. This scheme is a modern systematisation. The classical texts know the five elements, and the association of the south-east with Agni and the north-west with Vāyu follows from the guardians of those directions; but the full directional scheme of the elements, and the advice derived from it, is not found in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the Mayamata or the Mānasāra.

docs.title: 2.4 Orientation: Finding the Directions
docs.text:
Before a building is laid out its axes must be fixed. The texts describe the gnomon (śaṅku) method, which goes back to the Śulbasūtras: a vertical peg is set up on levelled ground and a circle drawn around it. The points where the tip of the shadow touches the circle in the morning and in the afternoon are marked; the line joining them runs east–west, and a line perpendicular to it, constructed with cords, runs north–south (Sen and Bag 1983; Dagens 1994). The method gives the cardinal directions to within a small error, which arises because the sun’s declination changes slightly between morning and afternoon; some texts add refinements. The gnomon was also the basic instrument of Indian astronomy (see Volume 12, Khagola Jyotiṣa). See Figure 2.3.

Figure 2.3. The gnomon method of finding the cardinal directions (plan view, for a site north of the Tropic of Cancer, where the noon shadow points north). The two points where the tip of the shadow meets the circle in the morning and in the afternoon give the east–west line; the perpendicular through the gnomon gives north–south.

Many Indian temples are aligned within a degree or two of the cardinal directions; others deviate considerably, sometimes because they follow a river, a street or an older building, and sometimes, it has been argued, because they were aligned on a particular sunrise. Archaeoastronomical studies have proposed intentional solar alignments at a number of sites (Malville and Gujral 2000). Popular claims that a given temple is lit by the sun on a particular day should, however, be checked against measurement: some are correct, while others are traditions that have not been confirmed.

docs.title: 2.5 Choosing and Testing the Site
docs.text:
The texts give detailed rules for the selection of a site (bhūparīkṣā). A good site is square or rectangular, level or sloping gently towards the north or east, with good soil and a supply of water, and free of bones, ant-hills, thorny trees and other inauspicious things. The soil is examined for colour, smell, taste and texture, and the texts assign soils of different colours to the four varṇas: white soil to brāhmaṇas, red to kṣatriyas, yellow to vaiśyas and black to śūdras. This allocation is found in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā and the Mayamata; the place of caste in the texts is discussed in Chapter 1 (Section 1.6) and in Chapter 10 (Section 10.3).

Several practical tests are described, with some variation between texts (Bhat 1981; Dagens 1994):

  1. The pit test. A pit is dug, for example a cubit deep, and refilled with the earth taken from it. If earth is left over, the site is excellent; if it just fills the pit, middling; if the pit is not filled, the site is bad.

  2. The water test. The pit is filled with water and observed after a fixed interval; if the water has not drained away, the site is good.

  3. Ploughing and sowing. The site is ploughed and seeds are sown; the speed with which they sprout is taken as a sign of the quality of the ground.

Modern commentators often point out that these tests give rough information about the density, drainage and fertility of the soil, which is true; but in the texts they are omens as much as engineering tests, and their outcome is expressed in terms of good or bad fortune for the owner.

docs.title: 2.6.1 Kinds of Measurement
docs.text: The Mānasāra and Mayamata distinguish six kinds of measurement: māna, pramāṇa, unmāna, parimāṇa, upamāna and lambamāna. Acharya and Dagens explain them as, approximately, height, breadth, thickness, girth, the measurement of intervals (for example between pillars) and measurement along plumb lines; the precise meaning of each term varies between texts and contexts (Acharya 1946; Dagens 1994). Buildings are dimensioned in whole numbers of hastas and aṅgulas (Chapter 1), and their parts are proportioned to a module, often the width of the sanctum or of a pillar.

docs.title: 2.6.2 Proportions of Height to Breadth
docs.text: The southern texts give five classes of proportion of height to breadth for buildings and their parts, rising by quarters from equal height and breadth to a height twice the breadth, each class bearing an auspicious name. Similar graded series of proportions are used for pillars, doorways and storeys. These are rules of thumb that ensured consistency within a workshop tradition; they do not form a single system based on “harmonic” or musical ratios, and the frequently repeated claim that Indian temples were designed on the golden ratio has no basis in the texts or in measured surveys.

docs.title: 2.6.3 The Āyādi Calculations
docs.text:
A distinctive feature of the southern texts is a set of calculations, usually called āyādi (“gain and the rest”) or ṣaḍvarga (“the six classes”), which test the chosen dimensions for auspiciousness. A dimension, usually the length, breadth or perimeter in hastas and aṅgulas, is multiplied by a fixed number and divided by another; the remainder gives a value for “gain” (āya), “loss” (vyaya), “origin” (yoni), lunar mansion (nakṣatra), weekday (vāra) and portion (aṃśa). The eight yonis are named after the flag (dhvaja), smoke (dhūma), lion (siṃha), dog (śvan), bull (vṛṣa), ass (khara), elephant (gaja) and crow (kāka), and the odd-numbered ones are auspicious. Gain should exceed loss. If the result is unfavourable the dimension is altered by a few aṅgulas and recalculated (Dagens 1994). The multipliers and divisors differ from text to text, and the calculations are still used by traditional builders in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.

These calculations belong to astrology rather than to geometry or engineering. They are of historical interest as evidence of the close relation between the builders’ craft and jyotiṣa, but they have no bearing on the strength, comfort or performance of a building.

docs.title: 2.7.1 Lines and Marmans
docs.text: The lines of the grid, and the diagonals drawn across it, are described in the texts as “veins” (sirā) or “beams” (vaṃśa) of the vāstupuruṣa, and the points where the principal lines cross as his vulnerable points (marman), a term also used in medicine and in the martial arts for vulnerable points of the body. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā and the Mayamata forbid placing a pillar, a door or a wall on these points, and predict misfortune for the owner if this is done (Bhat 1981; Dagens 1994). In practice the rule, combined with the grid, helped fix the positions of pillars and doors in a consistent way; but the texts present it as a matter of injuring or not injuring the being who lies beneath the building.

docs.title: 2.7.2 Obstructions and Defects
docs.text: The texts list many defects (doṣa) of a site or building. One of the most often mentioned is vedha, “piercing”: a tree, a post, a corner of another building, a well, a drain or a road directly in front of a door is said to “pierce” it and bring misfortune; the Bṛhatsaṃhitā exempts obstructions that stand at a sufficient distance from the door. Other defects include irregular plots, plots that slope the wrong way, and buildings that rise higher on one side than the other. The remedies the texts prescribe are mostly ritual: rites of pacification, offerings and the installation of protective images. Modern “vāstu remedies” (mirrors, pyramids, coloured lights, crystals) are recent inventions.

docs.title: 2.8 Trees, Gardens and the House
docs.text: The vāstu texts pay attention to the trees and plants around a house. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā lists trees that are auspicious near a dwelling and others, such as thorny trees and trees with milky sap, that should be avoided, and devotes a separate chapter (ch. 55, on vṛkṣāyurveda, “the science of the life of trees”) to the planting of gardens: choosing soil, propagating trees by seeds and cuttings, watering, and treating tree diseases (Bhat 1981). Water near the house, in tanks, wells and garden pools, is recommended, and the planting of trees along roads and near tanks is praised as a meritorious act in many inscriptions. In the house itself, the sacred basil (tulasī) planted in a raised stand in the courtyard is a common feature of Hindu homes. These prescriptions reflect a real attention to the setting of buildings, though again expressed largely in terms of auspiciousness.

docs.title: 2.9 Vāstu, Astrology and Ritual
docs.text: Every stage of building, in the texts, has its ritual and its auspicious moment (muhūrta), determined by astrology: the testing and ploughing of the site, the offering to the vāstupuruṣa, the laying of the first stones or bricks (śilānyāsa, iṣṭakānyāsa), the deposit of a sealed casket of precious materials in the foundations (garbhanyāsa), the raising of the door-frame and the main pillar, the placing of the crowning element, and the first entry of the owner (gṛhapraveśa) or the consecration of the temple. The Mayamata devotes separate chapters to several of these rites. They show that the vāstu texts are part of the larger world of ritual and astral science, and that their authors saw building as a sacred undertaking from beginning to end.

docs.title: 2.10 The Grid in Practice
docs.text: How far were real buildings laid out on the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala? Michael Meister and others have analysed the plans of northern temples and shown that many of them can be explained by grids of squares, with the sanctum, walls and projections set out on the lines of a grid of 64 or 81 squares, or on related subdivisions, and with diagonals and rotated squares used to fix the positions of projections. Adam Hardy has shown how the plans and elevations of temples were generated by combining and repeating a small set of elements according to rules of proportion (Hardy 2007). These studies suggest that the grid was a real working tool of the builders, used to proportion buildings and to coordinate the work of large teams, and not only a symbol. But they also show that real plans depart from the texts in many ways, and that no single grid explains all buildings. The temple’s ritual centre, the sanctum, and its geometric centre do not always coincide, and in large complexes, such as South Indian temple towns, the maṇḍala is at most a guiding idea.

docs.title: 2.11 Orientation in Other Traditions
docs.text: The vāstu texts discussed in this chapter belong to the Brahmanical tradition, and their deities and rites are Hindu. Other communities had their own rules. Jain builders used vāstu texts of their own, such as Ṭhakkura Pherū’s Vatthusāra (early 14th century) in Prakrit, which adapt the same body of knowledge to Jain needs, and Jain temples follow many of the same procedures. Buddhist monasteries and stūpas followed rules set out in the monastic codes (vinaya) and in later Tantric manuals, which prescribe the layout of a monastery and the rituals for consecrating a site. The orientation of a mosque is fixed by a different principle altogether: it must face the qibla, the direction of the Kaʿba at Mecca, which from India is roughly west (Chapter 6). Medieval Islamic astronomers developed methods for computing the qibla, and in practice Indian mosques are aligned more or less to the west, sometimes deviating considerably from the true direction. Hindu, Jain and Muslim builders often shared workshops and techniques while following these different rules.

docs.title: 2.12 Regional Traditions
docs.text:
Although the vāstu texts share a common core, each region developed its own tradition, adapted to its materials, climate and forms of building.

  • Tamil Nadu and the South: the Mayamata, the Mānasāra, the Kāśyapaśilpa and the architectural chapters of the Śaiva āgamas describe the Drāviḍa temple and South Indian houses and settlements.

  • Kerala: the Tantrasamuccaya of Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan (15th century), the Śilparatna and the Manuṣyālayacandrikā (on houses), all in Sanskrit, describe a timber architecture with steep sloping roofs, adapted to the heavy monsoon. Carpentry (taccuśāstram in Malayalam) has its own tradition and vocabulary.

  • Odisha: the Śilpaprakāśa and Bhuvanapradīpa use the Odishan terminology of the rekhā and pīḍhā deuḷa (Chapter 4) (Boner and Rath Śarmā 1966).

  • Western India: the Aparājitapṛcchā and the works of Maṇḍana (15th century), still used by the Sompurā builders, describe the Māru-Gurjara temple, as well as houses, palaces and stepwells.

  • Central India: Bhoja’s Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra describes, among other things, the bhūmija temple type found in Paramāra territory.

docs.title: 2.13 Geometry and the Builder
docs.text: The geometry used in laying out buildings was that of the cord and peg: squares and rectangles, circles, the subdivision of a square into a grid, diagonals, and the rotation of squares to produce stellate plans. The Śulbasūtras show that these constructions were known in the Vedic period, together with a good approximation to \(\sqrt{2}\), given in Baudhāyana’s Śulbasūtra as \(1 + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{3 \cdot 4} - \frac{1}{3 \cdot 4 \cdot 34} \approx 1.414216\) (Sen and Bag 1983; Plofker 2009). Medieval builders used similar methods to set out the complex plans of northern temples, in which the projections of the walls are derived from rotated squares and from proportional subdivisions of the plan (Hardy 2007). Their skill was practical and geometrical; it did not depend on algebra or on any knowledge of modern physics.

docs.title: 2.14 The Texts in Print and in Teaching
docs.text:
Until the 19th century the vāstu texts circulated in manuscripts, copied in families of architects and in temple and monastic libraries, often in regional scripts and with local variations; some survive only in a few copies, and many are incomplete or corrupt. From the early 20th century, the principal texts were printed in series such as the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series and the Gaekwad’s Oriental Series, and translated: P. K. Acharya’s edition and translation of the Mānasāra appeared between 1927 and 1934, Bruno Dagens’s edition and translation of the Mayamata in the 1970s and 1980s, with a revised English version in 1994 (Acharya 1934; Dagens 1994). Many other texts remain unedited or available only in uncritical editions. Printed editions changed the way the texts were used: traditional architects who had relied on family manuscripts and oral instruction began to consult printed books, and a new class of readers, including engineers, consultants and the general public, gained access to them.

Today the traditional disciplines are taught in a few institutions, such as the Government College of Architecture and Sculpture at Mamallapuram, alongside family apprenticeship, and vāstu is the subject of short courses and a large popular literature in English, Hindi and other languages, most of which follows the modern scheme described in this chapter rather than the classical texts. University departments of architecture teach the history of Indian architecture, including the texts, as part of their curricula.

docs.title: 2.15 Reading Vāstu Today
docs.text:
Vāstu has enjoyed a large revival since the 1980s, especially among urban house-buyers, builders and property developers, in India and in the diaspora. Builders advertise “vāstu-compliant” apartments; consultants advise on the orientation of plots, the position of rooms and the placement of furniture; and books, magazines and websites offer remedies for “vāstu defects”. Vibhuti Chakrabarti, in the one scholarly study of this revival, has examined how architects, traditional sthapatis and consultants reinterpreted the texts in the late 20th century, and how far their readings departed from them (Chakrabarti 1998). Much of what is now sold as vāstu differs from the classical texts in content and spirit. This section sets out the case once, for the whole volume; later chapters refer back to it. Some of the claims most often made are examined in Table 2.3, and two general points need to be made clearly.

Table 2.3. Some common modern claims about vāstu, and what can be said about them Claim Assessment Vāstu rules work by aligning a building with the earth’s magnetic field or with “cosmic energy”. Not found in the classical texts, which speak of deities, auspiciousness and omens. The earth’s magnetic field is weak and has no known effect of this kind on occupants; “cosmic energy” is not a defined physical quantity. One should sleep with the head to the south because of the magnetic field. Rules about the direction of the head in sleep are found in traditional texts as rules of auspiciousness; the magnetic explanation is modern and has no experimental support. The north-east is the “water” corner because groundwater lies higher there. The association of directions with the five elements is a modern scheme (Section 2.3); groundwater levels depend on local geology and topography, not on compass direction. Temples were designed on the golden ratio or on Fibonacci numbers. Not supported by the texts, which use whole-number ratios and grids, nor by measured surveys of temples. Following vāstu guarantees health, wealth or harmony. No controlled study supports this; outcomes depend on many factors. The classical texts themselves frame such results as predictions of fortune. Vāstu “remedies” (mirrors, pyramids, crystals, coloured lights) correct defects. These remedies are modern inventions; the classical texts prescribe rituals of pacification.

First, the classical texts do not claim that buildings work through “cosmic energy”, magnetic fields, electromagnetism or the earth’s rotation, and these ideas have no scientific basis as explanations of vāstu rules. There is no reliable evidence that the orientation of a door, the position of a kitchen or the shape of a plot, in itself, affects the health, wealth or happiness of the occupants. Statements to the contrary are claims made by modern consultants, not findings of research.

Secondly, some traditional practices, both those recorded in the texts and those found in vernacular building, do make sense in terms of climate and construction: shaded verandahs, courtyards that help ventilate deep houses, thick walls in hot dry regions, raised plinths in wet ones, and the orientation of openings to catch breezes and avoid the low western sun. These can be studied and used on their own merits, with the methods of building science (Krishan et al. 2001). It may help to compare vāstu with other traditions of geomancy, such as Chinese fengshui, which likewise combine practical knowledge of sites and climate with cosmology, divination and rules of auspiciousness, and which have likewise been revived and commercialised in modern times. Such traditions are valuable objects of historical and anthropological study, and they can preserve useful local knowledge; but they are not, and do not need to be, sciences in the modern sense.

Respect for the tradition is better served by reading the texts for what they are, a historical record of the knowledge and beliefs of Indian builders, than by attributing to them a modern science they did not contain.
