docs.title: Chapter 3: Stūpas, Monasteries and Rock-Cut Architecture
3.1 Introduction
docs.text:
The oldest surviving monuments of historical India, after the Harappan cities, are Buddhist, Jain and Ājīvika: stūpas, monasteries and halls of worship, many of them cut into living rock. India has one of the richest traditions of rock-cut architecture in the world, with well over a thousand excavated caves, most of them in the western Deccan. They range from simple cells for monks to vast halls and, at Ellora and Māmallapuram, whole temples carved as free-standing monoliths. This chapter begins with the stūpa and the monastery, the core forms of Buddhist architecture, and then follows the rock-cut tradition from the Mauryas to the Rāṣṭrakūṭas (Huntington 1985; Dehejia 1972; Harle 1994). It comes before the chapters on the temple because these are the oldest surviving religious monuments of historical India, and because forms first fixed in them, above all the horseshoe-shaped arch of the caitya window, run through the later temple architecture of both North and South (Chapter 4). The history and doctrines of the Buddhist and Jain traditions are treated in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā.

Rock-cut architecture is subtractive: nothing can be added once the rock is cut away, so the whole design must be planned in advance. The early caves reproduce in stone the forms of contemporary timber buildings, with ribbed vaults, rafters, railings and horseshoe-arched windows, and so preserve a record of a timber architecture that has otherwise vanished (Table 3.1).

Table 3.1. The principal types of early Indian religious architecture Type Form and function stūpa A solid hemispherical mound over relics of the Buddha or of revered monks, surrounded by a path for circumambulation and often by a railing with gateways caitya hall A hall of worship, usually apsidal, with a nave, aisles and a stūpa (or later an image) in the apse vihāra A monastery: cells for monks or nuns grouped round a court or hall maṇḍapa cave In Hindu and Jain caves, a pillared hall with a shrine cut into its rear wall monolith A free-standing temple carved from a single mass of rock

docs.title: 3.2.1 Form and Meaning
docs.text:
The stūpa began as a burial mound. According to the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta, the Buddha’s relics were divided after his cremation and enshrined in stūpas, and Buddhist tradition credits Aśoka with redistributing them among many more. A developed stūpa consists of a circular base or drum (medhi), a hemispherical dome (aṇḍa, “egg”), a square railing on top (harmikā), and a mast (yaṣṭi) carrying one or more umbrellas (chattra), symbols of honour (Figure 3.1). A path for circumambulation (pradakṣiṇāpatha) runs round the base and is enclosed by a railing (vedikā), entered through gateways (toraṇa) at the four cardinal points. The relics were placed in caskets, often of stone or crystal, deep within the mound; the inscriptions on these caskets are important historical documents. Later stūpas, in Gandhāra and elsewhere, were raised on high square platforms and became taller and more elaborate.

Figure 3.1. Schematic elevation of an early stūpa of the Sāñcī type: a drum (medhi) whose railed top forms an upper processional path, the solid dome (aṇḍa) with the relic deposit, the railing on top (harmikā), and the mast (yaṣṭi) with three umbrellas (chattra); the ground-level path is enclosed by a railing (vedikā) of uprights, crossbars and coping, entered through gateways (not shown). Not to scale.

The stūpa has been interpreted as a symbol of the Buddha’s final nirvāṇa, of the world mountain and the axis of the world, and of the Buddha himself; Buddhist texts support some of these readings and not others, and they should be presented as interpretations.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Sāñcī, Bhārhut and Amarāvatī
docs.text:
The Great Stūpa at Sāñcī (Figure 1.1) began as a brick stūpa of the Mauryan period, perhaps built under Aśoka, beside one of his pillars. In the 2nd century BCE it was doubled in size and cased in stone, with a stone railing, and around the turn of the Common Era four great gateways were added. Their pillars and architraves are carved with scenes from the life of the Buddha and from the jātaka stories of his previous lives, with yakṣīs (female tree spirits) as brackets; an inscription records that one carving was the work of the ivory-carvers of nearby Vidiśā. The railing and gateways bear hundreds of short inscriptions recording gifts by monks, nuns, householders and guilds from a wide region (Huntington 1985; Dehejia 1997).

At Bhārhut (2nd century BCE), the railing, now largely in the Indian Museum, Kolkata (Figure 3.2), carries labelled reliefs of jātakas and of yakṣas and yakṣīs. At Amarāvatī in Andhra (2nd century BCE–3rd century CE) the stūpa was cased in carved limestone slabs; many are now in the Government Museum, Chennai, and the British Museum. The stūpa of Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, also in Andhra, was built on a plan of radiating walls filled with earth, a technique used for other large stūpas.

Figure 3.2. The east gateway (toraṇa) and part of the railing (vedikā) of the stūpa of Bhārhut, Madhya Pradesh, 2nd century BCE, as reassembled in the Indian Museum, Kolkata. The railing posts carry lotus medallions and standing figures of yakṣas and yakṣīs, and the crossbars between them further medallions. Photo: Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.2.3 The Question of Aniconism
docs.text: In the early reliefs of Bhārhut and Sāñcī the Buddha is not shown in human form; his presence is indicated by a tree, a throne, footprints, a wheel or a stūpa. This has traditionally been explained as a deliberate avoidance of the human image of the Buddha (“aniconism”), lasting until images appear around the 1st century CE in Mathurā and Gandhāra. Susan Huntington challenged this explanation, arguing that many of these reliefs show the worship of sacred places and objects rather than events of the Buddha’s life; Vidya Dehejia and others have replied that the symbols could be read in several ways at once. Neither reading accounts for every relief (Huntington 1990; Dehejia 1991).

docs.title: 3.3 Monasteries
docs.text:
The monastic codes (vinaya) of the Buddhist schools regulate the dwellings of monks and nuns in some detail: the size of a cell, the furnishing of beds and seats, the provision of wells, latrines, bathhouses and walking places, and the rules for accepting gifts of buildings from lay donors. Monasteries were meant to stand at a suitable distance from towns, neither too near nor too far, so that monks could go on their alms rounds; many of the rock-cut monasteries of the western Deccan lie a short walk from the trade routes and towns they served.

Buddhist monks and nuns lived first in temporary shelters during the rainy season and then in permanent monasteries (vihāra, saṅghārāma). The standard plan, found in both rock-cut and structural monasteries, is a square court surrounded by cells, with a shrine opposite the entrance in later examples. Large monasteries had stūpas, halls, kitchens, wells and stores. The great monastic universities of eastern India, Nālandā (founded in the 5th century CE) and, later, Vikramaśilā and Somapura (Paharpur, in modern Bangladesh), consisted of rows of such monasteries and temples built of brick. Nālandā flourished until it was sacked around 1200, during the campaigns of Bakhtiyār Khaljī (c. 1193–1205); its activity was much reduced thereafter, although the Tibetan pilgrim Dharmasvāmin found a few monks teaching there in 1234. The decline of Buddhism in most of India in the following centuries, for which the destruction of the monasteries was one cause among several, left these sites in ruins until their excavation in the 19th and 20th centuries.

docs.title: 3.4 Nālandā
docs.text: The excavated remains of Nālandā in Bihar, uncovered by the Archaeological Survey from 1915 onward, show the plan of a great monastic institution. A line of large brick monasteries stands on the east side of the site, each a square court surrounded by cells on two or more storeys, with a shrine opposite the entrance, wells and kitchens; facing them on the west is a line of temples and stūpa-shrines, the largest of which (“Site 3”) was enlarged in at least seven phases into a massive stepped structure with corner towers. Clay sealings bearing the name of the “great monastery” (mahāvihāra) and inscriptions of the Gupta, Pāla and other rulers who endowed it have been found there. The Chinese monks Xuanzang (in the 630s) and Yijing (in the 670s) studied at Nālandā and described its learning, its discipline and its endowments of villages. The site was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016. The often-repeated claim that its library held “nine million manuscripts” has no historical basis.

docs.title: 3.5 Bodh Gayā, Sārnāth and the Buddhist Holy Places
docs.text:
The places associated with the life of the Buddha, Lumbinī (his birth), Bodh Gayā (his enlightenment), Sārnāth (his first sermon) and Kuśīnagara (his death), became centres of pilgrimage, and Aśoka visited several of them. At Bodh Gayā in Bihar, the Mahābodhi temple stands beside the descendant of the tree under which the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment, with a stone slab, the “diamond seat” (vajrāsana), marking the place. The present brick temple, with its tall pyramidal tower and four corner towers, probably goes back to the 5th–6th century in its basic form, but it was much rebuilt, notably by Burmese missions in the 11th–14th centuries and by the British in the 1880s. Parts of a stone railing of the 1st century BCE survive. The temple was inscribed by UNESCO in 2002. At Sārnāth, near Vārāṇasī, the great cylindrical Dhamekh stūpa (5th–6th century, on an earlier core), with its band of finely carved geometric and floral ornament, stands among the remains of monasteries and of the pillar of Aśoka whose lion capital is now in the site museum.

In the north-west, the monasteries of Gandhāra, such as Takht-i-Bāhī near Peshawar (1st–7th century), built on a hilltop with a court of votive stūpas, a main stūpa court and a monastery of cells, and the Dharmarājikā stūpa and monasteries of Taxila, show the architectural setting of Gandhāran sculpture. In Odisha, the monastic sites of Ratnagiri, Lalitgiri and Udayagiri (Lalitgiri from the early centuries CE; all three flourishing c. 7th–12th century) were important centres of Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna Buddhism, with brick monasteries, stūpas and fine sculpture. In the western Himalaya, the monasteries of Tabo in Spiti (founded 996) and Alchi in Ladakh (11th–12th century), with their mud-brick walls, timber roofs and painted interiors, preserve the architecture and art of the later spread of Buddhism to Tibet.

docs.title: 3.6 The Mauryan Caves
docs.text: The earliest Indian rock-cut chambers are the caves in the Barābar and Nāgārjunī hills near Gayā in Bihar. Their inscriptions record that they were given to the Ājīvikas, an ascetic order contemporary with early Buddhism and Jainism, by Aśoka (r. c. 268–232 BCE) and by his grandson Daśaratha. They are cut into hard granite and their interiors have the high polish characteristic of Mauryan stonework. Two of the Barābar caves carry Aśoka’s dedicatory inscriptions: the Sudāmā cave, a rectangular hall leading to a domed circular chamber, and the Karṇa Caupar, a single polished rectangular chamber. The Gopikā cave in the Nāgārjunī hills, a long vaulted hall, was dedicated by Daśaratha. The Lomas Ṛṣi cave is uninscribed but of the same period, and its entrance is the most important of all, because it reproduces in stone the curved roof, rafters and lattice of a timber building, with a frieze of elephants in the arch: the earliest instance of the horseshoe arch (caitya arch, gavākṣa) that would remain a basic motif of Indian architecture for more than a thousand years.

docs.title: 3.7 The Buddhist Caves of the Western Deccan
docs.text: From the 2nd century BCE, Buddhist communities excavated monasteries and halls along the trade routes that crossed the Western Ghats between the ports of the Konkan coast and the cities of the Deccan plateau. Their inscriptions record gifts by merchants, artisans, monks, nuns and members of the Sātavāhana and Western Kṣatrapa courts (Dehejia 1972).

docs.title: 3.7.1 The Caitya Hall
docs.text: The rock-cut caitya hall is an apsidal hall divided by rows of pillars into a nave and aisles, with a stūpa at the apse and a ribbed barrel vault over the nave. The façade is dominated by a great horseshoe-shaped window that lights the interior (Figure 3.4).

docs.title: 3.7.2 Bhājā, Kārlā and Other Sites
docs.text:
The caitya hall at Bhājā (c. 2nd century BCE) is one of the earliest; its façade was originally completed with timber, as the sockets for wooden fittings show, and its pillars lean inwards like the posts of a wooden building. The great caitya hall at Kārlā (Kārle), of about the 1st century CE, is the largest and most accomplished (Figure 3.3, left). It is about 38 metres long and some 14 metres high, and its vault still carries original teak ribs. Its pillars have pot-shaped bases and bell-shaped capitals crowned by sculptured pairs of riders on elephants and horses, and the entrance is flanked by large reliefs of donor couples. An inscription credits a merchant (seṭhi) named Bhūtapāla of Vaijayantī with the “rock mansion” (selaghara), which it describes as the finest in Jambudvīpa. Other important early sites include Kondāṇe, Pitalkhorā, Beḍsā, Nāsik (the Pāṇḍavleṇī caves, with important Sātavāhana inscriptions), Junnar and Kānheri.

Figure 3.3. Two rock-cut caitya halls. Left: the nave of the great caitya hall at Kārlā (Kārle), Maharashtra, about the 1st century CE, looking towards the stūpa in the apse, under a vault that keeps its original teak ribs; the capitals of the pillars carry sculptured riders. Right: the façade of cave 19 at Ajaṇṭā, later 5th century CE, with its horseshoe-shaped window above a pillared porch, and standing and seated Buddhas carved on the surrounding rock. Photo: Mouleesha, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons Figure 3.4. Schematic plan of a rock-cut caitya hall: an apsidal nave and aisles separated by rows of pillars, with a stūpa in the apse. Not to scale.

docs.title: 3.7.3 Kānheri and Nāsik
docs.text: At Kānheri, in the hills of what is now Mumbai, more than a hundred caves were cut over a long period, from about the 1st century BCE to the 10th century CE, with a caitya hall modelled on Kārlā, monasteries, water cisterns, stairways cut in the rock, and a burial ground of monks’ memorial stūpas: an entire monastic settlement. The caves at Nāsik (Pāṇḍavleṇī) bear some of the most important historical inscriptions of the Sātavāhanas and Western Kṣatrapas, recording gifts of caves, villages and money deposited with guilds of weavers and others, whose interest was to provide robes and food for the monks. These inscriptions show that monasteries were embedded in the economic life of the region.

docs.title: 3.8 Ajaṇṭā
docs.text:
The caves of Ajaṇṭā, cut into a horseshoe-shaped bend of the Waghora river in Maharashtra, were made known to Europeans in 1819 by a party of British officers. There are about thirty caves, made in two distinct phases (Spink 2005) (Table 3.2):

Table 3.2. The two phases of Ajaṇṭā Phase Period Principal caves Character Early c. 2nd–1st c. BCE 9, 10 (caitya halls), 12, 13, 15A No images of the Buddha in human form; some early paintings in caves 9 and 10 Later 5th c. CE (mainly c. 460–480, according to Spink) 1–7, 11, 14–29, incl. 19 and 26 (caitya halls) Vākāṭaka-period patrons; Buddha images in shrines; extensive painting

Walter Spink has argued that most of the later caves were made in a short burst of activity under the Vākāṭaka king Hariṣeṇa (d. c. 477) and his feudatories, and abandoned unfinished soon after; his short chronology is widely, though not universally, accepted. The later monasteries (for example caves 1, 2, 16 and 17) consist of a pillared hall surrounded by cells, with a shrine containing a large image of the seated Buddha at the back (Figure 3.5). The shrine turned the monastery into a place of image worship as well as a residence, a change that Spink traces through the sequence of excavation at the site.

Figure 3.5. Schematic plan of a later rock-cut monastery (vihāra) of the type found at Ajaṇṭā in the 5th century: a pillared verandah, a square hall with a ring of pillars, cells for monks opening off the side and rear walls, and at the back an antechamber and shrine containing a seated image of the Buddha. The shaded area is the living rock. Caves of this type differ in size and in the number of cells and pillars; not to scale.

The two later caitya halls, 19 and 26, place a Buddha image on the front of the stūpa and have richly sculptured façades (Figure 3.3, right). The paintings of the later caves, including the famous Bodhisattva of cave 1 known as Padmapāṇi, are discussed in Chapter 14.

Inscriptions in the caves name some of their patrons. Cave 16 was dedicated by Varāhadeva, a minister of Hariṣeṇa, and other caves by local rulers and monks; an inscription in cave 26 records its donation by the monk Buddhabhadra. The variety of donors, royal, official and monastic, and the evidence of unfinished work, interrupted shrines and later intrusive images, have allowed Spink and others to reconstruct the history of the site in unusual detail. Ajaṇṭā, like Ellora, was inscribed by UNESCO in 1983.

docs.title: 3.9 Hindu and Jain Caves of the 5th to 7th Centuries
3.9.1 Udayagiri (Madhya Pradesh)
docs.text: The caves at Udayagiri near Vidiśā, of the early 5th century, are among the earliest Hindu cave shrines. One bears an inscription of the reign of the Gupta emperor Candragupta II dated 401 CE. The most famous sculpture is the great relief of Viṣṇu as the Boar (Varāha) rescuing the Earth from the waters, surrounded by rows of sages and gods. Michael Willis has shown how the site was linked to the astronomy and ritual of the Gupta court (Willis 2009).

docs.title: 3.9.2 Udayagiri and Khaṇḍagiri (Odisha)
docs.text: Near Bhubaneswar, the twin hills of Udayagiri and Khaṇḍagiri contain Jain monastic caves, some of them two-storeyed with carved friezes. The Hāthīgumphā inscription of the Mahāmeghavāhana king Khāravela of Kaliṅga, probably of the 1st century BCE, is cut above one of them.

docs.title: 3.9.3 Elephanta
docs.text:
The main cave on the island of Gharapuri (Elephanta) in Mumbai harbour, of about the mid-6th century, is a Śaiva temple: a great pillared hall with entrances on three sides, a free-standing liṅga shrine with four doorways, and large relief panels of Śiva’s forms and deeds, including Śiva as Lord of Dance, as the half-female Ardhanārīśvara, receiving the Gaṅgā in his hair, at his marriage to Pārvatī, and subduing Rāvaṇa. Its focus is the colossal relief of a three-headed Śiva (Figure 3.6), over five metres high, set in a recess in the south wall. It was long called the “Trimūrti” and interpreted as Brahmā, Viṣṇu and Śiva; scholars now identify it as Maheśamūrti or Sadāśiva, the five-faced supreme form of Śiva, of whom three faces are visible: a calm central face, a fierce face (Aghora-Bhairava) on one side and a gentle, feminine face (Vāmadeva, associated with Umā) on the other (Harle 1994).

Figure 3.6. The Maheśamūrti (Sadāśiva) in the south wall of the main cave at Elephanta (Gharapuri), Mumbai harbour, about the mid-6th century. Three of the five faces of Śiva are shown: the calm central face, the fierce, moustached Aghora-Bhairava at the viewer’s left and the gentle Vāmadeva at the right. Photo: Saankav, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.9.4 Bādāmi
docs.text: At Bādāmi, the early Cālukya capital in Karnataka, four caves were cut into the red sandstone cliffs above a lake. Cave 3, dedicated to Viṣṇu, bears an inscription of 578 CE recording its dedication by Maṅgaleśa; its reliefs show Viṣṇu seated on the serpent, as Narasiṃha, as Trivikrama and as Varāha. Cave 1 is Śaiva and contains a dancing Śiva with eighteen arms; Cave 2 is Vaiṣṇava; and Cave 4, of the 7th century, is Jain, with images of Pārśvanātha, Bāhubali and other Jinas. The early Cālukyas also excavated caves at Aihoḷe, such as the Rāvaṇa Phaḍi.

docs.title: 3.10 Cave Temples of the South
docs.text: In the Tamil country, the earliest stone temples are cave shrines of the Pallavas and Pāṇḍyas of the 7th and 8th centuries. An inscription in the cave temple at Maṇḍagapaṭṭu, attributed to the Pallava king Mahendravarman I (early 7th century), states that he created a shrine for Brahmā, Īśvara and Viṣṇu without the use of brick, timber, metal or mortar, a statement that has often been taken to mark the beginning of stone architecture in the region, where earlier temples had been built of perishable materials. Mahendravarman’s caves, at Maṇḍagapaṭṭu, Mahendravāḍi, Tiruchirappalli and elsewhere, are simple pillared halls with massive square pillars and guardian figures; those of his successors at Māmallapuram are more elaborate. The Pāṇḍyas excavated many cave temples in the far south, at sites such as Tirupparankuṉṟam, Kuṉṉakkuḍi and Kaḻugumalai, where the unfinished monolithic temple of Veṭṭuvāṉ Kōyil (8th century) was carved from the top of a granite hill, like a smaller Kailāsa.

docs.title: 3.11 Māmallapuram
docs.text: At Māmallapuram (Mahabalipuram) on the Tamil coast, the Pallava kings of the 7th and early 8th centuries, especially Narasiṃhavarman I Māmalla (r. c. 630–668), from whom the place takes its name, and Narasiṃhavarman II Rājasiṃha (r. c. 690–728), created a group of monuments that was inscribed by UNESCO in 1984. They include pillared cave shrines (maṇḍapa) with relief panels, such as the Varāha and Mahiṣāsuramardinī caves; monolithic temples; the structural Shore Temple of Rājasiṃha’s time (Chapter 5, Section 5.6.3); and a great open-air relief. The style of their sculpture is discussed in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 3.11.1 The Five Rathas
docs.text:
The “Five Rathas” are monolithic shrines carved in the 7th century from a granite outcrop. Their names, after the five Pāṇḍava brothers and Draupadī of the Mahābhārata, are modern and have nothing to do with their original dedications. They reproduce in stone the principal forms of early southern buildings (Table 3.3 and Figure 3.7):

Table 3.3. The “Five Rathas”, Māmallapuram Name Form Draupadī ratha Small square shrine with a curved roof like that of a thatched hut Arjuna ratha Square two-storeyed Drāviḍa shrine with an octagonal cupola Bhīma ratha Oblong shrine with a barrel-vaulted roof (śālā) Dharmarāja ratha Square three-storeyed Drāviḍa shrine, the tallest of the group Nakula–Sahadeva ratha Apsidal shrine; a monolithic elephant stands beside it Figure 3.7. The “Five Rathas” at Māmallapuram, 7th century, monolithic shrines cut from a granite outcrop: at the right the three-storeyed Dharmarāja ratha, in the centre the oblong Bhīma ratha with its barrel-vaulted roof, and beyond them the smaller shrines of the group and the monolithic elephant. Photo: Vaibhav A. Gangane, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.11.2 The Great Relief
docs.text:
The relief carved across two great boulders (Figure 3.8), nearly thirty metres long, shows a crowd of gods, celestial beings, sages, hunters and animals converging on a natural cleft, down which water once flowed, with serpent deities in it. It is identified either as Arjuna’s penance to obtain a weapon from Śiva, or as the penance of Bhagīratha to bring the Gaṅgā down to earth; the debate between the two interpretations has never been settled, and some scholars think the ambiguity may be intended.

Figure 3.8. The great relief at Māmallapuram, 7th century, carved across two granite boulders: gods, celestial beings, sages, hunters and animals, among them life-size elephants, converge on the natural cleft in the centre, in which serpent deities rise. It is read either as Arjuna’s penance or as the descent of the Gaṅgā. Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.12 Ellora
docs.text:
The caves of Ellora, near Aurangabad in Maharashtra, comprise thirty-four principal excavations of three religions, made between about the 6th and the 10th century (Harle 1994) (Table 3.4):

Table 3.4. The cave groups at Ellora Group Caves Religion Period (approx.) Southern 1–12 Buddhist 6th–8th c. Central 13–29 Hindu 6th–9th c. Northern 30–34 Jain 9th–10th c.

The Buddhist caves include the caitya hall of cave 10 and the three-storeyed monasteries of caves 11 and 12. Cave 10, known locally as the Viśvakarmā cave after the divine craftsman, has a façade carved to imitate a structural building with a balcony and a window, and a large seated Buddha in front of the stūpa in its apse; caves 11 and 12 (Do Thal and Tin Thal) rise in three storeys of pillared halls, with rows of seated Buddhas, bodhisattvas and goddesses that reflect the growth of Vajrayāna Buddhism in the 7th and 8th centuries. Among the Hindu caves, cave 29 (Dhumar Leṇa) resembles the main cave at Elephanta, and caves 14, 15 and 21 have fine reliefs of Śiva and Viṣṇu.

docs.title: 3.12.1 The Kailāsa Temple (Cave 16)
docs.text:
The Kailāsa, dedicated to Śiva and attributed on inscriptional evidence to the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Kṛṣṇa I (r. c. 756–773), is the largest monolithic temple in India (Figure 3.9). The builders cut three deep trenches into the hillside to isolate a block of basalt and then carved it from the top downwards into a complete Drāviḍa temple: a two-storeyed shrine with a superstructure some thirty metres high, a hall, a porch, a pavilion for Śiva’s bull Nandī, a gateway and two free-standing pillars, linked by bridges and surrounded by a court whose walls are cut into galleries. The amount of rock removed is commonly estimated at about 200,000 tonnes. The temple is closely related in plan to the Virūpākṣa at Paṭṭadakal (Chapter 5), and its form is that of the Drāviḍa temple described in Chapter 4. Its reliefs, which include the famous scene of Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa, Śiva’s home, are discussed with the sculpture of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas in Chapter 13.

Figure 3.9. The Kailāsa temple (cave 16) at Ellora, Maharashtra, attributed to the Rāṣṭrakūṭa king Kṛṣṇa I (r. c. 756–773): the entrance front, with its gateway and screen wall, and the superstructure of the temple rising behind them, all cut from the basalt hillside whose scarp surrounds the court. Photo: World8115, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 3.12.2 The Jain Caves
docs.text: The Jain caves at the northern end of Ellora, of the 9th and 10th centuries, include the Indra Sabhā (cave 32), a two-storeyed excavation with a small monolithic shrine in its court, and the Jagannātha Sabhā (cave 33), with images of the tīrthaṅkaras, of the Jain goddesses Ambikā and Siddhāyikā, and of Bāhubali. Sittannavāsal in Tamil Nadu is an important Jain cave in the South, with remains of painting.

docs.title: 3.13 Jain Sacred Hills
docs.text: Jain communities created a distinctive kind of sacred landscape: hills covered with temples, to which pilgrims climb on foot. At Śatruñjaya, above the town of Pālitāṇā in Gujarat, several hundred shrines, most of them rebuilt from the 16th century onward after earlier destruction, are grouped in walled enclosures (ṭuṅk) along the two ridges of the hill; no one may stay on the hill overnight, for it belongs to the gods. Girnār near Junāgaḍh, sacred to Neminātha, has temples of the 12th century and later high on its slopes; Sammet Śikhar (Pārasnāth) in Jharkhand is revered as the place where twenty of the twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras attained liberation. At Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in Karnataka, the hill of Candragiri carries a group of early medieval basadis and inscriptions associated by tradition with the migration of Bhadrabāhu and Candragupta Maurya, and the facing hill of Vindhyagiri the colossal Bāhubali (Chapter 13). These sites illustrate the importance of pilgrimage, lay patronage and continuous renewal in Jain religious architecture.

docs.title: 3.14 How the Caves Were Made
docs.text: Unfinished caves at Ajaṇṭā, Ellora and elsewhere show how the work was done. The masons first cut the outline of the façade; they then worked into the rock from the top, so that they always worked downwards and never needed scaffolding below the working face. The interior was roughed out by cutting channels and removing blocks, leaving masses of rock from which pillars, images and other features were later carved; the finished surfaces were dressed and, where painting was planned, covered with plaster. Iron chisels and picks were the main tools. The rock had to be chosen with care: the Deccan basalt, in horizontal flows of varying quality, was well suited to cutting, while the granite of Barābar and Māmallapuram and the sandstone of Bādāmi each imposed their own constraints. Water was a constant concern, and many caves have cisterns cut into the rock and channels to carry rain away from the façade.

docs.title: 3.15 Decline and Rediscovery
docs.text: By the 13th century Buddhism had disappeared from most of India, except in the Himalaya and in parts of the east, and its monuments were abandoned. The reasons were many: the loss of royal and mercantile patronage, competition from Hindu devotional movements and the absorption of Buddhist ideas and sites into Hinduism, the concentration of Buddhism in a few great monasteries, and the destruction of those monasteries in the conquests of the late 12th and early 13th centuries. Many stūpas were quarried for bricks and stone, and many sites were forgotten. Their rediscovery began in the late 18th and 19th centuries, when British officers and Indian scholars identified sites with the help of the accounts of the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang, and the Archaeological Survey excavated and restored them (Chapter 1). The revival of Buddhist pilgrimage to Bodh Gayā and Sārnāth from the late 19th century, the conversion of B. R. Ambedkar and hundreds of thousands of his followers to Buddhism at Nagpur in 1956, and the building of new monasteries and temples by Buddhist communities from many countries have given the old sites new life.

docs.title: 3.16 The Stūpa beyond India
docs.text: The stūpa travelled with Buddhism and took new forms in each country. In Sri Lanka, the great dāgabas (from Pali dhātugabbha, “relic chamber”) of Anurādhapura, such as the Ruvanvälisāya and the Jetavanārāma, built between the 2nd century BCE and the 4th century CE, are enormous brick hemispheres; the Jetavanārāma was among the largest brick structures of the ancient world. In Myanmar, the stūpa became the tall, bell-shaped gilded pagoda of Bagan and the Shwedagon at Yangon; in Java, the stepped terraces of Borobudur (late 8th–early 9th century) carry hundreds of reliefs and small perforated stūpas around a central one; in Nepal, the white domes of Svayambhūnāth and Boudhanāth bear painted eyes on their harmikās (on the monasteries of the Kathmandu valley see Chapter 5, Section 5.7.6); and in Tibet and China, the chörten and the pagoda developed from the same ancestry. These monuments are part of the history of Asian Buddhism rather than of India alone, but they show how far the Indian stūpa travelled (Huntington 1985).

docs.title: 3.17 From Timber to Rock to Temple
docs.text: The monuments of this chapter record a double transfer. The earliest caves copied in rock the timber halls and monasteries that have otherwise vanished, so that the ribbed vault, the leaning post and the horseshoe window survive only because masons reproduced them in stone. Later, the rock-cut tradition became a laboratory for the temple: the cave shrines of the 5th to 7th centuries tried out the sanctum, the pillared hall and the sculptural programme, and the monoliths of Māmallapuram and Ellora carved whole Drāviḍa temples out of the hillside. Unlike the Brahmanical temple, however, these monuments were paid for by a very wide public: their inscriptions name monks and nuns, merchants, artisans and many women, alongside kings. The next chapter turns to the structural temple, whose forms grew in part out of this tradition.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Temple Architecture: Nāgara, Drāviḍa and Vesara
4.1 The Temple as the House of a God
docs.text:
The Hindu temple is, in the first place, a house for a deity who is present in a consecrated image or emblem. Its common names say as much: devagṛha or devālaya (“house of the god”), prāsāda (“palace”), mandira (“dwelling”), and in Tamil kōyil (“house of the lord”). Worship in the temple is modelled on the service of an honoured guest or a king: the deity is woken, bathed, dressed, fed, entertained and put to rest, and taken out in procession on festival days. The architecture serves these rites: a small, dark sanctum for the image, a hall or halls for the worshippers and the temple staff, space for circumambulation, kitchens, stores and tanks, and, in large temples, enclosures for festivals and processions.

The texts also give the temple a cosmic meaning. Its superstructure is compared to a mountain, and several temple types bear the names of mountains (Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa); the Bṛhatsaṃhitā (ch. 56) lists twenty kinds of temple beginning with Meru (Bhat 1981). The plan is laid out on the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala (Chapter 2), and the vertical axis that rises from the image through the centre of the superstructure has been interpreted, notably by Stella Kramrisch, as a link between the world of humans and the divine (Kramrisch 1946). Kramrisch’s reading has been very influential; later scholars have accepted much of it while warning against attributing a single symbolic programme to temples of every period and region (Michell 1977; Hardy 2007).

docs.title: 4.2 The Parts of a Temple
docs.text:
Despite great regional variety, most Hindu temples share a set of elements, shown for a northern temple in Figure 4.1; equivalent northern and southern terms are given in Table 4.1.

Garbhagṛha (sanctum) The “womb-house”, a small, usually square chamber containing the image, normally entered by a single door on the main axis and lit only through it. Superstructure The tower over the sanctum. Modern writers usually call it śikhara in northern temples and vimāna in southern ones. The terms are not used in quite this way in the southern texts, where vimāna refers to the whole shrine building from base to finial and śikhara to its crowning dome-like member. Antarāla (vestibule) A short passage between the sanctum and the hall. Maṇḍapa (hall) An open or closed pillared hall in front of the sanctum, sometimes several in a row: an entrance porch (mukhamaṇḍapa or ardhamaṇḍapa), a closed hall (gūḍhamaṇḍapa), an open hall for dance or assembly (raṅgamaṇḍapa, nṛttamaṇḍapa, sabhāmaṇḍapa). Pradakṣiṇāpatha (ambulatory) A path for clockwise circumambulation of the sanctum, either inside the building, between the sanctum wall and an outer wall (a sāndhāra temple), or outside it (a nirandhāra temple). Base A moulded base (adhiṣṭhāna in the South, pīṭha and vedībandha in the North), often standing on a further platform (upapīṭha, or jagatī in the North). Enclosure and gateways An enclosure wall (prākāra), with gateways (in the South, gopura), and subsidiary shrines, halls, tanks and kitchens within it. Enclosures are characteristic of southern temples but are also found in the North, for example in Odisha. Figure 4.1. Type plan and section of a northern temple with an inner ambulatory (a sāndhāra temple), drawn on one axis with the entrance on the right. (a) Section: the sanctum, containing the image, rises into the tower (śikhara), from whose front the śukanāsā projects over the vestibule; the hall and porch have lower roofs of stepped slabs; the whole stands on a platform (jagatī). (b) Plan: sanctum (garbhagṛha), ambulatory (pradakṣiṇāpatha, arrow showing the clockwise path), vestibule (antarāla), pillared hall (maṇḍapa) and porch (ardhamaṇḍapa). In a temple without an inner ambulatory (nirandhāra) the path runs round the outside of the sanctum walls. A schematic of the type, not of a particular temple; not to scale. Table 4.1. Some equivalent terms in the northern and southern traditions (simplified) Element Northern (Nāgara) Southern (Drāviḍa) Superstructure śikhara; in Odisha gaṇḍī tiered superstructure (tala) of the vimāna Crowning members āmalaka (ribbed disc) and kalaśa (pot) śikhara (cupola) and stūpi (finial) Base pīṭha, vedībandha upapīṭha, adhiṣṭhāna Wall jaṅghā bhitti (pāda) Cornice zone varaṇḍikā prastara with kapota Wall projections ratha: bhadra, pratiratha, karṇa bays answering to the śālā, kūṭa and pañjara above Gateway toraṇa, porch gopura

docs.title: 4.3.1 The Terms in the Texts
docs.text: The names Nāgara, Drāviḍa and Vesara come from the texts, but the texts use them in more than one way. In the southern texts (the Kāmikāgama, Mayamata and Mānasāra), they denote three classes of vimāna distinguished chiefly by the shape of the crowning parts (the “neck” and the cupola): square for Nāgara, octagonal for Drāviḍa, and circular (or apsidal) for Vesara. A temple of the southern type can therefore be “Nāgara” in this sense if its cupola is square (Dagens 1994). The northern texts, such as the Aparājitapṛcchā, use a different classification, which includes Nāgara, Drāviḍa, Bhūmija, Latina and other types (Mankad 1950).

docs.title: 4.3.2 The Terms in Modern Art History
docs.text: Modern art historians use Nāgara for the temple form of northern and central India with a curved tower, and Drāviḍa for the southern form with a tiered superstructure of miniature shrines. These two are genuinely distinct architectural languages, each with its own system of composition. The term Vesara has been used for the temples of the Deccan, between the two; but its meaning is disputed. Early Cālukya temples of the 7th and 8th centuries, at Aihoḷe, Bādāmi and Paṭṭadakal, are not hybrids: they include fully northern and fully southern temples standing side by side. Adam Hardy treats the southern temples of Karnataka, from the early Cālukyas to the Hoysaḷas, as a single “Karṇāṭa Drāviḍa” tradition, in which, from the 11th century, the tiers of the superstructure are broken into so many small, staggered elements that the tower acquires an almost continuous profile. He distinguishes from this tradition a separate mode, which he calls Vesara, that emerged in the later Cālukya period and combines the principles of Drāviḍa and Nāgara composition in a hybrid form (Hardy 1995, 2007). The Encyclopaedia of Indian Temple Architecture, edited by Michael Meister, M. A. Dhaky and Krishna Deva, follows a regional and dynastic arrangement that avoids forcing temples into three boxes (Meister et al. 1983).

docs.title: 4.4.1 Characteristics
docs.text: The Nāgara temple of northern and central India has a square sanctum and a superstructure (śikhara) that curves inward as it rises, crowned by a large ribbed disc (āmalaka) and a pot-shaped finial (kalaśa). The walls are broken by vertical projections (ratha): a central projection (bhadra), corner projections (karṇa) and, in larger temples, intermediate projections (pratiratha), which continue up through the tower. The surface of the tower is covered with a mesh of horseshoe-arch motifs (gavākṣa, candraśālā). Many northern temples stand on a high terrace (jagatī) instead of within an enclosure, but enclosed precincts are common in Odisha and elsewhere.

docs.title: 4.4.2 Types of Nāgara Superstructure
docs.text:
Art historians, following the northern texts, distinguish several types of Nāgara superstructure (Meister et al. 1983; Hardy 2007) (Table 4.2):

Table 4.2. Types of Nāgara superstructure Type Form Examples Latina A single curved spire with continuous bands (latā) running up each face Galaganātha, Paṭṭadakal (8th c.); early Odishan rekhā temples such as Paraśurāmeśvara, Bhubaneswar Śekharī A central spire clustered with smaller half-spires (uruśṛṅga) and miniature spires Kandariyā Mahādeva and Lakṣmaṇa temples, Khajuraho Bhūmija Rows of miniature spires arranged in storeys between vertical bands Udayeśvara, Udayapur (Paramāra, 11th c.); Gondeśvara, Sinnar Phāṃsanā A pyramidal roof of horizontal slabs Halls and smaller shrines; the Odishan pīḍhā roof Valabhī A barrel-vaulted (“wagon”) roof over an oblong sanctum Telī kā Mandir, Gwalior; Vaitāl Deuḷ, Bhubaneswar Figure 4.2. Schematic elevation of a Nāgara temple of the Latina type. The sanctum (dashed) lies within the wall zone; the curved tower is crowned by the āmalaka and kalaśa. Not to scale.

docs.title: 4.4.3 Anatomy of a Latina Tower
docs.text: A Latina tower is composed with great regularity (Figure 4.2). Its central projection carries a continuous band, the latā (“creeper”), covered with a mesh of interlocking horseshoe-arch motifs, which runs from the base of the tower to the top. The corner projections are divided into storeys (bhūmi) by small ribbed discs (bhūmi-āmalaka), five storeys being common in medium-sized temples, so that the tower is read as a stack of diminishing floors drawn inward along a curve. At the top, the tower narrows to a “shoulder” (skandha) and a recessed “neck” (grīvā) carrying the great āmalaka, the kalaśa and, in many temples, a flag-pole. On the front of the tower, above the vestibule, a large projecting gable called the śukanāsā (“parrot’s beak”) frames an image or an emblem of the deity. The curve of the tower was set out by geometrical methods, and its profile is one of the most characteristic features of each regional style.

docs.title: 4.4.4 Development
docs.text:
The earliest surviving stone temples of the North, of the 5th century, have flat roofs (temple 17 at Sāñcī); the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogaṛh (early 6th century) and the brick temple at Bhitargaon had towers, now partly ruined. The brick tradition reached its height in the Lakṣmaṇa temple at Sirpur in Chhattisgarh, usually dated to the first half of the 7th century, which its inscription records was built by the queen Vāsaṭā in memory of her husband, the Pāṇḍuvaṃśī king Harṣagupta. Its Latina tower, of finely moulded brick, preserves the pattern of horseshoe-arch motifs and corner storeys that stone towers of the period have often lost. By the 7th and 8th centuries the Latina temple had taken its classic form, in Odisha, central India, Rajasthan and the Deccan. From the 10th century the Śekharī and Bhūmija forms multiplied the miniature spires of the tower, producing the soaring, many-peaked temples of Khajuraho (c. 950–1050) and the Paramāra temples of Mālwā. Regional schools developed their own vocabularies:

  • Odisha (Kaliṅga): the sanctum tower (rekhā deuḷa) with its massive āmalaka, the hall (jagamohana) with a stepped pyramidal pīḍhā roof, and the oblong khākharā type with a barrel roof; from the Paraśurāmeśvara (7th century) through the Liṅgarāja (11th century) and the Jagannātha temple at Puri (12th century) to Konārak (13th century) (Donaldson 1985; Boner and Rath Śarmā 1966).

  • Western India (Māru-Gurjara): the temples of the Caulukya (Solaṅkī) period in Gujarat and Rajasthan, such as Moḍherā (1026–27) and the marble Jain temples of Dilwārā, with richly carved halls and ceilings.

  • Central India: the Candella temples of Khajuraho and the Kacchapaghāta and Paramāra temples.

  • Kashmir and the Himalaya: the stone temples of Kashmir (Mārtaṇḍ, 8th century), with pyramidal roofs, trefoil arches and pediments that reflect contact with Gandhāran and Western traditions; and the timber temples of Himachal and Uttarakhand.

  • Bengal: brick temples covered with terracotta reliefs and with curved roofs derived from village huts, especially of the 16th–18th centuries (Viṣṇupur).

docs.title: 4.4.5 The Māru-Gurjara Temple
docs.text:
In Gujarat and Rajasthan, the temples of the 10th to 13th centuries developed a distinctive and very richly carved form, called Māru-Gurjara (“of Marwar and Gujarat”) by M. A. Dhaky, which is still built today by the Sompurā architects using the texts of Maṇḍana. Its base and wall are built up of a long sequence of named mouldings and bands of figures, described in the western Indian texts; some of the principal ones are listed in Table 4.3 (Meister et al. 1983). The halls have corbelled domed ceilings and richly carved pillars, and many temples have a decorative arched gateway (toraṇa) in front. The sun temple at Moḍherā and the Jain temples of Mount Abu and Raṇakpur are among its masterpieces (Chapter 5).

Table 4.3. Some mouldings of the base (pīṭha) and wall base (vedībandha) of a Māru-Gurjara temple (bottom to top; simplified) Moulding Form jāḍyakumbha Large “pot” moulding at the foot of the base karṇikā Sharp-edged fillet grāsapaṭṭī Band of grimacing “faces of glory” (kīrttimukha) gajapīṭha, narapīṭha Bands of elephants and of human figures, in the larger temples khura, kumbha, kalaśa Hoof, pot and vase mouldings of the wall base kapotālī Cornice-like moulding completing the wall base

docs.title: 4.5.1 Characteristics
docs.text:
The Drāviḍa temple of southern India has a superstructure built in tiers (tala), each tier carrying a parapet of miniature buildings: square pavilions (kūṭa) at the corners, oblong barrel-roofed pavilions (śālā) in the middle of each side, and smaller elements (pañjara, nīḍa) between. Above the topmost tier is a “neck” (grīvā) and a dome-like crowning member (śikhara), square, octagonal or round, with a finial (stūpi) (Figure 4.3). The walls are articulated by pilasters and niches (devakoṣṭha) for images, and topped by an entablature (prastara) with a projecting, curved cornice (kapota) decorated with horseshoe-arch motifs (kūḍu, nāsī). Large temples stand within one or more enclosures (prākāra) entered through gateways (gopura), and often have a tank (Meister et al. 1983; Hardy 2007).

Figure 4.3. Schematic elevation of a four-storeyed Drāviḍa shrine (vimāna). The ground storey (base, wall and entablature) counts in the texts as the first storey (tala); three diminishing upper storeys follow, and the edge of each roof carries a parapet (hāra) of miniature pavilions, square kūṭas at the corners and an oblong śālā in the middle. The top storey carries the neck (grīvā), the crowning cupola (śikhara) and the finial (stūpi). Not to scale.

Kerala developed a distinct southern tradition: sanctums that may be square, circular, oblong or apsidal, built of laterite or stone below and timber above, with steep, overhanging roofs of tiles or copper sheets suited to the heavy rainfall.

docs.title: 4.5.2 The Base
docs.text:
The southern texts describe many types of moulded base (adhiṣṭhāna), built up from a standard set of mouldings. The two most common families are the pādabandha, whose principal moulding is a large rounded or faceted torus (kumuda), and the pratibandha, whose upper part carries a frieze of mythical lion-like beasts (vyāla) below a projecting member (Dagens 1994). The texts name many further types, and their names and definitions differ from text to text. See Table 4.4.

Table 4.4. Principal mouldings of a southern base (bottom to top; simplified) Moulding Form upāna Plain plinth course jagatī Tall, vertical base course kumuda Torus: rounded, octagonal or faceted kaṇṭha Recessed “neck” or dado, often framed by thin fillets (kampa) paṭṭikā Flat band; replaced by a kapota (cornice) in some types vyālavari Frieze of vyālas, in the pratibandha type

docs.title: 4.5.3 Development
docs.text: Pallava (7th–9th century) The monolithic rathas and the Shore Temple at Māmallapuram, and the Kailāsanātha temple at Kāñcīpuram (early 8th century), established the Drāviḍa vocabulary in Tamil country (Chapters 5 and 3). Early Cālukya and Rāṣṭrakūṭa (7th–9th century) In Karnataka, Drāviḍa temples such as the Virūpākṣa at Paṭṭadakal (c. 740s) stand beside northern ones; the rock-cut Kailāsa at Ellora (later 8th century; Section 3.12) is the largest Drāviḍa monument of its age. Chola (9th–13th century) Temples ranging from small, finely proportioned village shrines to the colossal royal temples of Thanjavur (completed 1010) and Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram (Dehejia 1990). Later Chola, Pāṇḍya and Vijayanagara (12th–16th century) Expansion of temple complexes with multiple enclosures, halls of a thousand pillars and ever larger gateways; under Vijayanagara, the great temple complexes of Hampi and of the Tamil country. Nāyaka (16th–18th century) The temple cities of Madurai, Śrīraṅgam and Rāmeśvaram, with towering gopuras covered with painted stucco figures and immense columned corridors.

docs.title: 4.5.4 The Gopura
docs.text: The gopura (in Sanskrit originally a town gate) is the gateway tower of the southern temple enclosure. Under the Pallavas and early Cholas gateways were modest and much lower than the main shrine; from the 12th century they grew taller, so that in the great temple complexes of the Pāṇḍya, Vijayanagara and Nāyaka periods the outer gateways, the tallest of them some 50 metres or more high, dwarf the sanctum. Several reasons have been suggested: rulers and donors could add new enclosures and gateways to an established temple without disturbing its sanctified centre; the gateways announced the temple to the city and framed its festival processions; and the old sanctum was valued for its age and sanctity rather than its size (Michell 1977).

docs.title: 4.6 The Temples of the Deccan: “Vesara”
docs.text:
The Deccan, between the Nāgara north and the Drāviḍa south, was the scene of the most varied experiments in Indian temple architecture.

  • Early Cālukyas of Bādāmi (6th–8th century): at Aihoḷe, Bādāmi, Mahākūṭa and Paṭṭadakal, rock-cut and structural temples in both the northern and the southern manner, together with distinctive early forms such as the apsidal Durgā temple and the Lāḍ Khān temple at Aihoḷe.

  • Rāṣṭrakūṭas (8th–10th century): the Kailāsa temple at Ellora and the Jain caves there (Chapter 3).

  • Later Cālukyas of Kalyāṇa (11th–12th century): temples at Lakkuṇḍi, Itagi, Kuruvatti and elsewhere, finely carved in greenish schist, in which the Drāviḍa superstructure is broken into close-set, staggered elements, with a stepped or stellate plan.

  • Hoysaḷas (12th–13th century): temples at Belūr (Cennakeśava, begun 1117), Haḷebīḍ (Hoysaḷeśvara) and Somanāthapura (Keśava, 1268), of chloritic schist, raised on stellate platforms, with lathe-turned pillars, densely sculptured friezes and bracket figures.

  • Kākatīyas (12th–13th century): in Telangana, temples such as the Thousand-Pillared temple at Hanamkonda (1163) and the Rāmappa temple at Palampet (1213), whose superstructure is built of unusually light brick; the popular claim that these bricks float on water has not been confirmed by any published test.

Further east, at Ālampur on the Tuṅgabhadrā in Telangana, a group of nine temples of the 7th and 8th centuries (the Navabrahma temples), built under the early Cālukyas, have northern Latina towers, showing that the boundary between “northern” and “southern” forms was not a simple geographical line. The Kākatīya temples mentioned above, with their richly carved black stone pillars and bracket figures, are a further regional variant; the Rāmappa temple was inscribed by UNESCO in 2021.

Whatever name is given to them, it is these later Deccan temples, rather than the early Cālukya ones, that mark the most distinctive contribution of the region; in Hardy’s usage the term Vesara is reserved for the hybrid mode among them, while the rest belong to the Karṇāṭa Drāviḍa tradition (Hardy 1995, 2007). See Figure 4.4.

Figure 4.4. Highly simplified profiles of a Nāgara temple (curved tower), a Drāviḍa temple (tiered superstructure) and a later Deccan temple of the 11th–13th centuries, in which many closely spaced tiers give a stepped but almost continuous profile. Such later Deccan temples are often called “Vesara”; Adam Hardy reserves that name for a hybrid Nāgara–Drāviḍa mode among them. Real temples are far more complex.

docs.title: 4.7 Composition: Temples Made of Temples
docs.text:
Both the Nāgara and the Drāviḍa traditions build their superstructures out of miniature representations of shrines. On a Drāviḍa temple, each tier carries a ring of small pavilions, square, oblong and apsidal, each a reduced image of a complete building with its own base, pillars, cornice and roof; on a Nāgara temple, the tower is covered with a mesh of horseshoe-arch motifs, and in the Śekharī and Bhūmija types with whole miniature spires. Adam Hardy has called these components “aedicules” and shown how the history of temple architecture can be understood as the progressive multiplication, overlapping and interpenetration of such miniature shrines, so that the temple appears to grow outward and upward from its centre (Hardy 1995, 2007). In the mature Śekharī temples of Khajuraho, for example, half-spires (uruśṛṅga) cling to the main tower in several layers, and smaller spires cluster on its lower parts, giving the impression of a mountain range rising to a summit. In the later Deccan temples, the tiers of the southern superstructure are broken into so many staggered elements that the tower acquires an almost continuous profile.

This way of thinking explains features that might otherwise seem merely decorative. The niches on the walls, framed by pilasters and crowned by miniature roofs, are themselves small shrines; the horseshoe arches on the tower are the gable-ends of miniature buildings; and the projections of the plan carry these miniature shrines up through the whole height of the temple. The temple is, in a sense, a temple made of temples.

docs.title: 4.8 Doorways, Ceilings and Halls
docs.text:
The doorway of the sanctum is one of the most carefully designed parts of the temple. In northern temples from the Gupta period onwards, the door-frame is made up of several vertical bands (śākhā), carved with creepers, couples, ganas, snakes and lotus scrolls; at the base stand the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā and door guardians (dvārapāla), and at the centre of the lintel is a small image of the temple’s deity or of a related deity. Southern temples have plainer door-frames but large guardian figures on either side of the entrance.

The halls of northern temples were often roofed by corbelled domes built of concentric rings of stone, carved on the underside with tiers of figures, lotus petals and a central pendant; those of the Māru-Gurjara temples of Gujarat and Rajasthan, and above all of the Jain temples of Mount Abu and Raṇakpur, are of extraordinary richness (Chapter 5). Southern halls are usually flat-roofed, carried on many pillars; the great pillared halls of the Vijayanagara and Nāyaka periods, such as the thousand-pillared halls of Madurai and Śrīraṅgam, are designed for festivals, assemblies and the display of processional images. Many temples also have a separate hall for dance and music (nāṭamaṇḍira in Odisha, nṛttamaṇḍapa in the South) and, in Kerala, a theatre (kūttambalam).

docs.title: 4.9.1 Projections
docs.text:
Northern temple plans are classified by the number of projections on each face of the sanctum: three (triratha: a central bhadra and two corner projections), five (pañcaratha), seven (saptaratha) and nine (navaratha). The projections are carried up through the base, the wall and the tower, so that the plan determines the whole three-dimensional form of the temple (Figure 4.5).

Figure 4.5. Schematic plans with three, five and seven projections per face (simplified; in real temples the projections are proportioned according to rule and are often further subdivided). ‘G’ marks the sanctum.

docs.title: 4.9.2 Groups of Shrines
docs.text: Many temples are not single buildings but groups. In the pañcāyatana (“five-shrined”) arrangement, found from the Gupta period at Deogaṛh and common in the North, a principal shrine stands at the centre of a terrace with four smaller shrines at its corners, often dedicated to related deities. Northern temples may have subsidiary shrines in their courts or on their terraces, and southern complexes have shrines for the consort goddess, for Gaṇeśa and Skanda, for the saints and for many other deities within their enclosures. Some temples have several sanctums in a row or round a common hall: double and triple temples, such as the Hoysaḷa temples of Haḷebīḍ and Somanāthapura, and the multiple shrines of Jain temples.

docs.title: 4.9.3 Stellate Plans
docs.text: From the 10th century, builders in central India and the Deccan produced stellate (star-shaped) plans by rotating a square about its centre, or by setting projections at angles, so that the walls form a sequence of sharp points. The Bhūmija temples of Mālwā and the later Cālukya and Hoysaḷa temples of Karnataka, such as the Keśava temple at Somanāthapura, have such plans, which multiply the faces of the walls available for sculpture and create a play of light and shadow (Hardy 2007).

docs.title: 4.10.1 The Northern Wall
docs.text: In the northern temple the wall (jaṅghā) is divided vertically by the projections. The central projection (bhadra, Odishan rāhā) carries the principal niche, often with an image of a form of the main deity or of a deity of the same family; the corner projections (karṇa) often carry the guardians of the directions; the recesses between projections (salilāntara, “water channels”) carry celestial women, ascetics and mythical beasts. In large temples, such as those of Khajuraho, the wall carries two or three registers of sculpture.

docs.title: 4.10.2 The Southern Wall
docs.text: In the southern temple the wall (bhitti) is articulated by pilasters into bays. The principal bays contain niches (devakoṣṭha) for images framed by pilasters and crowned by an arch or a miniature pavilion; smaller bays contain “cages” (pañjara) or decorative arches (toraṇa), sometimes with makara (crocodile-like monsters) at the ends. In Chola temples the niches carry a standard set of images: for a Śiva temple, Dakṣiṇāmūrti on the south, Liṅgodbhava or Viṣṇu on the west, Brahmā on the north, with Gaṇeśa, Durgā and others.

docs.title: 4.10.3 Pillars
docs.text: Pillars (stambha) are classified in the southern texts by their section: square pillars are called brahmakānta, octagonal ones viṣṇukānta, and round or sixteen-sided ones by other names (rudrakānta, indrakānta); many pillars combine sections, square at the base and octagonal or round above. A southern pillar is made up of a base, a shaft (daṇḍa), a series of capital mouldings (in the texts laśuna, kalaśa, tāḍi, kumbha, padma) and an abacus (phalaka), and carries a bracket (potikā) that supports the beam (Dagens 1994). Bracket forms are among the best guides to the date of southern buildings. In the Vijayanagara and Nāyaka periods pillars were carved with rearing horses and composite animals (yāḷi), or as clusters of colonnettes; Hoysaḷa pillars were turned on a lathe.

docs.title: 4.11.1 Construction
docs.text:
Indian temples are, with few exceptions, trabeate: they are built of posts and beams, and openings and roofs are spanned by lintels, slabs and corbelling, in which each course projects slightly beyond the one below until the gap can be closed. Ceilings of halls are often corbelled domes made of concentric rings of stone, richly carved on the underside, as in the Jain temples of Mount Abu. The true arch was known: brick voussoir arches are found in the Gupta-period temple at Bhitargaon, and the arch was used in some Buddhist and later buildings. But it was not adopted in temple building, which kept to the trabeate system even after Indo-Islamic architecture had made the arch and dome common (Chapter 6). See Figure 4.6.

Figure 4.6. Left: a corbelled arch, in which horizontal courses project step by step until the opening can be closed by a slab; the stones work as cantilevers. Right: a true arch, in which wedge-shaped voussoirs transmit the load to the supports by compression. Indian temple builders used the first; the second became common with Indo-Islamic architecture. Schematic.

Stone temples were usually built of finely dressed blocks laid dry, without mortar, held in place by their own weight and sometimes by iron clamps or dowels; iron beams were used at Konārak and Puri. Brick temples used mud or lime mortar, and lime plaster (sudhā) was used to coat walls and to model stucco figures, especially on southern superstructures and gopuras. The claim, often repeated, that dry-stone temples are “earthquake-proof” is not correct. Unmortared masonry can accommodate small movements, and the sheer mass of a temple helps it to stand; but many temples have been damaged or brought down by earthquakes, subsidence and the failure of their foundations, and those that survive have generally been repaired.

docs.title: 4.11.2 Materials
docs.text:
The principal building materials are listed in Table 4.5.

Table 4.5. Principal materials of Indian temple architecture Material Region Examples Sandstone North and central India, Odisha, Deccan Khajuraho, Bhubaneswar, Aihoḷe, Paṭṭadakal Khondalite Odisha Konārak Granite Tamil Nadu, Karnataka Thanjavur, Māmallapuram, Hampi Chloritic schist (“soapstone”) Karnataka Hoysaḷa temples (Belūr, Haḷebīḍ, Somanāthapura); later Cālukya temples Basalt (trap rock) Western Deccan Ellora, Elephanta, Ajaṇṭā (rock-cut) Marble Rajasthan, Gujarat Dilwārā (Mount Abu), Raṇakpur Laterite, timber, copper Kerala Kerala temples Brick and terracotta Gangetic plain, Bengal Bhitargaon, Viṣṇupur

docs.title: 4.12 The Ritual of Construction
docs.text: The Mayamata, the Mānasāra and the āgamas describe the building of a temple as a sequence of rites (Dagens 1994): the examination and purification of the site; the ploughing of the ground and the offering to the vāstupuruṣa; the laying of the first stones or bricks; the placing of a consecration deposit (garbhanyāsa) in the foundations; the raising of the door-frame; the placing of a further deposit and of the crowning finial at the top of the superstructure; the installation of the image; and the consecration of the temple. In modern South Indian practice the great consecration (kumbhābhiṣeka), in which sanctified water is poured over the finials, is repeated after major repairs, traditionally about every twelve years. The Āgamic rituals of temple worship and installation are treated in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama.

docs.title: 4.13.1 Quarries, Transport and Workshops
docs.text:
Stone for temples was usually quarried close to the site; the builders of Thanjavur, for example, used granite from quarries some distance from the delta, while the sandstone temples of Khajuraho and Bhubaneswar stand near outcrops of their stone. Blocks were split from the bedrock with wedges driven into lines of holes, a technique whose marks can still be seen at many ancient quarries, roughly dressed on the spot, and moved on rollers, sledges, carts or rafts, with animals and large teams of labourers. Final dressing and carving were done at the site, often after the blocks had been set in place: unfinished temples and sculptures show surfaces left in the rough, waiting to be carved.

Building was organised by workshops under a master architect, with masons, carvers, sculptors, carpenters and smiths, and unskilled labour drawn from the surrounding villages. Masons’ marks, cut on blocks to identify the team that dressed them or the position in which they were to be laid, are found at many sites, from Paṭṭadakal to the Vijayanagara capital. Some temples record the names of their architects and sculptors (Section 4.14).

docs.title: 4.13.2 Drawings and Templates
docs.text: Builders worked from drawings and full-size layouts. At Paṭṭadakal and a few other sites, outline drawings of temple superstructures and of mouldings are incised on rock surfaces and on the walls of temples, apparently as guides for the masons. At Bhojpur near Bhopal, where the 11th-century Paramāra temple was left unfinished, architectural drawings of the plan, elevation and details of the temple are engraved on the flat rock surfaces around it, and the earthen ramp by which stones were raised can still be traced; the site gives an unusually direct view of a medieval building in progress. Adam Hardy has shown that the Bhojpur drawings correspond closely to the procedures for designing temples set out in Bhoja’s own Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, so that here, unusually, a text and a building of the same court can be read together (Hardy 2015). Templates of wood or metal were probably used to repeat profiles of mouldings, and measuring rods carried the module from which the building was proportioned.

docs.title: 4.13.3 Raising the Stones
docs.text: How the upper parts of tall temples were built is not recorded in detail. Earthen ramps, timber scaffolding, levers and simple lifting tackle were all available, and the remains at Bhojpur show that ramps were used in at least some cases. Claims about specific methods at particular temples, such as the story of the ramp at Thanjavur (Chapter 5), rest on tradition unless there is archaeological evidence for them.

docs.title: 4.13.4 Time and Cost
docs.text: Inscriptions occasionally give the time a temple took to build. The Bṛhadīśvara at Thanjavur, whose inscriptions record its completion in 1010, appears to have been built within about seven years; many other temples took decades, were built in stages, or were never finished. Temples were enormously costly, and inscriptions record how they were funded: by royal treasuries, by gifts of land and villages whose revenue was assigned to the temple, by donations of gold and cattle, and by contributions from merchants, guilds and individual devotees.

docs.title: 4.14 Architects and Their Names
docs.text:
Indian temples are usually known by the names of their gods and their royal patrons, and the vāstu texts describe the ideal sthapati without naming any real one. Yet inscriptions name a fair number of architects and sculptors, and together they give a picture of the profession (see also Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru, and Chapter 11).

In the Deccan, inscriptions of the mid-8th century on the Virūpākṣa temple at Paṭṭadakal, built for the Cālukya queen Lokamahādevī, honour its builders: they name two masters, Guṇḍa, styled Anivāritācāri, who received honours and titles from King Vikramāditya II, and Sarvasiddhi Ācārya, whose name is linked with the southern part of the work. These records call their architect the sūtradhāri “of the southern quarter”, a phrase read by some as a reference to the Tamil country and by others to the south side of the temple. At Thanjavur, the inscriptions of Rājarāja I name the chief architect of the Bṛhadīśvara temple (Chapter 5). In the Hoysaḷa temples of the 12th and 13th centuries, sculptors signed individual images, sometimes with boastful titles, so that the work of masters such as Mallitamma, Dāsoja and his son Cāvaṇa can be identified and followed from temple to temple. The Kākatīya temple at Pālampet (1213), built by the general Recarla Rudra, is known locally as the Rāmappa temple, after the name, according to tradition, of its chief sculptor.

Western India has the richest record. The foundation inscriptions of Jain temples often name the sūtradhāra responsible: the Lūṇa Vasahī at Mount Abu (1230) is associated with the sūtradhāra Śobhanadeva, and the temple of Ādinātha at Raṇakpur (1439) with the sūtradhāra Depāka. The tower of victory built at Chittorgarh by Rāṇā Kumbhā of Mewar in the mid-15th century (the Vijaya Stambha, called Kīrtistambha in its inscriptions) records the names of its architect, Jaitā, and his sons. Kumbhā’s court architect Maṇḍana is the best known Indian architect before the modern period, because he was also an author: the Prāsādamaṇḍana on temples, the Rājavallabha on houses, palaces and towns, the Rūpamaṇḍana on images and other works are attributed to him, and members of his family are credited with further manuals. These books, written in plain Sanskrit for working builders, show a hereditary architect setting down the Māru-Gurjara practice of his own day rather than repeating an ancient canon (Meister et al. 1983).

The Sompurās of Gujarat, who regard themselves as brāhmaṇas and trace their origin to Somnāth (Prabhās Pāṭan), are the best documented of the hereditary architect families. For several centuries they have designed temples in the Māru-Gurjara manner for Jain and Hindu patrons, working from family manuscripts of the vāstu texts, drawings, and the knowledge of proportion handed down from father to son; much of the actual carving was done by other communities of stone-workers, such as the Salāṭs. In the 20th century Sompurā architects designed some of the most prominent new temples of India: Prabhashankar Sompura the rebuilt temple of Somnāth (consecrated 1951; Chapter 5), in the manner of the Caulukya period, and his successors many large temples in India and abroad, among them the Rāma temple at Ayodhya (consecrated 2024), designed by Chandrakant Sompura in the Nāgara style. Prabhashankar Sompura also edited Sanskrit texts of the western Indian tradition, such as the Dīpārṇava, with Gujarati commentary, bringing the family’s learning into print. In the South, the corresponding hereditary architects are the sthapatis of the Viśvakarma communities, whose modern training is described in Chapter 1.

The architect’s name has thus survived in three ways: in honorific and donative inscriptions, in signatures on individual works, and in the books that a few architects wrote. All three show the master builder as a respected professional, and in western India and the Deccan a literate one, while most of those who quarried, carried, laid and carved the stones remain anonymous.

docs.title: 4.15.1 Land, Wealth and Staff
docs.text: A great temple was not only a building but an institution with land, wealth and a large staff. South Indian inscriptions show temples holding villages and agricultural land, lending money, employing priests, accountants, cooks, garland-makers, musicians and dancers, and maintaining tanks, schools and feeding houses. The Thanjavur inscriptions list hundreds of temple servants by name and record the shares of land and produce assigned to them (Chapter 5). Temples were centres of local economic and political life as well as of worship, and kings used them to integrate their territories. Many were linked to monasteries (maṭha) of ascetic orders: Tamara Sears has shown how the Śaiva monastic lineages of central India in the 9th to 11th centuries built monasteries beside temples, served as royal preceptors and shaped the religious landscape of their kingdoms (Sears 2014). In the South, the great festivals in which images were carried out of the temple in procession shaped the architecture of the temple and of the town around it (Branfoot 2007).

docs.title: 4.15.2 Temple Women
docs.text: Many medieval temples employed women dancers and singers, called in Tamil inscriptions taḷiccēri peṇṭukaḷ and later known as devadāsīs (“servants of the god”). Leslie Orr’s study of the inscriptions of medieval Tamil Nadu shows that in the Chola period they were women of standing, who received land and made donations to temples in their own names, and that the “temple women” of the inscriptions were a more varied group than the later image of the devadāsī suggests (Orr 2000). Over later centuries their position changed, and under colonial rule the institution became associated with poverty and sexual exploitation; reformers, among them Muthulakshmi Reddy, campaigned against it, and the dedication of girls to temples was prohibited by law, in Madras by an act of 1947 and later elsewhere. Davesh Soneji has traced what followed for the communities concerned: the loss of their livelihoods and their stigmatisation, and the passage of their dance and music, reshaped by middle-class performers, into modern Bharatanāṭyam (Soneji 2012). Their history is more complex than either romantic or purely reformist accounts allow.

docs.title: 4.15.3 Caste and Temple Entry
docs.text:
For most of their history, Hindu temples did not admit everyone. Communities regarded as untouchable were excluded from the temple and often from the streets around it, and lower castes were restricted to particular parts of the precinct. The struggle against these exclusions was a major theme of social reform in the early 20th century. The Vaikom Satyagraha in Travancore (1924–25) demanded the right of all castes to use the roads around the Vaikom temple; the Guruvayur Satyagraha (1931–32) and B. R. Ambedkar’s campaign for entry to the Kalaram temple at Nashik (from 1930) followed. The Temple Entry Proclamation of the Maharaja of Travancore (1936) opened the state’s temples to all Hindus, and the Constitution of India (1950) abolished untouchability and, in Article 25, allowed laws throwing open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes of Hindus. The architecture of the temple, with its graded enclosures and thresholds, thus has a social history as well as a religious one (Figure 4.7).

Figure 4.7. Schematic plan of a large South Indian temple complex: the sanctum and its halls on an east–west axis, surrounded by concentric enclosures entered through gateways (gopura) that grow larger towards the outside. Not to scale; real complexes, such as Śrīraṅgam or Madurai, are far more complex.

docs.title: 4.16 Jain Temples
docs.text: Jain temples (jinālaya, basadi, derāsar) share the building techniques and much of the ornament of contemporary Hindu temples in each region, and were often built by the same workshops. But they have distinctive features of their own. The sanctum houses one or more images of tīrthaṅkaras, sometimes four facing outwards (caturmukha), as at Raṇakpur. Many temples are surrounded by a court lined with cells (devakulikā), each with its own image. The samavasaraṇa, the assembly hall in which a tīrthaṅkara preaches to all beings, is represented as a stepped, circular or square structure. Jain communities also built “temple cities” on sacred hills, such as Śatruñjaya (Pālitāṇā) and Girnār in Gujarat, where hundreds of shrines were added over centuries. The marble temples of Dilwārā and Raṇakpur are discussed in Chapter 5, and the Jain caves of Ellora and the colossal image of Bāhubali at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in Chapters 3 and 13.

docs.title: 4.17 Temple Building Today
docs.text: More temples are being built in India and abroad today than at almost any time in the past. Many are designed by hereditary architects, the Sompurās in the Māru-Gurjara tradition and the sthapatis of Tamil Nadu in the Drāviḍa tradition, who use the texts, their family drawings and modern engineering; the stone is often carved by machine and finished by hand, and parts may be carved in India and shipped abroad for assembly. Very large temple complexes, such as those built by modern devotional movements in Delhi, Gandhinagar and several cities overseas, combine traditional forms with modern planning, exhibition spaces and visitor facilities. In the diaspora, temples serve as community centres as well as places of worship, and often combine shrines of several deities, northern and southern, under one roof. Alongside these new buildings, the renovation of old temples raises the conservation questions discussed in Chapter 1.

docs.title: 4.18 Texts, Builders and Forms
docs.text: The chapter has moved between three kinds of evidence, the texts, the inscriptions and the buildings, and they do not tell the same story. The texts supply a vocabulary and a set of classifications, some of which, like the three classes of Nāgara, Drāviḍa and Vesara, mean something different in the texts from what they mean to art historians. The inscriptions name patrons, architects and endowments, and show the temple as an institution with land, staff and social exclusions. The buildings show what the texts cannot: a system of composition in which a temple is made of miniature temples, developed differently in each region and constantly reworked. The next chapter looks at individual temples in which these three kinds of evidence can be brought together.
