docs.title: Chapter 8: Town Planning: Villages, Towns and Cities
8.1 Introduction
docs.text: South Asia has a long history of planned settlements, from the Harappan cities of the 3rd millennium BCE to Jaipur in the 18th century and Chandigarh in the 20th. But “planning” meant very different things at different times. Some cities were laid out on a regular plan from the start; many more grew around a fort, a palace, a temple, a shrine or a market, and were reorganised by successive rulers. The texts describe idealised plans, which real towns resemble only in part. This chapter looks first at the textual prescriptions and then at the evidence of particular cities.

docs.title: 8.2.1 The Arthaśāstra
docs.text:
The Arthaśāstra (composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE; traditionally attributed to Kauṭilya and dated c. 300 BCE) describes the building of a fortified capital (book 2, chapters 3–4) (Olivelle 2013; Kangle 1965). The text prescribes that it be built at a suitable site, such as the confluence of rivers or the bank of a lake, and surrounded by three moats, of 14, 12 and 10 daṇḍas in width, an earthen rampart and a wall with towers and gates. Within, three royal roads running east–west and three running north–south divide the city into blocks. The royal palace is placed north of the centre, and the text assigns quarters to particular groups (2.4): priests, ministers and temples to the north; merchants, artisans, soldiers and others to their specified places; brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras to the north, east, south and west respectively; and heretics and the caṇḍālas, regarded as untouchable, to the area outside, near the cremation ground. The Arthaśāstra thus shares with the vāstu texts the practice of writing the hierarchy of caste into the plan of a settlement (Chapter 1, Section 1.6, and Chapter 10, Section 10.3).

The Arthaśāstra distinguishes four kinds of fort by their natural defences: forts protected by water, by mountains, by desert and by forest. The Manusmṛti (7.70) gives a list of six, adding forts of earth and forts defended by men.

docs.title: 8.2.2 The Vāstu Texts
docs.text:
The Mayamata, the Mānasāra and other texts describe the planning of villages (grāma) and towns (nagara, pura) on the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala, with a temple or a hall at the centre, streets on the lines of the grid, and quarters for different castes and occupations arranged in the zones of the grid (Chapter 2) (Dagens 1994; Acharya 1934). The Mānasāra names eight types of village plan, which also serve for towns (Table 8.1; four are drawn in Figure 8.1):

Table 8.1. The eight village plans of the Mānasāra (after Acharya’s interpretation; the descriptions in the text are brief and not always clear) Name Form daṇḍaka “Staff”: a simple plan with streets crossing at right angles sarvatobhadra “Auspicious on all sides”: a square plan with a temple at the centre nandyāvarta Named after an auspicious figure; streets arranged around a centre in a swastika-like pattern padmaka “Lotus”: a plan with radiating divisions svastika Named after the swastika; streets in a cross pattern with diagonal elements prastara “Spread out”: a rectangular or square grid kārmuka “Bow”: a curved plan for a site on a river or the sea caturmukha “Four-faced”: a plan with four main gates and cross streets Figure 8.1. Schematic interpretations of four of the Mānasāra’s plan types. The texts give few dimensions, and these diagrams follow modern reconstructions.

How far these prescriptions guided real settlements is an open question. Brāhmaṇa villages granted by kings in South India (agrahāra, brahmadeya) were often laid out with a temple and parallel streets, and temple towns were organised around the temple (below); but most villages grew organically, and the eight plan types cannot be matched one-to-one with surviving towns.

docs.title: 8.3 The Harappan Cities
docs.text:
The cities of the mature Harappan or Indus civilisation (c. 2600–1900 BCE) are among the earliest planned cities in the world (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002; Wright 2010). Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, the best known, covered some 200 hectares or more. It consisted of a raised western mound, often called the “citadel”, and a larger lower town, both built on massive platforms of mud brick to raise them above the floods of the Indus. Main streets ran roughly north–south and east–west, dividing the lower town into large blocks, within which lanes gave access to houses. The houses, of baked brick of standardised proportions (commonly 1:2:4), were built round courtyards, with bathing platforms, latrines and, in many cases, private wells; drains from the houses ran into covered drains along the streets, provided with soak pits and covers for cleaning. Several hundred wells have been recorded. On the citadel mound stood the “Great Bath”, a watertight brick tank about 12 by 7 metres and 2.4 metres deep, sealed with bitumen, and a large building usually called the “granary”, whose function is disputed. Population estimates for the city vary widely, typically from about 40,000 upwards.

Harappā in Punjab had a similar arrangement of mounds. Its so-called “granary” too has been reinterpreted by some archaeologists as a hall.

docs.title: 8.3.1 Dholāvīrā
docs.text: Dholāvīrā, on an island in the Rann of Kachchh in Gujarat, occupied from about 3000 to 1500 BCE and inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021, differs from the cities of the Indus plain. It is built largely of stone, and it is divided into a “castle”, a “bailey”, a “middle town” and a “lower town”, each walled. Its excavator, R. S. Bisht, interpreted a large open area between the castle and the middle town as a ceremonial ground. Most striking is its water system: a series of large reservoirs, partly cut into the rock, and dams and channels to capture the runoff of two seasonal streams, in a region of very low rainfall. Near the north gate of the castle were found ten large Harappan signs, made of inlaid gypsum, which may once have been mounted over the gate.

docs.title: 8.3.2 Lothal
docs.text: Lothal in Gujarat, a smaller Harappan town with a bead-making workshop and a warehouse, has a large brick-lined basin, about 214–219 metres long and 35–37 metres wide (published figures vary), which its excavator S. R. Rao interpreted as a dockyard connected to an estuary (Rao 1973). This interpretation has been widely repeated but is contested: others, notably Lawrence Leshnik, have argued that the basin was a reservoir for fresh water. Its function, dock or reservoir, remains debated (Leshnik 1968). Lothal certainly took part in long-distance trade, but it should not be described without qualification as the world’s earliest dockyard.

docs.title: 8.3.3 Who Planned the Harappan Cities?
docs.text: The regularity of Harappan cities, their standardised bricks and weights, and their shared material culture over a very large area have suggested to some archaeologists a powerful central authority, perhaps a state with kings and priests. Others point out that there are no palaces, royal tombs or monumental temples of the kind found in Mesopotamia and Egypt, and argue for a more decentralised society, perhaps governed by councils of merchants, landowners and religious specialists, in which shared conventions were maintained by trade and custom rather than by a single ruler. The absence of readable texts makes the question hard to settle (Kenoyer 1998; Possehl 2002; Wright 2010).

docs.title: 8.3.4 Continuity?
docs.text: How much the Harappan experience passed into later Indian urbanism is uncertain. The cities were largely abandoned by the early 2nd millennium BCE, more than a thousand years before the cities of the Gaṅgā valley and the earliest town-planning texts. Similarities, such as orthogonal planning and attention to drainage, can be explained by common needs as well as by transmission, and no direct line of descent has been demonstrated.

docs.title: 8.4 Early Historic Cities
docs.text:
The second urbanisation of South Asia began in the Gaṅgā valley around the middle of the 1st millennium BCE (Coningham and Young 2015). Its cities, such as Kauśāmbī, Śrāvastī, Rājagṛha and Pāṭaliputra, were surrounded by massive ramparts and moats. The Greek envoy Megasthenes (c. 300 BCE), quoted by later writers, described Pāṭaliputra, the Mauryan capital, as a long city defended by a timber palisade and a moat; excavations at Bulandibagh in Patna have found remains of such a palisade, and at Kumrahar the remains of a great pillared hall. At Taxila in the north-west the city of Sirkap, laid out under Indo-Greek rule in the 2nd century BCE, has a main street with regular cross streets, houses, shrines and a stūpa. These cities show that fortification and regular street plans were known, but none corresponds exactly to the ideal city of the Arthaśāstra.

The best-preserved early historic fortified city is Śiśupālgaṛh near Bhubaneswar in Odisha, occupied from about the 5th century BCE to the 4th century CE. Its earthen ramparts, later faced with brick and laterite, enclose an almost square area of more than a square kilometre, with two monumental gateways on each side, arranged roughly symmetrically; the gates were elaborately defended. Excavations since the 1940s, and more recent surveys, have revealed a dense city within the walls, with a group of stone pillars at its centre. Its regular, gated square plan is the closest archaeological parallel to the ideal cities described in the texts (Coningham and Young 2015).

docs.title: 8.4.1 Life within the Walls
docs.text: Excavated early historic towns show houses of mud brick and baked brick with tiled roofs, ring-wells and soak-pits lined with terracotta rings, drains, workshops for beads, shell, iron and pottery, and shrines. Literary sources, in Pali, Sanskrit and Tamil, describe streets of particular crafts, markets, assembly halls, parks and pleasure gardens, and the gates and watchtowers of the walls. The Tamil poems of the Caṅkam anthologies and the epic Cilappatikāram describe the port of Pukār (Kāvirippūmpaṭṭiṉam) and the city of Madurai, with their streets of merchants and artisans and quarters for foreign traders.

docs.title: 8.4.2 Ports
docs.text: Coastal trading towns, linked to the Roman world, the Persian Gulf and Southeast Asia, formed another kind of early city. At Arikamedu near Pondicherry, excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in 1945 and later by Vimala Begley, Roman amphorae and fine wares found alongside Indian pottery and beads show a trading settlement active from about the 2nd century BCE to the 2nd century CE. Excavations at Pattanam in Kerala, which some identify with the port of Muziris described in Roman sources, and at sites on the Gujarat and Bengal coasts have added to the picture. These ports had warehouses, wharves and craft quarters, and their populations included foreign merchants.

docs.title: 8.5 Temple Towns
docs.text:
In South India, many towns grew around great temples, and the temple shaped the plan of the town. The concentric enclosures of the temple were extended outwards by streets, often called in Tamil māḍa vīdhi or ratha vīdhi, along which the deity’s chariot was drawn at festivals; brāhmaṇa households, temple servants and merchants lived along them in an order that reflected their status and their role in the temple. Crispin Branfoot has shown how the processional festivals of the Nāyaka period, in which images left the sanctum to visit the halls, tanks and streets of the town, shaped both the architecture of the temple and the plan of the town around it (Branfoot 2007).

  • Madurai: the streets form concentric rectangles round the Mīnākṣī–Sundareśvara temple and are named after the Tamil months in which processions pass along them (Chapter 5).

  • Śrīraṅgam: the temple of Raṅganātha, on an island in the Kāverī, has seven concentric enclosures with twenty-one gateways; the outer enclosures contain streets of houses and shops, so that the town lies within the temple. Its huge outer gateway (rājagopuram), left unfinished for centuries, was completed only in 1987.

  • Chidambaram, Tiruvaṇṇāmalai, Kāñcīpuram and Kumbakonam are other towns whose plans are organised by temples and their processional routes.

docs.title: 8.6 Pilgrimage Towns
docs.text: Many Indian towns grew up around places of pilgrimage (tīrtha): at river crossings and confluences, on sacred hills, and at the sites of famous temples, shrines of saints and tombs. Their form was shaped by the movement of pilgrims: processional routes, bathing places, rest-houses (dharmaśālā), markets for offerings, and the houses of the priests and guides who served the pilgrims and kept their family records. Vārāṇasī (Kāśī), on the Gaṅgā, is the most famous: its riverfront of stone steps (ghāṭ), built mostly from the 18th century onward by rulers and nobles from all over India, is lined with temples, palaces and monasteries, and behind it lies a dense maze of lanes (Eck 1982). At Puri, the broad processional avenue (baḍa daṇḍa) along which the chariots of Jagannātha are drawn each year links the temple with a second shrine some three kilometres away. The Jain temple cities of Śatruñjaya and Girnār, the Buddhist holy places, and the Sufi shrines (dargāh) of Ajmer, Delhi and many other towns, with their courts, gateways and kitchens, have shaped their surroundings in similar ways.

docs.title: 8.7 Vijayanagara (Hampi)
docs.text:
Vijayanagara, “the city of victory”, on the Tuṅgabhadrā river in Karnataka, was the capital of the empire of the same name from the mid-14th century until its sack in 1565, after the battle of Tālikoṭa; the empire continued elsewhere until the mid-17th century. Its ruins, at and around the village of Hampi, were inscribed by UNESCO in 1986. Contemporary visitors, such as the Persian envoy ʿAbd al-Razzāq in the 1440s and the Portuguese Domingo Paes and Fernão Nunes in the 16th century, described a very large and wealthy city with seven lines of fortification; modern estimates of its population vary widely (Fritz and Michell 1991).

Archaeologists distinguish a “sacred centre” around the Virūpākṣa temple and other temples near the river, with long colonnaded bazaar streets running from their gateways, and a “royal centre” to the south, with palace platforms, audience halls, enclosures for the royal women, stepped tanks, and buildings such as the Lotus Mahal and the elephant stables, whose arches and domes derive from the architecture of the Deccan sultanates. The city was supplied by canals drawing water from the Tuṅgabhadrā, aqueducts and tanks. The arrangement of the city followed the rocky landscape and its sacred associations, especially with the Rāmāyaṇa, rather than a single geometrical plan. Its temples are described in Chapter 5 (Section 5.6.9), the borrowings of its courtly buildings from the sultanates in Chapter 6, and its canals, aqueducts and tanks in Chapter 9 (Michell 1995).

docs.title: 8.8 Sultanate and Mughal Cities
docs.text:
The Sultanates and the Mughals founded or refounded many cities: the successive cities of Delhi (among them Sīrī, Tughluqābād and Fīrūzābād), Ahmadābād (1411), Bīdar, Gulbarga, Bījāpur, Golconda and Hyderabad (1591) in the Deccan, Fatehpur Sīkrī and Shāhjahānābād. Their characteristic elements were the fortified citadel or palace, the congregational mosque, the bazaar street and the walled garden, with residential quarters (in Gujarat the pol, a gated street of houses) often organised by community or occupation (Asher 1992).

  • Fatehpur Sīkrī (1571–c. 1585), Akbar’s capital near Agra, was built on a ridge beside a lake, with the palace and the great mosque on the top of the ridge and the town below; it was largely abandoned after Akbar moved his court in 1585 (Brand and Lowry 1985). The site was chosen because the Sufi Shaikh Salīm Chishtī, who had predicted the birth of Akbar’s heir, lived there. The palace is not a single building but a sequence of courts and pavilions, aligned on a common grid but not symmetrically: a public audience hall (Dīwān-i ʿĀmm) with a great court, the private audience hall (Dīwān-i Khāṣṣ), the treasury, the five-storeyed open pavilion (Pañch Mahal), a square tank with a central platform (Anūp Talāo), and the residential palaces of the women of the household, of which the largest is the so-called palace of Jodh Bāī. The great mosque, with the marble tomb of Salīm Chishtī in its court, is entered from the south through the Buland Darwāza. The reasons for the abandonment of the city, whether shortage of water or the political needs of a moving court, are debated.

  • Shāhjahānābād (begun 1639), the walled city of Old Delhi, was laid out by Shāh Jahān with the Red Fort on the Yamunā, the Jāmiʿ Masjid on a natural rise, and two great bazaar streets, one of them Chāndnī Chowk, along which a canal ran. Its plan has been interpreted as a deliberate expression of Mughal ideas of sovereignty (Blake 1991).

  • Golconda, the Quṭb Shāhī fortress city, was surrounded by massive walls and its citadel rose on a granite hill. Visitors are still shown how a hand-clap at the entrance gate can be heard at the top of the citadel.

  • Bīdar is notable for its kārīz, underground channels that collect groundwater, a technique of Iranian origin.

docs.title: 8.9 Hill Forts and Sea Forts
docs.text: Fortresses were among the largest building works of pre-modern India, and the Arthaśāstra’s classification of forts by their natural defences (above) reflects a real strategic tradition. In the Deccan, rulers from the Sātavāhanas to the Marathas fortified the flat-topped hills of the Western Ghats, cutting cisterns into the rock to store the monsoon rain for the dry season. Daulatabad (Devagiri), the Yādava capital raided by ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī in 1296 and annexed by the Delhi Sultanate in 1318, has an isolated rock scarped all round, a moat and a tunnel entrance. In the 17th century the Maratha king Śivājī built or rebuilt a network of hill forts, among them Rajgad and Raigad, and sea forts on islands off the Konkan coast, such as Sindhudurg (1664–1667) and the earlier Janjira of the Siddis. In Rajasthan, Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore and Jaisalmer combine walls, palaces, temples and water tanks within their circuits (Chapter 7). These forts were often towns in their own right, with markets, temples, mosques and houses, and their water systems were as important as their walls.

docs.title: 8.10 Jaipur
docs.text:
Jaipur was founded in 1727 by the Kachhwāhā ruler Savāī Jai Singh II, who moved his capital from the hill fort of Amber to the plain below. Jai Singh, who also built the astronomical observatories known as Jantar Mantar, worked with the architect Vidyādhar Bhaṭṭācārya, a Bengali brāhmaṇa in his service. The city is laid out on a grid of large rectangular blocks (chokrī) separated by broad bazaar streets, with the palace complex occupying the centre of the northern part. The grid is not aligned to the cardinal directions but turned by about fifteen degrees, probably to suit the lie of the land. Because the hills to the north-west prevented the completion of one block of a nine-block arrangement, an extra block was added at the south-east.

The plan of Jaipur has often been explained as a direct application of a nine-square vāstu maṇḍala, with the palace at the sacred centre. Vibhuti Sachdev and Giles Tillotson have shown that the evidence is more complicated: the city combined traditional ideas of auspicious planning with the practical needs of a commercial capital, Mughal precedents and the specific site, and its regular form owes as much to its development by the court as a planned trading city as to any text (Sachdev and Tillotson 2002). See Figure 8.2.

Figure 8.2. Schematic plan of the walled city of Jaipur (founded 1727): rectangular blocks separated by broad bazaar streets, the palace complex in the centre of the northern part, and an extra block at the south-east replacing the one that could not be built against the hills. The grid is in reality turned about 15 degrees from north; not to scale.

docs.title: 8.11 Delhi: A City of Many Cities
docs.text:
Delhi illustrates how Indian capitals were repeatedly refounded. Tradition counts “seven cities” of Delhi, but the real number of successive settlements is larger. The earliest fortified city to survive in part is Lāl Kot, associated with the Tomar Rajputs, enlarged by the Cauhāns as Qilʿa Rāi Pithorā; the Delhi sultans made it their first capital, building the Qutb mosque within it (Chapter 6). ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī built a new walled city at Sīrī (c. 1303) and the great reservoir of Ḥauẓ Khāṣ; Ghiyāth al-Dīn Tughluq built the massive fortress city of Tughluqābād (1320s); Muḥammad bin Tughluq enclosed the space between the older cities as Jahānpanāh; and Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq founded Fīrūzābād on the Yamunā, where he set up an Aśokan pillar brought from Topra. The Mughal emperor Humāyūn and the Sūr ruler Sher Shāh built Dīn Panāh, the Purānā Qilʿa; Shāh Jahān founded Shāhjahānābād (1639); and the British built New Delhi (1911–1931; Chapter 7, Section 7.2.4). Each new city reused materials, sites and water sources of its predecessors, and their ruins, tombs and mosques now lie scattered across the modern metropolis (Table 8.2).

Table 8.2. Some of the successive cities of Delhi (dates approximate) City Date Builder and notes Lāl Kot, Qilʿa Rāi Pithorā 11th–12th c. Tomar and Cauhān Rajputs; first capital of the Delhi sultans Sīrī c. 1303 ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī Tughluqābād 1320s Ghiyāth al-Dīn Tughluq Jahānpanāh 1320s–1330s Muḥammad bin Tughluq; walls joining earlier cities Fīrūzābād 1354 Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq, on the Yamunā Dīn Panāh (Purānā Qilʿa) 1530s–1540s Humāyūn and Sher Shāh Sūr Shāhjahānābād 1639 Shāh Jahān; Red Fort and Jāmiʿ Masjid New Delhi 1911–1931 British imperial capital

docs.title: 8.12 Neighbourhoods
docs.text: Within the walled cities of the Sultanate and Mughal periods, and in older cities generally, most people lived in neighbourhoods organised by community, caste or occupation. In Ahmadābād, the pol was a street or group of streets of houses, entered through a single gate that could be closed at night, inhabited by families of one caste or occupation and managed by its own council; each pol had its shrines, wells, and bird-feeders (cabūtrā). Old Delhi was divided into mohallas and kaṭrās, and similar arrangements are found in many old cities. These neighbourhoods combined dense, shaded housing with shared spaces and strong local institutions, and their social structure reflected the divisions of caste and community.

docs.title: 8.13 Colonial and Modern Cities
docs.text:
The colonial port cities of Madras (founded 1639 around Fort St George), Bombay (developed by the East India Company from the 1660s) and Calcutta (from 1690) grew in a new pattern: a fort and a European “white town” beside a much larger and denser Indian “black town”, with markets, temples, mosques and neighbourhoods of merchants and artisans who came to trade with the Company. In the 19th century they acquired docks, railways, mills, broad avenues, public buildings and parks, together with crowded tenements and slums, and became the largest cities of India.

Colonial rule also brought other new kinds of planned settlement: the cantonments and “civil lines” laid out beside older Indian towns; hill stations; railway colonies; and the new imperial capital of New Delhi, whose avenues and vistas centred on the Viceroy’s House are described in Chapter 7 (Section 7.2.4) (Metcalf 1989). After independence, new capitals were built for Punjab at Chandigarh (Section 7.3.1), on a grid of self-contained sectors, and for Odisha at Bhubaneswar, planned by Otto Koenigsberger. These cities drew on international modernist ideas rather than on the vāstu texts, although their designers often described their work in terms of Indian climate and ways of life. Since the 1990s, new planned towns, special economic zones and “smart cities” have continued the tradition of planning from above, alongside the unplanned growth that accounts for most of India’s urbanisation.

docs.title: 8.14 Plans and Cities
docs.text: The cities of this chapter show the distance between the planned city of the texts and the cities that were actually built. Only a few, Śiśupālgaṛh, Jaipur and the colonial and modern capitals among them, were laid out on a regular plan from the start, and even Jaipur, so often explained as a vāstu maṇḍala, turns out on examination to owe as much to its site, its court and its trade. Most cities grew around a fort, a temple, a shrine or a market, and were reshaped by water, defence and the movement of processions. What the texts and many real cities do share is an ordering of space by social rank, in which caste and community decided where people could live. The qualities that modern planners admire in old Indian towns, compact neighbourhoods, mixed uses and shaded streets, are real, but they were the product of particular histories rather than of a single ancient science of planning.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Water Architecture: Wells, Tanks, Dams and Gardens
9.1 Water in Indian Building
docs.text: Over most of South Asia rain falls in a few months of the year, and must be stored, or drawn from the ground, for the rest. Wells, tanks, reservoirs, dams, canals and stepwells were therefore among the most important works a ruler, a community or a private donor could build, and the inscriptions and texts of every religious tradition count them among the most meritorious of gifts. Water structures were also places of ritual: bathing in a sacred tank or river (tīrtha) purifies, temple tanks are the scene of festivals, and stepwells contain shrines. This chapter surveys the main types, from the Harappan reservoirs to the Mughal gardens (Agarwal and Narain 1997; Livingston 2002).

docs.title: 9.2 Early Reservoirs and Dams
docs.text:
Water management is visible in the earliest cities of South Asia. Mohenjo-daro had several hundred brick-lined wells, many of them inside houses, and an extensive network of covered street drains with soak pits; the Great Bath on the citadel mound, a watertight brick tank sealed with bitumen and reached by flights of steps, may have had a ritual purpose (Kenoyer 1998).

The Harappan city of Dholāvīrā in Kachchh, with its reservoirs, dams and channels, shows that rainwater harvesting on a large scale was practised in the 3rd millennium BCE (Chapter 8).

The best-documented early historic water work is the Sudarśana lake near Junāgaḍh in Gujarat, known from inscriptions on a rock that also bears the edicts of Aśoka. The Sanskrit inscription of the Western Kṣatrapa ruler Rudradāman (dated 150 CE) records that the lake was made under Candragupta Maurya by his provincial governor Puṣyagupta, provided with conduits under Aśoka by the governor Tuṣāspha, and repaired by Rudradāman after a storm breached the dam. A later inscription records a further repair in the reign of the Gupta emperor Skandagupta in the 450s. Together they give a unique record of the construction, maintenance and failure of an embankment dam over more than seven centuries.

In the 11th century the Paramāra king Bhoja is credited with the creation of a great lake near Bhopal by damming the Betwā; the huge unfinished temple at Bhojpur stands beside the remains of its dams.

docs.title: 9.3.1 Irrigation Tanks of the South
docs.text:
In the peninsula, where rivers are seasonal, the commonest water work is the irrigation tank (Tamil ēri, Kannada kere, Telugu ceruvu): an earthen embankment (Tamil karai) built across a shallow valley to hold back the monsoon run-off. A sluice (maḍai) releases water into channels (vāykkāl) that serve the fields below; a surplus weir (kalingal) lets excess water flow on, often into the next tank downstream, so that whole valleys are occupied by chains or cascades of tanks. Tamil Nadu alone has tens of thousands of tanks; many are known from inscriptions of the Pallava and Chola periods.

Some tanks are very large. The Vīranam tank (Vīranārāyaṇa ēri), on the northern edge of the Kāverī delta and fed from the Kollidam, attributed to the Chola period in the 10th century, has an embankment many kilometres long and still supplies water, now partly to the city of Chennai. In Karnataka, Andhra and Telangana, the Hoysaḷa, Kākatīya and Vijayanagara kings built great tanks, such as those at Ramappa and Pakhal in Telangana, which irrigated wide areas and were recorded in inscriptions as acts of royal merit.

Inscriptions show how tanks were built and maintained. The famous inscriptions of 919 and 921 CE at Uttaramērūr, a brāhmaṇa village (brahmadeya) near Kāñcīpuram, set out rules for choosing by lot the members of the village’s committees, including a tank committee (ēri vāriyam). They are often cited as evidence of early democracy. But eligibility was restricted to men of the village who owned land and a house and had Vedic learning: in effect to brāhmaṇa landholders. The work of maintenance was done by others. David Mosse’s study of tank irrigation in Tamil Nadu shows how the management of water was bound up with caste, kingship and temple honours, and how this changed under colonial rule (Mosse 2003).

docs.title: 9.3.2 Temple Tanks
docs.text: Most large South Indian temples have one or more tanks (puṣkariṇī, kalyāṇī, Tamil kuḷam), square or rectangular, with steps on all sides and often a pavilion in the middle. They are used for ritual bathing, for the water used in worship, and for festivals in which the deity is taken on a raft round the tank (teppam). Examples include the Tank of the Golden Lotus in the Mīnākṣī temple at Madurai, associated in Tamil legend with the assembly of poets, and the very large Teppakkuḷam at Madurai, about three hundred metres on each side, built in the 17th century. At Vijayanagara the royal centre contains a fine stepped tank built of dressed schist blocks, many marked with masons’ signs, which was excavated in the 1980s. In the North, tanks (kuṇḍa) were built at temples and pilgrimage places, such as the stepped tank of the Sun temple at Moḍherā (Chapter 5).

docs.title: 9.3.3 Tanks of the Sultanates
docs.text: The rulers of Delhi built reservoirs to supply their cities: the Ḥauẓ-i Shamsī of Iltutmish (c. 1230) at Mehrauli, and the Ḥauẓ-i ʿAlāʾī (Ḥauẓ Khāṣ) of ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī, on whose bank Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq built a madrasa in the 14th century. Fīrūz Shāh also cut or restored canals from the Yamunā and the Sutlej, the ancestors of the later Western Yamunā canal (Asher 1992).

docs.title: 9.3.4 Lakes and Reservoirs
docs.text: In central and western India, rulers created large artificial lakes by damming valleys. The Candella kings of Bundelkhand (10th–13th century) built many embanked tanks around their towns and fortresses, which still supply water and irrigation in a region of hard rock and unreliable rain. In Rajasthan, the lakes of Udaipur, among them the Pichola, enlarged in the 14th and 16th centuries, and the Fateh Sagar, together with the Gaḍīsar tank of Jaisalmer (14th century) and the lakes of Ajmer and Bundi, were central to the life and the architecture of their cities, lined with steps (ghāṭs), temples, pavilions and palaces. The great embankment of the Rāj Samand near Kankroli (17th century) carries a long series of carved marble pavilions and steps, with a long Sanskrit inscription. In the Deccan, the Quṭb Shāhī ruler Ibrāhīm Quli Quṭb Shāh built the Hussain Sāgar (1562), which later supplied the city of Hyderabad, founded in 1591. Many of these lakes are now threatened by silting, encroachment and pollution.

docs.title: 9.3.5 Water and Pilgrimage
docs.text: Many of the greatest gatherings of Indian religious life take place at water. The Kumbh Melā is held in rotation at four places on sacred rivers, Prayāgrāj (Allahabad), at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik, at intervals determined by astrological calculation, and draws millions of pilgrims to bathe at auspicious moments. Pilgrimage towns throughout India are organised around their tanks, ghāṭs and river fronts (Chapter 8), and the temporary cities built for such gatherings, with their roads, bridges, water supply and camps, are themselves remarkable feats of planning.

docs.title: 9.4.1 Form and Function
docs.text:
The stepwell (Gujarati vāv, Hindi bāolī or baoṛī) is a well that can be reached on foot by a long flight of steps, punctuated by landings and pavilions, descending to the water table. It is most characteristic of Gujarat and Rajasthan, where the water table falls sharply in the dry season and the steps allow access to water at any level. Stepwells were built by rulers, queens, nobles and merchants, Hindu, Jain and Muslim, as charitable works; many stood on trade routes and served travellers as well as local people. Their cool, shaded galleries were also places of rest and gathering, and many contain shrines of goddesses and of Viṣṇu (Jain-Neubauer 1981; Livingston 2002).

Texts of western India, such as the Rājavallabha of Maṇḍana, classify stepwells as nandā, bhadrā, jayā and vijayā according to the number of their entrances, from one to four. Most surviving examples consist of a long stepped corridor, roofed at intervals by pillared pavilions several storeys high, leading to a cylindrical well shaft at the far end (Figure 9.1).

Figure 9.1. Schematic longitudinal section of a stepwell: a stepped corridor, roofed at intervals by pillared pavilions, descends in stages to the water level and to a well shaft at the far end. The water level rises and falls with the seasons. Not to scale.

docs.title: 9.4.2 Rāṇī kī Vāv, Pāṭaṇ
docs.text:
The “Queen’s stepwell” at Pāṭaṇ, the Caulukya capital in Gujarat, was built in the later 11th century and is traditionally attributed to Queen Udayamatī in memory of her husband Bhīma I. It is the largest and most richly sculptured of the Gujarati stepwells: its stepped corridor (Figure 9.2, left) is over sixty metres long and descends some twenty-seven metres, in seven levels, to the well. Its walls carry hundreds of sculptures, chiefly of the incarnations of Viṣṇu, of goddesses and of celestial women. Long buried in silt, it was excavated and restored by the Archaeological Survey of India in the late 20th century and was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.

Figure 9.2. Two stepwells. Left: Rāṇī kī Vāv, Pāṭaṇ, Gujarat, later 11th century, looking down the stepped corridor, framed by storeys of pillared pavilions, towards the well. Right: the Chānd Baoṛī at Ābhāneri, Rajasthan, 8th or 9th century, with flights of steps in a zigzag pattern on three sides of the shaft and pavilions on the fourth. Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 9.4.3 Chānd Baoṛī, Ābhāneri
docs.text: The stepwell at Ābhāneri in Rajasthan, of the 8th or 9th century, is a deep square shaft with flights of steps on three sides arranged in a zigzag pattern (Figure 9.2, right) of extraordinary regularity, said to number some 3,500, descending about twenty metres in thirteen stages; the fourth side has pavilions. Local tradition credits it to a king named Cānd. It stands beside the ruined temple of Harṣat Mātā.

docs.title: 9.4.4 Stepwells of the Sultanate Period
docs.text: Stepwell building flourished under the sultans of Gujarat. The stepwell at Aḍālaj near Ahmadābād (1499), built according to its inscription by Queen Rūḍā, combines a Hindu and Jain sculptural vocabulary with Islamic geometric ornament; the Dāḍā Harir stepwell in Ahmadābād, of the same year, was built by a lady of the sultan’s household. In Delhi, the Rājon kī Bāolī at Mehrauli (early 16th century) and the Agrasen kī Bāolī are fine examples, and stepwells continued to be built in Mughal and Rajput territory into the 18th century.

docs.title: 9.4.5 Decline and Revival of Stepwells
docs.text: With the introduction of piped water and tube-wells in the 19th and 20th centuries, most stepwells fell out of use; many silted up, became dumps, or were filled in as hazards. Some, such as the Rāṇī kī Vāv, were rediscovered under silt and excavated. Since the 1990s, stepwells have attracted renewed interest from conservationists, photographers and architects, and several have been cleaned and restored, both as monuments and, in some places, as sources of water and points of groundwater recharge (Livingston 2002).

docs.title: 9.5.1 The Grand Anicut (Kallaṇai)
docs.text: The Kallaṇai (“stone dam”), known as the Grand Anicut, diverts the waters of the Kāverī at the head of its delta into channels serving the Thanjavur plain. Tamil tradition, based on later inscriptions and literature, attributes its construction to the early Chola king Karikāla, placed in about the 2nd century CE. The structure has been repaired and rebuilt many times, especially in the 19th century, when British engineers, including Arthur Cotton, studied it and drew on its example for their own works, such as the barrage on the Kollidam (1836). It is a diversion weir rather than a storage dam: a low, massive barrier of stone that raises the level of the river enough to divert its water. It is among the oldest water-diversion works in the world still in use, although little of the original fabric can now be identified.

docs.title: 9.5.2 Ghāṭs and River Architecture
docs.text: Along the great rivers, flights of stone steps (ghāṭ) give access to the water for bathing, washing, ritual and cremation. The ghāṭs of Vārāṇasī, built largely in the 18th and 19th centuries by Maratha, Rajput and other rulers and nobles, are the most famous (Chapter 8), but similar riverfronts line the Narmadā at Maheshwar, the Kṣiprā at Ujjain, the Godāvarī at Nashik and the Gaṅgā at Haridwar, with temples, palaces and memorials (chhatrīs) above them. The ghāṭs must withstand seasonal floods and the scouring of the current, and many have been rebuilt repeatedly.

docs.title: 9.5.3 Water at Vijayanagara
docs.text: The Vijayanagara capital (Chapter 8) depended on a system of dams (anicuts) across the Tuṅgabhadrā, canals cut along the contours, aqueducts carried on stone pillars, and storage tanks, together with large reservoirs outside the city that held back the run-off of the surrounding hills. Several of the canals built in the Vijayanagara period are still used for irrigation. Within the royal centre, stone channels and aqueducts carried water to the palace enclosures, the stepped tanks and the bath known as the “Queen’s bath” (Fritz and Michell 1991).

docs.title: 9.5.4 Community Systems
docs.text:
Many forms of water harvesting were developed and managed by local communities, adapted to very different environments (Agarwal and Narain 1997) (Table 9.1):

Table 9.1. Some traditional water-harvesting systems of India System Region Form ēri / kere Tamil Nadu, Karnataka Irrigation tanks, often in cascades vāv / bāolī Gujarat, Rajasthan Stepwells giving access to groundwater kuṇḍ, ṭāṅkā Western Rajasthan Covered cisterns collecting rainwater from a prepared catchment johaḍ Rajasthan Earthen embankments holding run-off and recharging groundwater āhar–pyne South Bihar Embanked catchment basins fed by channels phaḍ Maharashtra (Tapi basin) Community-managed diversion of river water kuhl Himachal Pradesh Gravity-flow channels from mountain streams surangam Northern Kerala, Karnataka Horizontal tunnels driven into laterite hillsides to tap groundwater zabo Nagaland Combined system of forest, ponds, cattle-yards and terraced fields

Many of these systems declined under colonial and post-colonial water policies, which favoured large canals, dams and tube-wells. Since the 1980s, organisations such as the Centre for Science and Environment and many local groups have documented and revived them; in Alwar district of Rajasthan, for example, the revival of johaḍs by the Tarun Bharat Sangh is credited with restoring the seasonal flow of small rivers.

docs.title: 9.5.5 Lifting Water
docs.text: Water was lifted from wells by rope and bucket, by the counterpoised lever (ḍhenklī), by bullock-drawn leather bags (mhoṭ, charsā) and by pot-wheels (Sanskrit araghaṭṭa, ghaṭīyantra), on which pots tied to a rope or wheel are raised by a wheel turned by animals. The geared pot-wheel known as the “Persian wheel” became widespread in the Sultanate and Mughal periods.

docs.title: 9.6 Finding Water: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā
docs.text:
Chapter 54 of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā, called dakārgala (“water-bar”), explains how to find underground water (Bhat 1981). Its premise is that water runs beneath the earth in veins, like the veins of the body. It lists signs of water: particular trees and shrubs growing in dry places, termite mounds near certain trees, the colour and texture of soil and rocks, frogs, fish and other animals, and steam rising from the ground. For each sign it states the direction and distance from the indicator at which to dig, the depth, measured in puruṣas (the height of a man with arms raised), and the kind of water and rock to be met. The chapter also describes how to break hard rock and how to purify water.

Some of these signs reflect real relationships: deep-rooted trees in dry country often do indicate groundwater, and termite mounds need moisture. Others are omens. The chapter is an interesting record of empirical observation mixed with traditional lore, but the precise depths it gives are not reliable guides, and there are no published systematic tests that confirm them.

docs.title: 9.7 Gardens and Water
docs.text:
Sanskrit literature describes royal pleasure gardens with pools, fountains and water-machines (yantra), and Bhoja’s Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra, in its chapter on machines, describes water devices, including a pavilion with showers of water (dhārāgṛha). Few early gardens survive. The great surviving gardens of South Asia are those of the Mughals and their contemporaries (Ruggles 2008). The chahār bāgh (“four gardens”), a walled garden divided into four by raised walkways and water channels, came to India from Iran and Central Asia with Bābur, who complained in his memoirs about the lack of running water in Hindustan. The Mughals used it for palace gardens and for tombs, such as Humāyūn’s tomb and the Tāj Mahal (Chapter 6). In Kashmir, the Mughal emperors and nobles built terraced gardens on the slopes above the Dal lake, in which water flows down from terrace to terrace over carved cascades (chādar) and through rows of fountains, past pavilions placed across the central channel. The Shālīmār Bāgh was laid out by Jahāngīr in about 1619 and extended by Shāh Jahān; the Nishāt Bāgh, with twelve terraces descending to the lake, was built by Āṣaf Khān, Nūr Jahān’s brother, in the 1630s; and at Vernāg and Achabal, gardens were built around great natural springs, the source of the Jhelum at Vernāg being enclosed in an octagonal tank with arcades. Jahāngīr’s memoirs record his delight in these places. At Agra, Ebba Koch has reconstructed a whole riverfront of gardens along the Yamunā, of which the Tāj Mahal was one (Koch 2006). Rajput palaces, such as those of Amber, Udaipur and Deeg, adopted and adapted these gardens and their fountains (Figure 9.3).

Figure 9.3. Schematic plan of a Mughal chahār bāgh: a walled garden divided into four quarters by raised walkways with water channels, each quarter subdivided again, with a pavilion or tomb at the centre (as at Humāyūn’s tomb) and gateways on the axes. At the Tāj Mahal the tomb stands instead at the far end of the garden, on the river. Not to scale.

docs.title: 9.8 Baths
docs.text: Bathing was a ritual as well as a practical act, and Indian architecture provided for it in many forms: the bathing platforms of Harappan houses, the steps of tanks and ghāṭs, the bathing pavilions of palaces and the “Queen’s bath” at Vijayanagara. The Sultanates and Mughals introduced the ḥammām, the steam bath of the Islamic world, with a sequence of rooms for undressing, warm and hot bathing, heated by furnaces beneath the floor and supplied by water channels; fine examples survive in the Red Fort at Delhi, at Fatehpur Sīkrī, in the Agra Fort and in the palaces of the Deccan and Rajasthan. Inscriptions and texts also record the building of public baths and drinking-water pavilions (prapā, Persian sabīl) as acts of charity.

docs.title: 9.9 Summary
docs.text: Indian water architecture ranges from village tanks to monumental stepwells and imperial gardens. It was the work of rulers, temples, merchants and communities, Hindu, Jain, Buddhist and Muslim. Its best-known monuments are works of art of the first rank; its humbler structures sustained agriculture for centuries. Both deserve study, and the revival of traditional water harvesting is one area in which historical knowledge has had real practical value. That value is best served by an honest account of how these systems worked, including the social hierarchies within which they were managed, rather than by idealising them.

docs.text:

docs.title: Chapter 10: The House: Residential Vāstu and Vernacular Architecture
10.1 The House in the Texts
docs.text: For the authors of the Sanskrit texts, the house (gṛha, veśman, śālā) was the setting of the householder’s religious life: the place of the domestic fire, of the daily offerings, of the rites of passage from birth to death, and of hospitality. The domestic ritual manuals of the Vedic schools, the Gṛhyasūtras, already describe rites for choosing a site, building a house and entering it; the Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra (3.4), for example, gives the procedure for building a house and for its first occupation. The vāstu texts develop these into a full doctrine of the dwelling: how to choose and test the site (Chapter 2), lay it out on the grid, dimension it, assign its rooms, raise its door and main post, and consecrate it.

docs.title: 10.1.1 Houses by Rank and Caste
docs.text: The texts do not describe a single ideal house but a hierarchy of houses. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā (ch. 53) gives the dimensions of houses for a king, a crown prince, a commander, ministers and others, and then for brāhmaṇas, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas and śūdras, the size diminishing at each step (Bhat 1981). The Mayamata and Mānasāra likewise prescribe the number of storeys, the forms of roof and the ornaments appropriate to each rank and caste (Dagens 1994). Such rules were not merely theoretical. In several regions, caste customs and, in some cases, the orders of rulers restricted the kinds of house that low-ranking castes could build: in Kerala, for example, customary rules long reserved certain house forms and features, such as gatehouses and tiled roofs, for high-caste households. How these rules shaped the village as well as the house is discussed below (Section 10.3).

docs.title: 10.1.2 House Types
docs.text: The southern texts classify houses by the number of ranges (śālā) of rooms built round a central court: houses of one range (ekaśālā), two (dviśālā), three (triśālā) and four (catuḥśālā), with many named variants of each, and larger houses with several courts and storeys (Dagens 1994; Acharya 1934). The four-range house enclosing a courtyard is the type most fully described, and it corresponds to real houses in many regions.

docs.title: 10.1.3 Assigning the Rooms
docs.text:
The texts assign rooms and activities to parts of the grid, but they do not agree with each other, and the assignments differ from region to region. Common prescriptions include placing the domestic shrine or the store of grain in favoured positions, keeping the centre of the house open as a court, and placing the kitchen and the fire in a direction associated with Agni or in some other position prescribed by local custom. The plan in Figure 10.1 shows the scheme now most often recommended in popular books on vāstu. It is not found in this form in any classical text; it is a modern synthesis, drawing on the guardians of the directions and on the modern scheme of the five elements described in Chapter 2.

Figure 10.1. The arrangement of rooms most often recommended in modern popular books on vāstu (north at the top). This scheme is a modern synthesis; the classical texts give varying and often different assignments, and regional traditions differ again.

docs.title: 10.1.4 The Door
docs.text: The texts give great importance to the main door. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā predicts the fortunes of the household from the square of the grid in which the door is placed (Chapter 2); the texts also regulate its proportions, its height in relation to the house, the wood of which it is made, and the rite performed when the door-frame is raised. Doors should not be “pierced” by a tree, post or corner directly in front of them, and doors on the same axis should be aligned. In temples, door-frames were carved with several bands (śākhā) of ornament, with the river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā at the base and guardian figures, and an image of Lakṣmī or of the temple’s deity at the centre of the lintel; houses of the wealthy adopted simpler versions of these doorways.

docs.title: 10.1.5 Rites of the House
docs.text: The building of a house was punctuated by rites, as described for temples in Chapter 4: offerings to the vāstupuruṣa, the laying of the first stone or brick, the raising of the main post and the door, and finally the entry into the house (gṛhapraveśa) at an astrologically chosen moment, with a rite of pacification of the site (vāstuśānti). Customs associated with the entry vary by region and community and include the entry of a cow, the boiling over of milk on the new hearth, and the feeding of guests. These rites remain widely observed today.

docs.title: 10.2 Houses of the Past
docs.text: Archaeology shows something of how ordinary people lived before the texts were written. In the Harappan cities, houses of baked brick were built round courtyards, entered from side lanes rather than main streets, with rooms for bathing and, in many cases, a private well and a latrine draining into the street drains; staircases show that many had upper storeys or flat roofs used as living space. In the early historic cities of the Gaṅgā valley, houses of mud brick and baked brick with tiled roofs, ring-wells and soak-pits have been excavated, and the reliefs of Bhārhut, Sāñcī and Amarāvatī show houses and palaces of several storeys with barrel-vaulted roofs, balconies and railings, built largely of timber. The paintings of Ajaṇṭā show palaces with pavilions and courts. These images and remains suggest that the courtyard house, the verandah and the upper-storey balcony have a very long history in South Asia.

docs.title: 10.3 Caste and the Layout of the Village
docs.text: The vāstu texts and the Arthaśāstra assign soils, house sizes and the quarters of a settlement according to varṇa, and place those regarded as impure at its edges (Chapters 1, 2 and 8). These prescriptions had their counterpart in the actual layout of many villages. In much of South India, the main village (Tamil ūr) was occupied by landowning castes, while the hamlets of Dalit communities (the cēri) stood apart, often on lower or poorer land, with their own wells and shrines; in the villages of the North, too, the houses of the lowest castes were commonly placed on the edges. Access to wells, tanks, temple streets and cremation grounds was restricted. These spatial arrangements were enforced by custom and sometimes by violence, and they have proved remarkably persistent. A survey of 565 villages in eleven states, published in 2006, found that the denial of equal access to water sources, temples and other shared spaces persisted in a large proportion of them, and that in many villages Dalit households still lived in separate quarters (Shah et al. 2006). The struggles of the 19th and 20th centuries for the right to use public roads, wells and tanks, such as B. R. Ambedkar’s Mahad Satyagraha of 1927 for access to a public tank, were also struggles over the use of space. Any account of Indian domestic and village architecture that celebrates its harmony with nature should also recognise this aspect of its history.

docs.title: 10.4 Women and the House
docs.text: The house was also the domain of women’s knowledge and art. In many regions women decorate thresholds, courtyards and walls with drawings made of rice flour, chalk, coloured powders or clay: kōlam in Tamil Nadu, raṅgolī in Maharashtra and Gujarat, ālpanā in Bengal, māṇḍaṇā in Rajasthan, aripan in Mithila. Drawn afresh each morning or at festivals, these designs mark the threshold between the house and the street and are associated with auspiciousness and welcome. Women also plastered and re-plastered floors and walls with clay and cow-dung, built and maintained hearths and storage bins, and painted walls for weddings and festivals; the Mithilā paintings now sold on paper grew from this domestic tradition (Chapter 14). In many households, and especially among elite families of the Mughal and Rajput courts and of high castes elsewhere, the house was divided into men’s and women’s quarters, with the women’s quarters (zanāna, antaḥpura) secluded from visitors, and screens, inner courts and roof terraces gave women space and light while limiting their visibility. The architecture of the house thus reflected and reproduced the gender norms of its society.

docs.title: 10.5 Vernacular Architecture
docs.text:
Most Indian houses were never built by architects who knew the texts. They were built by their owners and by local masons and carpenters, in local materials, using forms refined over generations to suit climate, available resources, family structure and social custom. This vernacular architecture is as much a part of the Indian building tradition as the temples and palaces (Oliver 1997; Cooper and Dawson 1998). See Table 10.1.

Table 10.1. Some regional house types of South Asia Region Type Principal features Kerala nālukeṭṭu Four ranges round a small court; timber frame on laterite base; steep tiled roofs with wide eaves Tamil Nadu agrahāram house; Chettinad house Row houses with raised front verandah (tiṇṇai) and inner courts; very large merchant houses with sequences of courts Rajasthan, Gujarat havelī; pol house Inward-looking courtyard houses of stone or brick and timber; carved façades, balconies (jharokhā) and screens (jālī) Kachchh bhuṅgā Circular houses of mud and wattle with conical thatched roofs Maharashtra wāḍā Courtyard mansions with high outer walls and timber interiors Bengal bāṅglā hut Mud or bamboo walls with curved thatched roofs of two or more slopes (do-cālā, āṭ-cālā) North-east stilt houses Bamboo and timber houses raised on posts, with steep thatched roofs Kashmir dhajjī dīwārī, tāq Timber-laced masonry, with walls of brick or stone set in timber frames Ladakh Thick mud-brick walls, flat earth roofs, small openings, south-facing living rooms Goa Laterite houses with lime-plastered façades, raised entrance verandahs (balcão) and windows glazed with flat oyster shells

docs.title: 10.5.1 The Kerala Nālukeṭṭu
docs.text:
The nālukeṭṭu (“four blocks”) of Kerala is the regional form of the four-range courtyard house, built for the joint households of landowning families. Four ranges, named after their directions (vaṭakkini, north; kiḻakkini, east; tekkini, south; paṭiññāṟṟini, west), enclose a small open court (naṭumuṟṟam) which admits light and rain (Figure 10.2); larger houses have two or four courts. The house stands on a raised laterite base, has a timber frame and walls of laterite, timber or mud, and is covered by steep, wide-eaved roofs of tiles over a timber structure, designed to shed the heavy monsoon rains and shade the walls. A gatehouse (paṭippura) marks the entrance to the compound, which usually contains a tank or well, a family shrine and groves. The Sanskrit Manuṣyālayacandrikā (16th century) and the living tradition of Kerala carpenters (taccan) regulate its dimensions and joinery.

Figure 10.2. Schematic plan of a Kerala nālukeṭṭu: four ranges of rooms, named after their directions, round a small open court with a surrounding verandah. The use of each range, and the position of the kitchen and the household shrine, varied with region and community. Not to scale.

docs.title: 10.5.2 The Havelī
docs.text: In Rajasthan and Gujarat, and in the old cities of north India, merchants and nobles lived in havelīs: courtyard houses of two to five storeys, often with an outer court for men and visitors and an inner court for the women of the household. The thick walls, small and screened windows, shaded courts and roof terraces respond to the hot, dry climate. The havelīs of Jaisalmer, carved in yellow sandstone, are famous: the Paṭvoṃ kī Havelī, a group of five houses begun in the early 19th century by a merchant family, and the Nathmal kī Havelī (1885), whose façade is said to have been carved by two brothers working on its two halves. In the Shekhawati region the havelīs built by Marwari merchants in the 19th and early 20th centuries are covered with wall paintings that show deities, legends, and novelties of the time such as railway trains and motor cars.

docs.title: 10.5.3 Town Houses of North India
docs.text: In the old cities of north India, such as Delhi, Lucknow, Agra, Varanasi and Ahmadābād, the houses of merchants, officials and nobles were inward-looking courtyard houses, often of several storeys, entered through a single doorway from a narrow lane. Larger mansions had a men’s court for receiving visitors and a separate court for the women of the household (Section 10.4), with roof terraces used for sleeping in the hot season, and basements (tahkhāna) for coolness. Facades were decorated with carved stone or timber balconies, brackets and screens. Many such houses in Old Delhi and other cities have been subdivided, rebuilt or demolished in recent decades, and their conservation is a pressing problem.

docs.title: 10.5.4 The Chettinad House
docs.text: In the Chettinad region of Tamil Nadu, the Nāṭṭukkōṭṭai Cheṭṭiyār bankers and merchants, whose business extended across Burma, Malaya and Ceylon, built very large houses in their home villages in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. A typical house has a raised front verandah (tiṇṇai), a sequence of pillared courts (vaḷavu) surrounded by rooms, and kitchens and service courts at the rear. The houses combine local materials and craftsmanship, including locally made floor tiles and polished lime plaster, with Burmese teak, European glass, tiles and cast iron.

docs.title: 10.5.5 The Wāḍā
docs.text: The wāḍā of Maharashtra is a courtyard house, sometimes fortified, of the Maratha period. The Shaniwār Wāḍā in Pune (built 1730–32), the seat of the Peshwās, was the grandest; it was largely destroyed by fire in 1828, and only its fortified walls and gateways survive. Smaller wāḍās in Pune, Nashik and other towns preserve fine timber courts and carved brackets.

docs.title: 10.5.6 The Houses of Goa
docs.text: Four and a half centuries of Portuguese rule produced in Goa a distinctive house that combines the local courtyard plan with European façades. The large houses built by Catholic and Hindu landowning families, mostly in the 18th and 19th centuries, have thick walls of laterite set in lime mortar and plastered and painted in strong colours, steep roofs of clay tiles on timber frames, and raised plinths reached by flights of steps. Their street fronts are symmetrical, with pilasters, mouldings and tall windows, and the entrance is often through a balcão, a covered porch with built-in seats where the family received visitors and watched the street. Windows were traditionally glazed with thin, translucent squares of the polished windowpane-oyster shell set in wooden lattices, which admit a soft light and keep out the glare. Behind the formal rooms of the front, the reception hall, the chapel or shrine and, in the grandest houses, a ballroom, the house is organised round one or more courtyards, with the kitchen, stores and service rooms at the back, as in houses elsewhere on the west coast. The Goan house shows how a colonial society built in a local material and climate, and how forms from Europe were absorbed into an Indian plan rather than replacing it. Many such houses are now threatened by division among heirs, emigration and the cost of upkeep.

docs.title: 10.5.7 Mountain, Forest and Pastoral Houses
docs.text: Some of the most remarkable vernacular buildings of India belong to communities that lived far from the cities. The Todas, pastoralists of the Nilgiri hills, built barrel-vaulted huts of cane and thatch with a tiny low entrance, and conical dairy-temples of similar materials. In Ladakh, houses of two or three storeys are built of sun-dried brick and stone with flat roofs of earth on poplar beams; the ground floor shelters animals and stores, the family lives above, and the living rooms face south to catch the sun in a cold desert climate. In the North-east, Naga, Khasi, Mizo, Adi and other communities build houses of timber and bamboo, often raised on stilts, with steep thatched roofs; the great communal houses of the Naga villages, with their carved posts, were centres of village life. In the Himalaya of Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand, houses and temples of stone and timber, with slate roofs and carved wooden balconies, use the timber-lacing techniques described below.

docs.title: 10.5.8 Bamboo and Timber in the North-east
docs.text:
The North-east, with its heavy rainfall, frequent floods and earthquakes, and abundance of bamboo, cane, timber and thatch, has building traditions unlike those of the rest of India. The social institutions housed in these buildings, such as the young men’s houses of the Naga villages, are discussed in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti; here the concern is with how they were built.

Bamboo is used in almost every part of the house. Whole culms serve as posts, beams and rafters; split bamboo is flattened into boards for floors and walls or woven into mats and screens; and the parts are joined not with nails but by lashing with strips of cane or bamboo, by notches and by pegs. Roofs are steep, to shed the rain, and covered with thatch grass or with the leaves of palms such as the tokou palm of Assam. Many houses stand on posts above the ground, which keeps the floor dry and clear of floodwater, insects and animals, ventilates it from below and gives sheltered space beneath for livestock, looms and firewood. The Miśiṅ communities of the Brahmaputra floodplain build long houses of this kind (cāṅ ghar) raised well above the level of the annual floods; in the hills, houses are often built against the slope, with the front on posts and the back on the ground. A hearth near the centre of the main room, with a rack above it for drying and storing grain, meat and firewood, is the focus of domestic life in many hill communities, and its smoke helps to protect the bamboo and thatch above it from insects and decay.

In the plains of Assam, the characteristic house of the colonial and modern periods, the so-called Assam-type house, has a frame of timber posts and beams, walls of ekarā (split bamboo or reed lath plastered with mud or lime on both sides) set between the posts, and a light roof, first of thatch and later of corrugated iron. Its light walls and flexible frame are well suited to a region of strong earthquakes, and it is said to have been widely adopted after the great earthquake of 1897, which destroyed many masonry buildings in Shillong and the Assam valley. Such buildings need regular maintenance: bamboo and thatch decay and are attacked by insects, and roofs must be renewed every few years. Over the last half century concrete, brick and corrugated iron have replaced bamboo in many places, but architects and engineers have also begun to treat bamboo as a modern structural material, preserving it chemically and joining it with bolts and steel connectors.

docs.title: 10.5.9 The Bungalow
docs.text: The word “bungalow” comes from the Bengali bāṅglā, the thatched hut with a curved roof. In the 17th and 18th centuries Europeans in Bengal adopted the form of a single-storey house with a verandah on all sides, and the colonial bungalow, set in its own compound, became the standard residence of officials and planters throughout British India and, later, a type of house found around the world. Anthony King has traced this history (King 1984), which shows how a vernacular Indian form was transformed by colonial needs and returned to India as a symbol of modern, suburban living.

docs.title: 10.5.10 Building with Earth, Bamboo and Timber
docs.text:
Much of India’s vernacular architecture is built of earth, in the form of rammed earth, cob, sun-dried brick or wattle and daub, with roofs of thatch, tiles or earth on timber. Bamboo is the principal material of the North-east and of parts of Bengal and the Western Ghats. In earthquake-prone Kashmir and the Himalaya, masonry walls are laced with horizontal timbers or built within timber frames (tāq and dhajjī dīwārī). Randolph Langenbach, who studied these buildings after the Kashmir earthquake of 2005, found that they had often survived better than unreinforced masonry and many concrete-framed buildings, because the timber holds the masonry together and the many joints absorb the energy of the shaking (Langenbach 2007). The circular bhuṅgās of Kachchh have likewise been reported to have withstood the earthquake of 2001 comparatively well, although these reports rest mainly on observations made during relief and rebuilding rather than on systematic engineering surveys. None of this means that any traditional building is “earthquake-proof”; performance depends on the quality of construction and maintenance.

Lime was the most important binding and plastering material of historic Indian masonry. Builders prepared it by burning limestone or shells, slaking the quicklime and mixing it with sand, brick dust and, in many regional recipes, organic additives such as jaggery, the fruit of the myrobalan (Tamil kaḍukkāy) or plant extracts, which modify its setting and water resistance. Polished lime plasters, such as Rajasthani ārāish, achieve a marble-like finish. Lime mortars and plasters have good durability and are compatible with historic masonry, which is why conservation architects use them in repairs; but claims that traditional lime mortars generally match the strength of modern cement are not supported by systematic testing.

docs.title: 10.5.11 Roofs
docs.text: Roofs are among the most regionally distinctive elements of Indian houses. Thatch of grass, palm leaf or straw, laid on bamboo or timber frames, covered most village houses until the 20th century and is still widespread; it is light, cool and cheap but must be renewed frequently. Clay tiles, either half-round “country” tiles or, from the later 19th century, the interlocking “Mangalore” tiles first made by the Basel Mission at Mangalore, cover pitched roofs in the wetter regions. Flat roofs of earth on timber, or of lime concrete on stone slabs, prevail in the dry north-west and in the Deccan, and serve as terraces for sleeping and drying grain. Slate and stone slabs are used in the Himalaya. The shape and material of the roof largely determine the outline of a village, and their replacement by corrugated iron and reinforced concrete has transformed the Indian landscape in the last century.

docs.title: 10.6 Furniture and the Use of Space
docs.text: The vāstu texts include furniture among the kinds of vāstu, and the Mayamata and Mānasāra give rules for the proportions of beds, couches, seats and thrones (Chapter 2). Yet traditional Indian houses contained little furniture by modern standards. People sat on the floor, on mats, carpets and low stools; ate from leaves or plates set on the floor; and slept on mats, mattresses or the light rope-strung bed (cārpāī, khaṭiyā), which could be carried outside to the courtyard or the roof in the hot season. Wall niches, shelves, chests and storage jars held possessions; swings (Tamil ūñcal, Hindi jhūlā) hung in verandahs and halls. Rooms were therefore flexible, used for different purposes at different times of day and year, and the courtyard and roof were as important as the rooms. European furniture spread with colonial rule, first in elite houses, and has changed the use of domestic space profoundly.

docs.title: 10.7 Climate and the Traditional House
docs.text:
Many features of traditional Indian houses respond intelligently to climate: courtyards that bring light and air into deep plans and act as reservoirs of cool night air; verandahs, deep eaves and screens that shade walls and openings; thick walls of earth or stone that even out the swing of temperature between day and night in dry regions; light, raised, well-ventilated structures in hot humid regions; and roof terraces for sleeping in the hot season. These features vary with climate: houses in Kerala and in Rajasthan are designed in almost opposite ways. They can be analysed, and used in new buildings, with the methods of building science (Krishan et al. 2001). Several 20th-century Indian architects drew on these lessons in their own work, among them Laurie Baker in Kerala, Charles Correa and B. V. Doshi, whose work, including Doshi’s self-built housing at Aranya, is described in Chapter 7 (Section 7.3).

Traditional knowledge has also been drawn on in rebuilding after disasters. After the Kachchh earthquake of 2001, organisations such as the Hunnarshala Foundation at Bhuj worked with local masons, carpenters and village communities to rebuild houses using improved versions of local techniques, including the circular bhuṅgā and stabilised earth, combined with modern earthquake-resistant features such as ring beams; similar approaches have been tried in the Himalaya. Such projects show that the lessons of vernacular architecture are best applied critically, adapting traditional forms to modern needs and safety standards rather than copying them.

These climatic advantages belong to particular regional forms; they do not depend on following a vāstu scheme of directions. A house built to the popular vāstu plan in Kerala and one built to the same plan in Rajasthan would not be equally well adapted to their climates.

docs.title: 10.8 Vāstu and the Modern House
docs.text: It is in house-building that modern popular vāstu is most visible: builders advertise “vāstu-compliant” apartments, and consultants advise on plots, rooms and furniture. The claims on which this advice rests, and their relation to the classical texts, are examined in Chapter 2 (Section 2.15 and Table 2.3). For the house, the practical point is that where vāstu advice coincides with good design, as in admitting winter sun, excluding the low western sun, providing cross-ventilation and avoiding poorly drained sites, the benefits come from the design principles themselves, which can be justified directly; and that buyers should not be persuaded to demolish sound structures or spend large sums on the strength of claims that have no evidential basis.

docs.title: 10.9 Two Kinds of Knowledge
docs.text: The house is where the two kinds of knowledge discussed in this volume are furthest apart. The classical texts describe a hierarchy of houses, laid out on the grid, dimensioned by astrological calculation, consecrated by ritual and assigned according to rank and caste; the same plan, in principle, served from the Himalaya to the far south. The vernacular houses of India’s regions show a knowledge of a different kind, practical, local and closely adapted to climate, materials and family life, so that the house of Kerala and the house of Rajasthan answer their climates in almost opposite ways. The best of modern Indian architecture, and the best of disaster rebuilding, has drawn on the second kind of knowledge rather than the first.
