docs.title: Chapter 11: Śilpaśāstra: The Making of Images
11.1 Śilpa and the Śilpin
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word śilpa means a craft, an art, or a work of skill, and the śilpin is the person who practises it: the carpenter, the mason, the smith, the sculptor, the painter, the weaver. Lists of the arts in Sanskrit literature, such as the sixty-four kalās enumerated in the Kāmasūtra (1.3), include painting, modelling and carpentry alongside music, dance and many other accomplishments. Śilpaśāstra, the “science of the crafts”, is a modern umbrella term for the texts that deal with these skills; in practice it usually refers to the texts on architecture and, above all, on the making of images.

The texts on image-making (pratimālakṣaṇa, “the characteristics of images”) are found in the same works that deal with architecture: chapter 58 of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā, the later chapters of the Mayamata and Mānasāra, the āgamas, the Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa (book 3), the Matsya and Agni Purāṇas, the Aparājitapṛcchā, Maṇḍana’s Rūpamaṇḍana (15th century) and the Kerala Śilparatna (Bhat 1981; Dagens 1994; Acharya 1934). Buddhist iconometric texts, such as the Pratimāmānalakṣaṇa, and the Citralakṣaṇa attributed to Nagnajit, survive mainly in Tibetan translation, and were used by the image-makers of Tibet and Nepal. The Jain author Ṭhakkura Pherū, an official at the court of the Delhi sultan ʿAlāʾ al-Dīn Khaljī, wrote a work on architecture and images in Prakrit, the Vatthusāra (Vāstusāra), in the early 14th century.

These texts tell the image-maker what to make: the proportions of an image, its posture, gestures, attributes, ornaments and attendants. They say rather less about how to make it, which was learned in the workshop. The modern standard surveys of their iconographic content are T. A. Gopinatha Rao’s Elements of Hindu Iconography and J. N. Banerjea’s Development of Hindu Iconography (Gopinatha Rao 1914; Banerjea 1956).

docs.title: 11.2 The Image and Its Meaning
docs.text:
In the Brahmanical, Jain and Buddhist traditions alike, images are made to be worshipped, and the texts treat their making as a religious act. The image-maker is told to purify himself and to visualise the deity, often with the help of a descriptive verse (dhyānaśloka), before he begins; the material is chosen and brought from the quarry or the forest with ritual; and the finished image is consecrated before it is worshipped (below). The rules of proportion and iconography were meant to ensure that the image was a fit dwelling for the deity, and in the temple traditions an image that was broken or defective was replaced.

At the same time, Indian images were works of art, made by trained craftsmen for patrons who valued beauty and skill, and their styles changed constantly with region and period. Richard Davis has shown how individual images acquired “lives” of their own as they were made, consecrated, worshipped, captured as trophies, lost, rediscovered and displayed in museums (Davis 1997). Diana Eck’s account of darśan, the reciprocal “seeing” between deity and devotee, explains why images are made with large, open eyes and placed so as to be seen (Eck 1981).

docs.title: 11.3.1 The Image’s Own Measure
docs.text: Images are proportioned not in absolute units but in units relative to the image itself. The height of the face, from hairline to chin, is one tāla (literally “palm”); it is divided into twelve aṅgulas, and the aṅgula into eight yavas. Because these units are derived from the image (dehalabdhāṅgula, “finger obtained from the body”), the same set of proportions can be used for an image of any size. The texts also describe ways of fixing the size of an image in relation to the sanctum and the doorway of the temple in which it is to be placed, or to the height of the donor.

docs.title: 11.3.2 Classes of Proportion
docs.text:
The texts give different proportional canons for different classes of being, named by the number of tālas in the total height. In broad terms, and with variation between texts, the great gods are made in ten tālas (daśatāla), with “highest”, “middle” and “lowest” variants; goddesses and many lesser deities in nine or eight; human beings in eight or seven; and dwarfish or child-like beings, such as the gaṇas who attend Śiva, in five or fewer (Gopinatha Rao 1914; Ganapati Sthapati 2002). Gaṇeśa is commonly given squat proportions. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā and the Viṣṇudharmottara also classify human figures into five types named after auspicious creatures (haṃsa, bhadra, mālavya, rucaka and śaśa), each with its own proportions (Table 11.1 and Figure 11.1).

Figure 11.1. The classes of proportion (tāla) of the image-making texts, drawn to a common face-length. The height of each class is a whole number of face-lengths, and the face-length is divided into twelve aṅgulas of the image’s own measure, so that the same rules serve for an image of any size. The bars show nominal heights only: the texts adjust the totals within each class (for example into “highest”, “middle” and “lowest” daśatāla) and distribute the face-lengths over the parts of the body in different ways, and the assignment of classes to kinds of being varies between texts. Table 11.1. Classes of proportion in the image-making texts (simplified; the assignments vary between texts) Canon Tālas in height Typical use daśatāla (uttama, madhyama, adhama) 10 The principal gods (Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā), Buddhas and Jinas navatāla 9 Goddesses and many lesser deities aṣṭatāla 8 Human beings, sages, attendant figures saptatāla 7 Human beings in some texts pañcatāla and smaller 5 or fewer Dwarfish attendants, gaṇas, child forms

Within each canon the texts give the measurements of every part of the body, from the length of the face and the height of the neck to the width of the fingers, in aṅgulas and yavas. A sculptor laying out an image marks these measurements on the block with a cord and a measuring rod, using vertical and horizontal guide lines (sūtra); the central vertical line (brahmasūtra) and the plumb-lines on either side govern the pose. Ganapati Sthapati’s manual, written from within the living Tamil tradition, shows how these measurements are applied in practice (Ganapati Sthapati 2002).

docs.title: 11.3.3 Proportion and Style
docs.text: The canons did not produce uniform images. Mathurā, Gupta, Pāla, Chola and Hoysaḷa images, all made in the same broad tradition, differ greatly in their proportions and in the way the body is modelled (Chapter 13). The canons were applied flexibly and adapted to local taste; they fixed the relations of the principal parts and left much to the sculptor’s judgment.

docs.title: 11.4.1 Choosing the Stone
docs.text:
The texts describe how to choose stone for images: it should be of uniform colour and texture, free of cracks, veins and spots, and should “ring” when struck. Many texts assign stones to sexes (“male”, “female” and “neuter” stones, distinguished by sound and texture) and prescribe male stone for male deities and female stone for goddesses; the neuter stone is used for pedestals. The stone is ritually selected and transported. In practice the choice of stone was determined by what was available locally (Table 11.2).

Table 11.2. Some stones used for Indian sculpture Stone Region Examples Spotted red sandstone Mathurā Kuṣāṇa and Gupta sculpture of Mathurā Buff (Chunār) sandstone Sārnāth, Gaṅgā valley Mauryan pillars; Gupta Buddhas of Sārnāth Grey schist Gandhāra Gandhāran Buddhist sculpture Limestone (“Palnad marble”) Andhra Amarāvatī and Nāgārjunakoṇḍa reliefs Basalt Western Deccan Elephanta, Ellora Granite Tamil Nadu Pallava and Chola stone images Chloritic schist Karnataka Later Cālukya and Hoysaḷa sculpture Dark phyllite or schist (often called “black basalt”) Bihar, Bengal Pāla sculpture Marble Rajasthan, Gujarat Jain images and temple carving

docs.title: 11.4.2 From Block to Image
docs.text: The stages of work can be reconstructed from unfinished images and from present-day practice. The block is squared and the guide lines and principal measurements are drawn on it. The figure is then roughed out with heavy chisels, working round the block so that the masses of the body are established before details are cut; then the forms are refined with lighter chisels and points, the details of ornament and hair are cut, and the surface is rubbed and polished with abrasives. The eyes are usually finished last, and in many traditions the final opening of the eyes is a ritual act performed during the consecration. The principal tools are iron chisels of various shapes, mallets and hammers, points, drills and abrasive stones, with the cord, plumb-line, measuring rod and compass for setting out.

docs.title: 11.5.1 The Lost-Wax Process
docs.text:
Most Indian metal images were made by the lost-wax process (madhūcchiṣṭavidhāna, “the method with beeswax”), which is described in the Mānasāra and in other texts and is still practised (Acharya 1934). In the solid-casting method used in South India (Figure 11.2):

  1. The image is modelled in a mixture of beeswax and resin, with all its details.

  2. Wax rods are attached to serve as channels for the molten metal and vents for air.

  3. The wax model is covered with several coats of fine clay, the first of which takes the impression of the details, and then with coarser clay, to form a mould.

  4. The mould is heated and the wax runs out, leaving a cavity in the shape of the image.

  5. Molten metal is poured into the hot mould.

  6. When the metal has cooled the mould is broken away, the channels are cut off, and the image is finished with chisels, files and burnishers; fine details are often re-cut at this stage.

In eastern India and the Himalaya images were often cast hollow, around a core of clay. Because the mould is destroyed, every lost-wax image is unique.

Figure 11.2. The lost-wax process (madhūcchiṣṭavidhāna) of solid casting, as practised in South India, in five stages: (1) a model of wax is made and wax rods are attached to serve as channels and vents; (2) the model is coated with fine and then coarse clay; (3) the mould is heated and the wax runs out, leaving a cavity in the shape of the image; (4) molten metal is poured in; (5) when it has cooled the mould is broken away, the channels are cut off and the surface is finished with chisels and files. Because the mould is destroyed, every image is unique. The position of the channels and of the pouring cup varies between workshops. Schematic.

Metal-casting as a craft, including the ḍhokrā tradition, is treated more fully in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

docs.title: 11.5.2 Alloys
docs.text: Texts and tradition speak of images made of “five metals” (pañcaloha), usually listed as copper, tin, zinc or lead, silver and gold. In practice the so-called bronzes of South India are alloys based on copper, with varying amounts of tin and lead and often some zinc; precious metals, where present, occur only in small quantities. Kashmiri and Himalayan images are often of brass, an alloy of copper and zinc, and are frequently inlaid with silver and copper. The surface of temple images used in worship is constantly altered by bathing, anointing and polishing.

docs.title: 11.5.3 Centres
docs.text: The great historic schools of metal images were those of the Pallavas and Cholas in Tamil Nadu, the Pālas in eastern India (with the hoards found at Nālandā and Kurkihār), Kashmir, Nepal and the western Himalaya, and the Jain workshops of western India and Karnataka (Chapter 13). At Swamimalai near Kumbakonam, families of Viśvakarma image-makers still cast bronzes by the solid lost-wax method described above, using fine clay from the bed of the Kāverī for the inner coat of the mould and re-cutting faces and ornaments after casting; larger images are cast in parts and joined. Among tribal and rural communities of central and eastern India, the ḍhokrā metal-smiths make figures by a lost-wax technique in which the wax is applied as fine threads.

docs.title: 11.6.1 Wood
docs.text:
Wood was certainly the most common material of early Indian architecture and probably of much early sculpture, and it remains important in Kerala, Odisha, Gujarat, Rajasthan, the Himalaya and the North-east. Kerala temples are rich in carved timber ceilings, brackets and figures; Gujarati houses and Jain shrines had elaborately carved wooden façades and interiors; and the hill temples of Himachal Pradesh are famous for their carved doorways and verandahs.

The most famous wooden images in India are those of Jagannātha, Balabhadra and Subhadrā at Puri. They are periodically renewed in the navakalevara (“new body”) ceremony, which falls in years in which an extra lunar month (adhika Āṣāḍha) is inserted into the calendar, at intervals of between eight and nineteen years; the most recent took place in 2015. Servitors called daitās, a hereditary group whom tradition connects with the tribal origins of the cult, search for neem trees (dāru) bearing prescribed signs, such as marks resembling a conch or discus and the proximity of a river, a cremation ground and an anthill. The trees are felled with ritual, the new images are carved in secret, and the sacred substance (brahma) is transferred from the old images to the new ones at night.

Temple chariots (ratha, Tamil tēr) are among the largest wooden sculptures in India. In the South, the processional chariots of temples such as Tiruvārūr and Śrīraṅgam are permanent structures of carved wood several storeys high, covered for festivals with cloth and decorations and pulled through the streets by thousands of devotees; their carved panels show deities, epic scenes and guardian figures. At Puri, the three chariots of the rathayātrā are built anew every year by hereditary carpenters, to fixed dimensions and designs.

docs.title: 11.6.2 Clay and Terracotta
docs.text: Fired clay (terracotta) is the oldest and most widespread sculptural medium of South Asia. Harappan sites have yielded many terracotta figurines of humans and animals; the early historic cities of the Gaṅgā valley, such as Kauśāmbī, Chandraketugaṛh and Ahicchatrā, produced moulded plaques of great refinement in the last centuries BCE; and Gupta-period temples such as Bhitargaon were decorated with large terracotta panels. In Bengal, where building stone is scarce, the brick temples of the 16th to 19th centuries are covered with narrative terracotta plaques (Chapter 13). Living traditions include the votive terracotta horses of Tamil Nadu (offered to the village god Aiyaṉār), Bankura in Bengal and Gorakhpur, and the painted terracotta plaques of Molela in Rajasthan. The unfired, painted clay images made for festivals, such as those of Durgā made in the Kumartuli quarter of Kolkata, are immersed in water at the end of the festival.

docs.title: 11.6.3 Stucco
docs.text: Lime stucco (sudhā) allowed rapid modelling and was used for figures and ornament on buildings. It was important in Gandhāra and Afghanistan, where stucco heads of Buddhas and bodhisattvas were made in great numbers between the 3rd and 5th centuries CE, and in the Deccan and South India, where the superstructures of temples and the great gopuras of the Vijayanagara and Nāyaka periods are covered with stucco figures, painted and periodically renewed. Recipes for stucco and plaster in the texts and in living practice include lime, sand and organic additives (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 11.6.4 Ivory
docs.text: Ivory carving was an important craft in ancient and medieval India, and its skills passed into stone: the inscription on the southern gateway of the Great Stūpa at Sāñcī recording a carving by the ivory-carvers of Vidiśā suggests how closely the two crafts were related. The history of Indian ivory work, from the Indus cities to its end under modern wildlife law, is treated in Volume 17, Śilpa–Kāru.

docs.title: 11.7 Image-Making in the Buddhist Himalaya
docs.text: The Buddhist traditions of Nepal and Tibet preserved Indian iconometric knowledge long after Buddhism had declined in India. Tibetan treatises, drawing on Indian texts such as the Pratimāmānalakṣaṇa and on the commentarial literature of the Kālacakra and other tantras, set out grids of proportion for Buddhas, bodhisattvas, peaceful and wrathful deities, and monks, based on a unit equal to the width of a finger or of the face; painters still learn to draw deities on these grids before they paint them. Newar craftsmen of the Kathmandu valley (on its architecture see Chapter 5, Section 5.7.6), renowned for their lost-wax casting and repoussé, made images for Tibetan monasteries as well as for their own temples, and the Newar artist Arniko (13th century) worked at the court of the Mongol emperors in China. This living tradition is one of the best places to see how Indian rules of proportion were applied in practice.

docs.title: 11.8 Consecration
docs.text:
An image becomes an object of worship through consecration (pratiṣṭhā). The rites, described at length in the āgamas and Purāṇas and still performed in modified forms, typically take several days (Davis 1997). They include the sowing of seeds in pots as an auspicious preliminary (aṅkurārpaṇa); the immersion of the image in water and then in grain, and its laying on a bed (adhivāsa); bathing with auspicious substances (snapana); the opening of the eyes (netronmīlana or nayanonmīlana), traditionally performed by the sculptor or priest with a golden needle, after which the image is shown its reflection in a mirror or auspicious objects such as grain or a cow; the installation of the image on its pedestal, with a deposit of precious materials beneath it; and the invocation of the deity into the image (prāṇapratiṣṭhā, “establishment of breath”), with mantras and the placing of syllables on the parts of the image (nyāsa). Thereafter the image is treated as the living presence of the deity, and receives daily worship. Images that are damaged may be “de-consecrated”, the deity being transferred to another image, and the old one immersed in water.

The Āgamic theology of the consecrated image is discussed in Volume 6, Tantra–Āgama. Jain and Buddhist images are consecrated by their own rites. In Nepal and Tibet the consecration of Buddhist images includes filling the hollow interior with scriptures, relics and other sacred materials.

docs.title: 11.9.1 Evidence of Guilds
docs.text: Inscriptions show that craftsmen in ancient India were organised in guilds (śreṇī) as well as in families and castes. Apart from the ivory-carvers of Vidiśā, a famous inscription at Mandasor in Madhya Pradesh records that a guild of silk-weavers who had migrated from Lāṭa (Gujarat) built a temple of the Sun in 436 CE and repaired it in 473. Many temple inscriptions record the names of individual sculptors and architects, and some sculptures are signed: at Paṭṭadakal, Ellora and Hoysaḷa sites such as Belūr and Haḷebīḍ, sculptors’ names are carved on or near their work. The Hoysaḷa temples in particular preserve the names of many sculptors, such as Mallitamma at Somanāthapura.

docs.title: 11.9.2 Training
docs.text: Skills were transmitted mainly within families and workshops, by apprenticeship. A boy began by preparing materials and roughing out blocks under the eye of a master, and only after years of practice was allowed to carve the faces and hands of principal images. Drawings, measuring rods and templates carried the workshop’s proportions from generation to generation; some families kept manuscripts of the relevant texts or of their own notes. Modern institutions, such as the Government College of Architecture and Sculpture at Mamallapuram (founded in 1957), now teach traditional sculpture and architecture alongside family workshops.

docs.title: 11.9.3 Social Position
docs.text: The social position of image-makers was ambiguous. Their skill was admired, and kings and temples rewarded master builders with land and titles; yet the dharmaśāstra texts rank craft work low, and artisan communities were subject to the disabilities of caste. In South India the Viśvakarma (Kammāḷar) groups of smiths, carpenters and sculptors long claimed a status equal to that of brāhmaṇas, wearing the sacred thread and employing their own priests, while other castes contested their claims; disputes between artisan castes and others over precedence and honours are recorded from the medieval period onward. Women’s labour in craft households, in preparing materials, finishing and painting, is rarely recorded in texts but is evident in ethnographic accounts.

docs.title: 11.10 Living Traditions
docs.text:
Image-making in the traditional manner continues in many centres:

  • Mamallapuram and other centres in Tamil Nadu: granite images and architectural carving for temples in India and abroad;

  • Swamimalai, Tamil Nadu: solid lost-wax casting of bronzes;

  • Jaipur and Makrana, Rajasthan: marble images for Hindu and Jain temples;

  • Puri and Bhubaneswar, Odisha: stone carving, and the wooden images of the Jagannātha cult;

  • Kumartuli, Kolkata: unfired clay images for the festivals of Durgā and other deities;

  • Bastar and other parts of central India: ḍhokrā metal-casting;

  • Nepal and the Himalaya: lost-wax casting and repoussé for Buddhist and Hindu images.

These traditions are adaptive. Modern sculptors use power tools for roughing out, print editions of the texts, photographs and plaster casts as models, and work to the expectations of new patrons, including temple trusts in the diaspora and the market for decorative images. The continuity they represent is real, but it is a continuity of practice that has always changed with its circumstances.

docs.title: 11.11 Dating, Provenance and Authenticity
docs.text: Few Indian sculptures are dated by inscription, and most are dated by comparing their style with dated works, by the archaeological context in which they were found, or by the buildings to which they belong. Inscribed images, such as the Kuṣāṇa sculptures of Mathurā with their regnal years, the dated bronzes of the Pāla period, and Jain images with dedicatory inscriptions on their pedestals, provide fixed points. Scientific methods can help: thermoluminescence dating of the clay cores of hollow-cast bronzes, analysis of metal composition, and study of tool marks and weathering. Because Indian sculpture is valuable on the art market, forgeries and re-carved or restored pieces are common, and many objects in collections lack a documented history. Establishing where and when an image was made, and how it left its original site, is therefore an essential part of its study, and has become central to the return of stolen images (Chapter 1).

docs.title: 11.12 Rule and Workshop
docs.text: The image-making texts are strongest where the workshop needed rules that could be written down: the relative measures of the body, the classes of proportion, the attributes to be held, and the rites that turn a finished object into a dwelling for a deity. They are weakest on what the workshop could teach only by example: how to choose and cut a stone, model wax, build a mould or finish a face. That division explains why images made under the same canon look so different from one region and century to another, and why the living workshops of Swamimalai, Mamallapuram and the Kathmandu valley are as important a source for the history of the craft as the texts themselves. The next chapter turns from how images were made to what they represent.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Iconography: The Forms of the Gods, Buddhas and Jinas
12.1 Reading an Image
docs.text:
Indian religious images communicate through a shared visual vocabulary. The posture of the figure, the number of its heads and arms, the gestures of its hands, the objects it holds, its ornaments and dress, its mount and its attendants together identify the deity and the particular form or episode represented. This vocabulary is set out in the image-making texts (Chapter 11) and in the Purāṇas and āgamas, and it was used across religious traditions: Buddhist and Jain images share many postures, gestures and ornaments with Hindu ones.

The iconographic rules were never uniform. They changed over time, as new forms of deities emerged and old ones were reinterpreted, and they differed between regions and sects. A modern reader should therefore treat the descriptions below as typical, not as fixed laws; the standard reference works, Gopinatha Rao for Hindu iconography, Banerjea for its development, Bhattacharyya for Buddhist and U. P. Shah for Jain iconography, document the many variants (Gopinatha Rao 1914; Banerjea 1956; Bhattacharyya 1924; Shah 1987).

docs.title: 12.2.1 Standing Postures
docs.text:
The texts distinguish standing postures by the number of bends (bhaṅga) in the body (Table 12.1 and Figure 12.1).

Table 12.1. Principal standing postures Posture Form Typical use samabhaṅga Upright and symmetrical, weight evenly distributed Principal images of Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Jinas standing in meditation ābhaṅga A slight bend of the body Many deities, Buddhas and bodhisattvas tribhaṅga Three bends, at neck, waist and knee, giving an S-shaped curve Goddesses, attendants, Kṛṣṇa playing the flute, many Chola bronzes atibhaṅga An exaggerated, dynamic bend Fierce and dancing forms, such as Naṭarāja and Kālī Figure 12.1. Schematic diagrams of the four standing postures, from the symmetrical samabhaṅga to the strongly flexed atibhaṅga. The dashed line marks the vertical; the coloured line traces the axis of the body, which in the tribhaṅga changes direction three times: the head inclines one way at the neck (1), the torso the other way at the waist (2), and the hips swing back over the bent knee of the free leg (3).

docs.title: 12.2.2 Seated Postures
docs.text:
The principal seated postures are listed in Table 12.2.

Table 12.2. Some seated postures (āsana) Posture Form and typical use padmāsana Legs crossed with both soles turned upwards; Buddhas and Jinas in meditation, Brahmā, Lakṣmī on the lotus vajraparyaṅka A form of the same with legs firmly locked; seated Buddhas ardhaparyaṅka, lalitāsana One leg folded on the seat, the other pendant; seated goddesses, bodhisattvas, Śiva with Pārvatī vīrāsana One leg folded over the other; seated forms of Viṣṇu and others sukhāsana At ease, one leg raised, sometimes with an arm resting on it utkuṭikāsana Squatting with the knees raised, often held by a meditation band (yogapaṭṭa); Yoga-Narasiṃha, Yoga-Dakṣiṇāmūrti pralambapādāsana Seated on a throne with both legs pendant; Maitreya and some Buddha images

docs.title: 12.3 Gestures
docs.text:
Hand gestures (mudrā, hasta) are among the most important signs. Several are shared by Hindu, Buddhist and Jain images; others belong to particular deities or to dance, from which iconography borrowed much of its vocabulary (Table 12.3; four are drawn in Figure 12.2).

Table 12.3. Principal gestures Gesture Form Meaning and use abhaya Hand raised, palm outward, fingers up “Do not fear”: protection; very many deities, Buddhas varada Hand lowered, palm outward Granting a boon; many deities, especially goddesses and bodhisattvas dhyāna Hands resting in the lap, palms upward, one on the other Meditation; Buddhas, Jinas, ascetic forms of Śiva bhūmisparśa Right hand reaching down to touch the earth “Calling the earth to witness”: the Buddha’s enlightenment dharmacakra Both hands at the chest, fingers forming circles “Turning the wheel of the law”: the Buddha’s first sermon vitarka, vyākhyāna Thumb and index finger joined in a circle, other fingers raised Teaching or argument; Buddhas, Dakṣiṇāmūrti (in this form often called cinmudrā) añjali Palms joined Salutation and devotion; devotees, Garuḍa, saints kaṭaka, kaṭakāmukha Fingers curled as if holding a flower Holding an attribute; goddesses sūci, tarjanī Index finger pointing or raised Pointing; threatening kaṭyavalambita Hand resting on the hip Relaxed standing figures gajahasta Arm swung across the body like an elephant’s trunk Dancing Śiva (Naṭarāja) Figure 12.2. Schematic diagrams of four gestures: abhaya (reassurance), varada (granting a boon), dhyāna (meditation) and vitarka (teaching).

docs.title: 12.4.1 Attributes
docs.text:
Multi-armed images hold attributes (āyudha, “weapons”, and other emblems) that identify them. Many attributes are shared, so that identification depends on their combination (Table 12.4).

Table 12.4. Some common attributes Attribute Principal deities cakra (discus) Viṣṇu and his forms; Vaiṣṇavī śaṅkha (conch) Viṣṇu; Vaiṣṇavī gadā (club) Viṣṇu; Vaiṣṇavī; Hanumān padma (lotus) Viṣṇu, Lakṣmī, Sūrya (a lotus in each hand), Padmapāṇi triśūla (trident) Śiva; Durgā ḍamaru (hourglass drum) Śiva, especially Naṭarāja paraśu (axe) Śiva; Gaṇeśa; Paraśurāma mṛga (deer) Śiva (held in a raised hand in South Indian images) pāśa (noose) and aṅkuśa (goad) Gaṇeśa; Varuṇa (noose); Lalitā (noose and goad) kamaṇḍalu (water-pot) and akṣamālā (rosary) Brahmā; Sarasvatī; ascetic forms; Maitreya pustaka (manuscript) Brahmā; Sarasvatī; Mañjuśrī vīṇā (lute) Sarasvatī; Vīṇādhara Śiva vajra (thunderbolt) Indra; Vajrapāṇi and many Vajrayāna deities khaḍga (sword) Durgā; Mañjuśrī; fierce deities kapāla (skull-cup) Bhairava; fierce goddesses; Vajrayāna deities dhanus and bāṇa (bow and arrow) Rāma; Śiva as Tripurāntaka; Durgā; Kāma

Modern devotional and popular books attach symbolic meanings to many of these attributes, such as the lotus as purity or the noose as attachment. Some of these interpretations are found in Purāṇas and later commentaries; others are recent. They should not be confused with the descriptive rules of the iconographic texts.

docs.title: 12.4.2 Mounts
docs.text:
Many deities have an animal mount or emblem (vāhana), shown beneath or beside the image (Table 12.5).

Table 12.5. Mounts of some principal deities Deity Mount Śiva Nandī, the bull Viṣṇu Garuḍa, the eagle-man Brahmā haṃsa, the goose Sarasvatī haṃsa; in some regions the peacock Lakṣmī lotus; in Bengal the owl Durgā lion (in some regions tiger) Gaṇeśa rat or mouse Kārttikeya (Skanda) peacock Sūrya chariot drawn by seven horses Yama buffalo Gaṅgā; Yamunā makara (crocodile-like monster); tortoise

docs.title: 12.4.3 Crowns and Ornaments
docs.text: The headdress is an important sign. The tall, cylindrical kirīṭamukuṭa is worn by Viṣṇu and by kings; the jaṭāmukuṭa, a crown of matted locks, by Śiva, Brahmā and ascetic figures; the smaller, tiered karaṇḍamukuṭa by goddesses and attendant deities. Images are adorned with ear ornaments (kuṇḍala), necklaces (hāra), armlets (keyūra), bracelets (kaṅkaṇa), a waistband (udarabandha) and girdle (mekhalā), anklets (nūpura), the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), and, in some periods, a chain crossing the chest (channavīra). A halo or aureole (prabhāmaṇḍala, prabhāvalī) surrounds the head or the whole figure. Buddhas wear only the monastic robe and have a cranial protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), elongated ear lobes and a tuft of hair between the eyebrows (ūrṇā), signs from the list of thirty-two marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa); Jinas are unadorned.

docs.title: 12.5 Viṣṇu
docs.text:
The standard image of Viṣṇu, established by the Gupta period, is a standing, four-armed figure wearing a tall crown, holding the discus, conch, club and lotus (the lotus sometimes replaced by a gesture). The Purāṇas and the Rūpamaṇḍana name twenty-four forms (caturviṃśatimūrti), from Keśava to Kṛṣṇa, distinguished solely by the order in which the four attributes are held in the four hands (Gopinatha Rao 1914).

The Pāñcarātra tradition describes five modes of the deity’s presence: the supreme (para); the four emanations (vyūha), Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha, of whom Vāsudeva possesses all six divine qualities while each of the others manifests two; the incarnations (vibhava); the inner controller (antaryāmin); and the consecrated image (arcā), which in this theology is a full and gracious form of God. Images of the vyūhas, including composite four-faced images from Kashmir and Mathurā, testify to the early importance of this doctrine.

Viṣṇu reclining on the serpent Śeṣa (Anantaśayana or Śeṣaśāyin), with Brahmā emerging on a lotus from his navel, is one of the great themes of Indian sculpture, from the Gupta relief at Deogaṛh to the colossal image at Śrīraṅgam. The incarnations (avatāra) are listed in different ways; the familiar list of ten (fish, tortoise, boar, man-lion, dwarf, Paraśurāma, Rāma, Balarāma or Kṛṣṇa, the Buddha, and Kalki) became standard only gradually, and some lists include both Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa and omit the Buddha (Table 12.6).

Table 12.6. Some forms of Viṣṇu and his incarnations in sculpture Form Usual representation Matsya, Kūrma As a fish or tortoise, or with human upper body and animal lower body Varāha A man with a boar’s head lifting the Earth goddess on his tusk or shoulder (e.g. Udayagiri, Bādāmi, Māmallapuram) Narasiṃha A man with a lion’s head, tearing apart the demon Hiraṇyakaśipu, or seated in yogic posture Vāmana–Trivikrama A dwarf with an umbrella and water-pot, or a giant striding across the universe with one leg raised Rāma A prince with bow and arrow, often with Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa and Hanumān Kṛṣṇa As a child dancing with a butter-ball, lifting Mount Govardhana, subduing the serpent Kāliya, or playing the flute Anantaśayana Reclining on the serpent Śeṣa, with Brahmā on a lotus from his navel

docs.title: 12.6.1 The Liṅga
docs.text: Śiva is worshipped above all in the liṅga, a cylindrical stone set in a pedestal (pīṭha) with a spout. In the texts, a “manufactured” liṅga has three parts: a square lower part (the brahmabhāga), an octagonal middle part (the viṣṇubhāga), both hidden in the pedestal, and a cylindrical upper part (the rudrabhāga) which is worshipped (Gopinatha Rao 1914). Self-manifested (svayambhū) liṅgas are natural stones. Many early liṅgas bear one or more faces of Śiva (mukhaliṅga). In the story of the Liṅgodbhava, Śiva appears in a pillar of fire to Brahmā and Viṣṇu, who fail to find its top and bottom; the scene is represented in Chola temples in the niche on the back wall of the sanctum.

docs.title: 12.6.2 Anthropomorphic Forms
docs.text:
The Śaiva tradition, especially in the South, counts many forms of Śiva (lists of twenty-five and sixty-four forms are known), several of which are important in sculpture (Table 12.7).

Table 12.7. Some forms of Śiva in sculpture Form Usual representation Naṭarāja Dancing with four arms in a ring of flames, holding drum and fire, one foot on the dwarf Apasmāra (Tamil Muyalakaṉ), the other raised Dakṣiṇāmūrti Seated under a banyan tree, facing south, teaching sages, with the teaching gesture Ardhanārīśvara Half male and half female: Śiva on the right, Pārvatī on the left Umāmaheśvara, Somāskanda Seated with Pārvatī; in the Somāskanda group the child Skanda sits between them Kalyāṇasundara At his marriage to Pārvatī Gaṅgādhara Receiving the river Gaṅgā in his hair Tripurāntaka As an archer destroying the three cities of the demons Bhikṣāṭana As a naked mendicant with a skull-bowl, followed by a deer Bhairava Fierce, naked, with skull-cup and fangs, accompanied by a dog Liṅgodbhava Emerging from the fiery pillar, with Brahmā as a goose above and Viṣṇu as a boar below Rāvaṇānugrahamūrti Seated on Kailāsa while Rāvaṇa tries to shake the mountain

docs.title: 12.6.3 Naṭarāja
docs.text:
The image of Śiva as Lord of Dance (Naṭarāja), in the form perfected in Chola bronzes, became one of the best-known images in Indian art (Figure 12.3). Ananda Coomaraswamy’s essay “The Dance of Śiva” interpreted it, following later Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta texts, as an image of the five acts of the god: creation (the drum), protection (the gesture of reassurance), destruction (the fire), concealment (the foot planted on the dwarf) and grace or release (the raised foot) (Coomaraswamy 1918). This interpretation is attested in Tamil Śaiva literature and is widely accepted, but the image itself is older than some of the texts used to explain it, and its earliest meaning may have been simpler; the connection with Chidambaram, where Śiva is worshipped as the dancer, is central to its history (Smith 1996; Sivaramamurti 1974).

Figure 12.3. Śiva as Lord of Dance (Naṭarāja), bronze, Tamil Nadu, Chola period, about 1000 (Cleveland Museum of Art). The god dances within a ring of flames, holding the drum and the fire in his upper hands; one lower hand makes the gesture of reassurance, the other points to the raised foot, and the other foot is planted on the dwarf. Photo: Cleveland Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 12.7 The Goddess
docs.text:
The iconography of the goddess is as varied as her worship. The Devīmāhātmya (c. 5th–6th century), part of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, provides the narrative of her fierce forms, above all her slaying of the buffalo demon Mahiṣa, which was represented in sculpture from the Kuṣāṇa period onward and on a monumental scale at Māmallapuram and Ellora (Table 12.8).

Table 12.8. Some forms of the goddess Form Usual representation Durgā Mahiṣāsuramardinī Multi-armed, with weapons of the gods, riding a lion and killing the buffalo demon Pārvatī, Umā Gentle consort of Śiva, often standing in tribhaṅga Lakṣmī, Śrī On a lotus, holding lotuses; as Gajalakṣmī, bathed by two elephants pouring water Sarasvatī With manuscript, rosary, water-pot and vīṇā; often white; with goose Kālī, Cāmuṇḍā Fierce and emaciated, with skull garland, severed head, chopper; Cāmuṇḍā often on a corpse, with owl or jackal Lalitā Tripurasundarī Four-armed, with noose, goad, sugar-cane bow and flower arrows Annapūrṇā Holding a ladle and a vessel of food The Seven Mothers (saptamātṛkā) Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Indrāṇī and Cāmuṇḍā, each with the attributes and mount of the corresponding male deity; often flanked by Vīrabhadra and Gaṇeśa

The river goddesses Gaṅgā and Yamunā, on their mounts the makara and the tortoise, stand at the base of temple doorways from the Gupta period, signifying the purification of those who enter. The sixty-four yoginīs, fierce female deities, were installed in circular, roofless temples in central India and Odisha, at Hirapur, Ranipur-Jharial, Bheraghat and Mitaoli (Dehejia 1986).

docs.title: 12.8 Other Deities
docs.text:
• Gaṇeśa, with an elephant’s head and a pot belly, holding his broken tusk, a sweet (modaka), the noose and the goad, and with a rat as his mount; images become common from the Gupta period.

  • Kārttikeya (Skanda, Murukaṉ), a youthful warrior with a spear and a peacock, sometimes with six heads; especially important in Tamil Nadu.

  • The guardians of the directions (dikpāla), each with his mount and weapon, placed at the corresponding corners and faces of temple walls (Chapter 2). Sūrya and the nine planets are described below.

  • Yakṣas and yakṣīs, nāgas and nāginīs, nature deities shown in human form, which appear in the earliest stone sculpture and were absorbed into Buddhist, Jain and Hindu iconography as guardians and attendants.

docs.title: 12.9 Yantra and Maṇḍala
docs.text: In Tantric worship, Hindu and Buddhist, the deity may be worshipped not in an anthropomorphic image but in a geometric diagram, the yantra or maṇḍala, in which the deity and its retinue are present as syllables, lines and figures. The best known is the śrīcakra (or śrīyantra) of the goddess Tripurasundarī, composed of nine interlocking triangles, four pointing upwards and five downwards, surrounded by circles of lotus petals and a square enclosure with four gates; it is engraved on metal or carved in stone, sometimes in three dimensions (meru), and installed in temples and homes. In Vajrayāna Buddhism, maṇḍalas of a central deity surrounded by concentric rings of other deities, enclosed in a square palace with four gateways, are painted on cloth and on the walls of monasteries, as at Alchi and Tabo, and created in coloured sand for particular rituals. The square and the circle, the centre and the four gates of these diagrams relate them to the plans of temples and stūpas, and to the vāstupuruṣamaṇḍala (Chapter 2).

docs.title: 12.10 Village Deities, Hero Stones and Memorials
docs.text: Much of the religious imagery of India lies outside the Sanskrit iconographic texts. Village goddesses (grāmadevatā), often worshipped as a stone, a head or a pot, protect communities from disease and disaster; in Tamil Nadu the guardian god Aiyaṉār and his companions receive offerings of large terracotta horses and figures, set up in groves at the edge of villages. Across the peninsula and in western India, memorial stones commemorate men who died defending cattle or villages (Tamil naṭukal, Kannada vīragal), with carved panels showing the fight, the hero’s death and his ascent to heaven; the earliest Tamil examples, inscribed in Tamil-Brāhmī, go back to the last centuries BCE or the early centuries CE, and thousands survive in Karnataka. Memorial stones for women who died on their husbands’ funeral pyres (satī stones), showing a raised arm with bangles, are found especially in Rajasthan, Gujarat and Karnataka; they record a practice that was celebrated in its time and was prohibited by law in 1829. Tribal communities make figures of wood, metal and clay for their own deities and ancestors. Because these images are rarely described in texts, their history has to be reconstructed from the objects themselves and from ethnography, and it is still only partly written.

docs.title: 12.11 The Sun and the Planets
docs.text: Sūrya, the Sun, was widely worshipped from the Kuṣāṇa period, and Sun temples were built at Moḍherā, Konārak, Mārtaṇḍ and many other places (Chapter 5). Northern images of Sūrya show him standing, holding a full-blown lotus in each hand, often wearing a tunic, a belt and high boots, a costume associated with Central Asia and with the Sun cult of the Magas, priests said to have come from Iran; he is attended by his charioteer Aruṇa, by the archer-goddesses Uṣā and Pratyuṣā, and by his attendants Daṇḍa and Piṅgala, and his chariot is drawn by seven horses. Southern images usually omit the boots. The nine planets (navagraha), Sūrya, Candra (the Moon), Maṅgala (Mars), Budha (Mercury), Bṛhaspati (Jupiter), Śukra (Venus), Śani (Saturn), and the eclipse-demons Rāhu and Ketu, are carved in a row on the lintels of northern temple doorways, and in the South are installed as a group of nine images on a platform, each facing a different direction; worship of the planets to avert their malign influence is common.

docs.title: 12.12.1 The Buddha
docs.text: Images of the Buddha in human form appear around the 1st century CE in Gandhāra and Mathurā. Alfred Foucher argued that the first images were made in Gandhāra under Greek and Roman influence; Ananda Coomaraswamy argued for an independent origin at Mathurā. Most scholars now think that both centres produced Buddha images at about the same time, in the Kuṣāṇa period, each in its own style (Rosenfield 1967; Huntington 1985). The earlier representation of the Buddha by symbols is discussed in Chapter 3. The Buddha is identified by the marks of a great man (the uṣṇīṣa, the ūrṇā, elongated ear lobes and others), his monastic robe and his gestures, which identify episodes of his life: enlightenment (touching the earth), the first sermon (turning the wheel), protection, and meditation.

docs.title: 12.12.2 Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna
docs.text:
The Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna traditions developed a large pantheon (Bhattacharyya 1924); some of its principal figures are listed in Table 12.9.

Table 12.9. Some Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna figures Figure Usual representation Avalokiteśvara (Padmapāṇi) Bodhisattva of compassion, with a lotus; a small seated Buddha (Amitābha) in his crown; in later forms with eleven heads and many arms Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva of wisdom, with a sword and a manuscript on a lotus Vajrapāṇi Holding a thunderbolt (vajra) Maitreya The future Buddha, often with a water-pot, sometimes seated with legs pendant Tārā Female saviour; Green Tārā seated with one leg pendant, with varada gesture and a blue lotus; White Tārā with eyes on palms, soles and forehead The five Jinas (Tathāgatas) Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha and Amoghasiddhi, distinguished by colour, gesture and direction Heruka, Hevajra, Cakrasaṃvara Wrathful tutelary deities, often embracing a female partner

docs.title: 12.13 Jain Iconography
docs.text:
The central figures of Jain art are the twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras or Jinas. They are shown in only two postures: standing erect with arms hanging free in the pose of “abandoning the body” (kāyotsarga), or seated in meditation. They are unadorned and, in Digambara images, naked; Śvetāmbara images are shown clothed in a lower garment and are often given inlaid eyes and ornaments in worship. Northern images often bear the śrīvatsa mark on the chest. Since the Jinas look alike, they are identified by an emblem (lāñchana) on the pedestal and by other signs (Shah 1987) (Table 12.10).

Table 12.10. Some tīrthaṅkaras and their emblems No. Name Emblem Other signs 1 Ṛṣabhanātha (Ādinātha) bull locks of hair falling on the shoulders 2 Ajitanātha elephant 7 Supārśvanātha svastika canopy of snake hoods (in some images) 16 Śāntinātha deer 22 Neminātha conch associated with Kṛṣṇa’s clan 23 Pārśvanātha snake canopy of seven snake hoods 24 Mahāvīra lion

Jain art also represents the structure of the universe and the assembly of the Jina. Painted cloths (paṭa) show the central continent of Jambūdvīpa with Mount Meru at its centre, surrounded by rings of oceans and continents, or the cosmos as a giant human figure; the samavasaraṇa, the circular or square assembly hall in which a Jina preaches to gods, humans and animals, is shown in painting and built in three dimensions in temples. Diagrams of auspicious symbols and of holy places such as Śatruñjaya were also painted for worship.

The Jinas are attended by pairs of guardian deities (yakṣa and yakṣī), of whom some, such as Ambikā (with a child and a mango tree) and Padmāvatī (with a snake canopy), became the objects of independent cults. Bāhubali, son of Ṛṣabhanātha, is not a tīrthaṅkara, but is revered for his meditation standing so still that creepers grew up his body; his colossal image at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa is discussed in Chapter 13.

docs.title: 12.14 Narrative Sculpture
docs.text: Besides cult images, Indian sculptors carved narratives. The early Buddhist reliefs of Bhārhut, Sāñcī, Amarāvatī and Gandhāra tell the jātaka stories and the life of the Buddha, using several narrative methods: a single scene representing a whole story, a sequence of scenes in separate panels, or “continuous narration”, in which the same figure appears several times within one composition to show successive moments (Dehejia 1997). Hindu temples carry narrative friezes of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata and of the life of Kṛṣṇa: on the base of the Virūpākṣa at Paṭṭadakal, on the walls of the Kailāsa at Ellora, around the Hazāra Rāma temple at Vijayanagara, and in long bands on the Hoysaḷa temples. The stories of the Tamil Śaiva saints are carved at Dārāsuram, and Jain temples show the lives of the tīrthaṅkaras. Reading these narratives requires knowledge of the texts and of the regional versions of the stories that the sculptors followed.

docs.title: 12.15 Saints, Teachers and Portraits
docs.text: Images of human beings also have a place in Indian religious art. In Tamil Nadu, bronze and stone images of the Śaiva poet-saints (the sixty-three Nāyaṉmār) and of the Vaiṣṇava Āḻvār, together with the teachers of the Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition such as Rāmānuja, are installed and worshipped in temples. Jain temples have images of revered monks and nuns and footprints (pādukā) of teachers; Buddhist monasteries had images of famous teachers. Royal and donor portraits appear from the Kuṣāṇa statues at Māṭ to the Pallava royal reliefs at Māmallapuram, the portrait bronzes of Kṛṣṇadevarāya and his queens at Tirupati, and the Nāyaka portrait sculptures of Madurai. These images are usually idealised rather than individual likenesses, identified by inscriptions and by their posture of devotion, often with hands joined in añjali.

docs.title: 12.16 Expression and Rasa
docs.text: The image-making texts distinguish broadly between peaceful (śānta, saumya) and fierce (ugra, raudra) forms of deities, and prescribe appropriate expressions: a calm face with half-closed eyes for meditating figures, bulging eyes and fangs for fierce ones. The Viṣṇudharmottara goes further and discusses how the nine sentiments (rasa) of dramatic theory should be represented in painting (Chapter 14). Sculptors were clearly familiar with the conventions of dance and drama, and many images, especially of dancing deities and celestial women, use the gestures and stances of dance. But the detailed correspondences between particular rasas and particular deities given in some modern books are not found in the texts.

docs.title: 12.17 Iconographic Programmes and Regional Variation
docs.text:
Images were not made in isolation: on temple walls they formed programmes. In northern temples the principal niches on the three outer walls of the sanctum often held forms or companions of the main deity (for a Śiva temple in Odisha, Gaṇeśa, Kārttikeya and Pārvatī), the corners held the guardians of the directions, and the recesses held celestial women and ascetics. Chola temples have a standard programme of niche images (Chapter 4). Doorways carry river goddesses and guardians; lintels the planets or the incarnations of Viṣṇu.

Regional traditions developed their own forms and emphases: the importance of processional bronze images (utsavamūrti) in Tamil Nadu; the wooden Jagannātha triad of Odisha; the Tantric goddesses of Bengal, Assam and Odisha; the inlaid brass images of Kashmir; the syncretic Hindu and Buddhist iconography of Nepal; and the marble Jinas of western India. Local deities, such as Viṭhobā at Pandharpur, Ayyappaṉ in Kerala or Khaṇḍobā in Maharashtra, have their own iconographies that do not fit neatly into the pan-Indian scheme.

docs.title: 12.18 A Shared Language
docs.text: The striking fact about Indian iconography is how much of it was shared. The same postures, gestures, crowns and ornaments identify a Jina, a Buddha or a Hindu god, and the same sculptors often made all three; what distinguishes them is the combination of signs, not the signs themselves. This is why iconography could absorb new deities so easily, from the village goddess to the bodhisattva, and why the rules changed with region and sect. It is also why an image can rarely be identified from a single attribute, and why the texts, which set out the combinations, are most useful when read alongside the images that show how the combinations were actually used.

docs.title: 13.1 Introduction
docs.text:
Art historians group Indian sculpture into “schools”, named after dynasties (Maurya, Kuṣāṇa, Gupta, Chola, Pāla, Hoysaḷa) or after regions and sites (Mathurā, Gandhāra, Amarāvatī). These labels are conveniences. Sculptors worked for patrons of every religion, moved between courts, and drew on neighbouring traditions; a dynastic name does not mean that the king paid for the sculpture, and the boundaries between “schools” are often blurred. With these cautions, this chapter follows the main traditions in rough chronological order (Harle 1994; Huntington 1985; Dehejia 1997; Mitter 2001). The principal centres of sculpture, and those of painting discussed in the next chapter, are shown in Figure 13.1.

Figure 13.1. Principal centres of sculpture and painting discussed in Chapters 13 and 14. Gandhāra, Kashmir and the Pahāṛī states (Basohli, Guler, Kangra) lie north of the frame and are not shown. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude and are approximate where several places share one symbol; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no rivers or political boundaries are shown.

docs.title: 13.2.1 Harappan Sculpture
docs.text: The Harappan cities produced small sculptures in stone, bronze and terracotta: the steatite bust of a bearded man from Mohenjo-daro (often called the “priest-king”, a modern label), the small bronze figure of a young woman known as the “dancing girl”, the red sandstone male torso from Harappā, and thousands of terracotta figurines, together with the carved steatite seals with their animals and script (Kenoyer 1998).

docs.title: 13.2.2 Mauryan Sculpture
docs.text:
Monumental stone sculpture appears under the Mauryas. The polished sandstone columns set up by Aśoka carried capitals with animals: the lion capital from Sārnāth, with four lions back to back above a frieze of animals and wheels (Figure 13.2, left), which became the emblem of the Republic of India; the bull from Rāmpurvā; and the single lions of Lauriyā Nandangaṛh and Vaiśālī. The origins of this polished, monumental style, with its Achaemenid Persian echoes, are much debated. Large stone figures of yakṣas and yakṣīs, such as the Parkham yakṣa near Mathurā and the polished yakṣī found at Didarganj near Patna (Figure 13.2, right), belong to the Mauryan or immediately post-Mauryan period; the date of the Didarganj figure in particular is disputed.

Figure 13.2. Polished sandstone sculpture. Left: the lion capital of Aśoka from Sārnāth, 3rd century BCE (Archaeological Museum, Sārnāth): four lions back to back on a drum carved with animals, among them a galloping horse, and wheels, above a bell-shaped lotus. Right: the yakṣī from Didarganj, holding a fly-whisk over her shoulder, photographed in the Patna Museum (now in the Bihar Museum, Patna); whether she is Mauryan or later is disputed. Photo: lisa bat, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 13.2.3 Bhārhut and Sāñcī
docs.text: The railings and gateways of the stūpas of Bhārhut (2nd century BCE) and Sāñcī (2nd century BCE to 1st century CE) carry the first great programmes of narrative relief in Indian art: scenes from the life of the Buddha and the jātakas, worshippers, animals, yakṣas and yakṣīs, and lotus and creeper ornament (Chapter 3). The yakṣī brackets of the Sāñcī gateways, embracing trees, are among the earliest images of the celestial woman that runs through all later Indian sculpture.

docs.title: 13.3 Mathurā
docs.text:
Mathurā, on the Yamunā, was a major centre of sculpture from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE and later, producing images for Buddhists, Jains and Hindus alike in a distinctive spotted red sandstone (Quintanilla 2007). Under the Kuṣāṇa rulers (1st–3rd century CE) Mathurā’s workshops produced:

  • some of the earliest Buddha and bodhisattva images: robust, broad-shouldered figures with smooth heads crowned by a coiled protuberance, a large scalloped halo, and a thin robe leaving the right shoulder bare, such as the seated Buddha from Katrā (Figure 13.3, left);

  • Jain images of tīrthaṅkaras and inscribed votive tablets (āyāgapaṭa) from the Kaṅkālī Ṭīlā stūpa site;

  • early images of Hindu deities, including Viṣṇu, Śiva (as liṅgas with faces), Durgā killing the buffalo, the Seven Mothers, Sūrya and others;

  • portrait statues of Kuṣāṇa rulers, among them the headless standing figure of Kaniṣka, inscribed with his name, from the dynastic shrine at Māṭ.

Many Mathurā images carry inscriptions naming their donors, often monks, nuns, merchants and women of the city, which make Mathurā one of the best-documented early schools.

docs.title: 13.4 Gandhāra
docs.text:
Gandhāra, the region around Peshawar in north-western Pakistan, and neighbouring areas of Afghanistan produced a large body of Buddhist sculpture between about the 1st and the 5th centuries CE, in grey schist and later in stucco (Zwalf 1996; Rosenfield 1967). Its style draws on the art of the Hellenistic and Roman world: the Buddha is shown with wavy hair gathered in a topknot, a classicising face and a heavy, deeply folded robe covering both shoulders (Figure 13.3, right); reliefs from stūpas narrate his life in a series of panels, with figures and motifs borrowed from Roman art. Bodhisattvas are shown as richly dressed princes. This was not a “Greek” art in India but a Buddhist art of the borderlands, produced by local workshops for local patrons in a region where several cultures met (Table 13.1).

Table 13.1. Kuṣāṇa-period Buddha images: Mathurā and Gandhāra (typical features) Feature Mathurā Gandhāra Material Spotted red sandstone Grey schist; later stucco Head Smooth head with coiled protuberance; round face Wavy hair in a topknot; classicising face Robe Thin, clinging; right shoulder often bare Heavy, with deep folds; usually both shoulders covered Body Broad-shouldered and powerful More slender Halo Large, with scalloped edge Plain Figure 13.3. Kuṣāṇa-period Buddha images (Table 13.1). Left: the inscribed seated Buddha from Katrā, Mathurā, spotted red sandstone, with the right hand raised in reassurance, a large scalloped halo and attendants (Government Museum, Mathurā). Right: a standing Buddha from Gandhāra, grey schist, with wavy hair gathered in a topknot and a heavy robe covering both shoulders (Tokyo National Museum). Photo: Biswarup Ganguly, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 13.5 Amarāvatī and Nāgārjunakoṇḍa
docs.text: In the lower Kṛṣṇā valley in Andhra, Buddhist stūpas were decorated from the 2nd century BCE to the 4th century CE with reliefs carved in a fine greenish-white limestone (Huntington 1985). At Amarāvatī, under the Sātavāhanas, and at Nāgārjunakoṇḍa, under the Ikṣvākus in the 3rd century CE, the sculptors developed a style of slender, animated figures in crowded, dynamic compositions, often arranged in roundels, with great skill in depicting movement and depth. Other sites include Jaggayyapeṭa, Goli and Ghaṇṭaśālā. Buddha images of the Andhra type travelled to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, where they influenced early Buddhist sculpture.

docs.title: 13.6 The Gupta Period
docs.text:
The sculpture of the Gupta period (c. 320–550 CE) and of contemporary dynasties such as the Vākāṭakas has long been regarded as “classical” in Indian art (Williams 1982). Its images combine a smooth, softly modelled body with a calm, inward expression. At Mathurā, the Buddha’s robe falls in regular, string-like folds; at Sārnāth, carved in buff Chunār sandstone, the robe is rendered as a transparent film, visible only at its edges, over a body of idealised smoothness. The seated Buddha preaching the first sermon, in Sārnāth, is the best-known example.

Hindu sculpture of the period includes the great Varāha relief at Udayagiri (Chapter 3), the panels of Viṣṇu reclining on the serpent, of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, and of Gajendramokṣa at the Daśāvatāra temple at Deogaṛh, mukhaliṅgas, and terracotta panels from brick temples. A copper Buddha over two metres high from Sultanganj in Bihar, now in Birmingham, shows the scale of metal casting in the 6th or 7th century.

At Eraṇ in Madhya Pradesh, a colossal free-standing image of Viṣṇu as a boar, its body covered with rows of small figures of sages and gods, bears an inscription of the first year of the Hūṇa ruler Toramāṇa (late 5th or early 6th century), recording its dedication by a local ruler; nearby stands a tall pillar set up in 484–85 under the Gupta king Budhagupta. The site shows the continuity of Vaiṣṇava patronage across a period of political upheaval.

docs.title: 13.7 Western India and the Deccan, 6th to 10th Centuries
docs.text:
The caves of Elephanta and Ellora and the temples of the early Cālukyas at Aihoḷe, Bādāmi and Paṭṭadakal contain some of the most powerful sculpture in India (Chapters 5 and 3): the Maheśamūrti and the great panels of Elephanta; the dancing Śiva, Durgā and Varāha of Bādāmi; and, at Ellora, Rāvaṇa shaking Mount Kailāsa. These works are characterised by large, dramatically lit compositions, cut deep into the rock.

Under the Rāṣṭrakūṭas (8th–10th century), the sculptors of the Kailāsa at Ellora carved monumental panels on the walls of the court and the base of the temple: Śiva in many forms, the river goddesses at the entrance to the shrine of the three rivers, the epic battles of the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata along the base, and the great elephants and lions that seem to carry the temple on their backs. The Jain caves at Ellora continue the style in a more ornate manner. In the early Cālukya temples at Paṭṭadakal, by contrast, the sculpture is set in niches and panels on the walls in a manner close to that of the Pallavas, and narrative friezes run along the bases and pillars, illustrating the epics and the Pañcatantra.

docs.title: 13.8.1 Pallava Sculpture
docs.text: The Pallava monuments of Māmallapuram and Kāñcīpuram (7th–8th century) established the southern sculptural idiom: slender, elegant figures with long limbs and small, oval faces, as in the relief of the Descent of the Gaṅgā (or Arjuna’s Penance), the Mahiṣāsuramardinī cave and the Somāskanda panels in the shrines of the caves and of the Shore Temple (Chapter 3, Section 3.11, and Chapter 5, Section 5.6.3).

docs.title: 13.8.2 Chola Stone Sculpture
docs.text: The early Chola temples of the 9th and 10th centuries, many of them small village shrines, carry niche images of great refinement, such as the Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Brahmā and Durgā of the temples at Puḷḷamaṅgai and Kumbakonam (Nāgeśvara). The great royal temples of Thanjavur, Gaṅgaikoṇḍacōḻapuram and Dārāsuram added monumental guardian figures, narrative friezes and the dance poses of the upper storey at Thanjavur (Dehejia 1990).

docs.title: 13.8.3 Chola Bronzes
docs.text: The bronze images made in the Chola country between the 10th and 13th centuries are among the masterpieces of world sculpture. Most were processional images (utsavamūrti), cast solid by the lost-wax process (Chapter 11) and fitted with lugs on their pedestals so that they could be carried on poles; in worship they are dressed, garlanded and decorated with jewels, so that the bronzes now in museums are seen as they were not seen in their temples. They include Śiva as Naṭarāja and in many other forms, Pārvatī, the Somāskanda group, Viṣṇu with Śrīdevī and Bhūdevī, Rāma with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, Kālī, and the Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava poet-saints (Nāyaṉmār and Āḻvār) (Dehejia 2002). Some of the finest early bronzes were commissioned by Sembiyaṉ Mahādevī, a Chola queen of the 10th century, who was also a great builder of temples. Vidya Dehejia has used the inscriptions that record such gifts, and the bronzes themselves, to reconstruct the “material life” of these images: who paid for them, how they were adorned and used in festivals, and how their makers were rewarded (Dehejia 2021). The Naṭarāja image is discussed in Chapter 12.

docs.title: 13.9 Eastern India: The Pālas and Senas
docs.text:
Under the Pāla (c. 750–1160) and Sena dynasties of Bihar and Bengal, sculptors produced Buddhist and Hindu images in a fine-grained, dark grey to black stone and in bronze (Huntington and Huntington 1990). Typical stone images are steles: the principal figure stands or sits before a pointed back-slab carved with attendants, flying figures and ornament, and the surfaces are crisp and finely detailed (Figure 13.4).

Figure 13.4. The composition of a stone stele of the Pāla period (8th–12th century), shown schematically: the principal deity stands on a lotus seat before a back-slab with a pointed top, with a halo behind the head, smaller attendants at the sides, flying figures bearing garlands above, and a face of glory (kīrttimukha) at the apex; the pedestal carries the donors and, in many examples, an inscription. Real steles vary greatly in their attendants and ornament; not to scale.

The great monasteries of Nālandā and Vikramaśilā and the shrine at Bodh Gayā were major centres; the hoards of bronzes found at Nālandā and at Kurkihār show the importance of portable metal images. Through pilgrims and monks, the Pāla style had a deep influence on the Buddhist art of Nepal and Tibet, and also reached Myanmar and Southeast Asia.

docs.title: 13.10 Central and Western India, 10th to 13th Centuries
docs.text: The temples of Khajuraho and other Candella sites, of the Paramāras of Mālwā, of the Kalacuris and of the Caulukyas of Gujarat carry very large programmes of sculpture in which deities, celestial women, couples and mythical beasts are carved in high relief and arranged in registers on the walls (Chapter 5) (Desai 1996). At Khajuraho the walls of the larger temples carry several hundred figures each, arranged in two or three registers between the projecting balconies: deities in the principal niches; the guardians of the directions at the corners; celestial women, shown adorning themselves, writing letters, removing thorns or playing with children and animals; rearing vyālas in the recesses; and couples. The figures are tall and slender, with sharply cut features and elaborate ornament, and their poses are animated by twisting and bending. Similar sculpture adorned the temples of the Kacchapaghātas at Gwalior and Suhania and of the Kalacuris of central India, and the Paramāra temples of Mālwā, such as the Udayeśvara at Udayapur. In western India, Jain patrons commissioned marble temples and images in great numbers; the carving of ceilings and pillars at Dilwārā and Raṇakpur is among the most intricate in Indian art.

docs.title: 13.11 Odisha
docs.text: The temples of Bhubaneswar, Puri and Konārak preserve a continuous sequence of sculpture from the 7th to the 13th century (Donaldson 1985). Among its high points are the Mukteśvara temple (10th century), with its arched gateway (toraṇa) and finely carved small panels; the Rājarāṇī temple (11th century), famous for its graceful female figures and guardians of the directions; and Konārak (13th century), where the platform, wheels and walls carry thousands of sculptures, from monumental horses and elephants to courtly scenes, musicians, dancers and couples, and green chlorite images of Sūrya.

docs.title: 13.12 Karnataka before the Hoysaḷas
docs.text: Between the early Cālukyas and the Hoysaḷas, several dynasties of Karnataka and its borders patronised fine sculpture. The Western Gaṅgas, rulers of southern Karnataka from the 4th to the 10th century, were great patrons of Jainism, and their minister Cāmuṇḍarāya commissioned the Bāhubali at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa (below). The Nolambas, a dynasty of the border region between Karnataka and Andhra in the 9th and 10th centuries, are known for their exquisitely carved black stone pillars, ceilings and images, as at Hemāvatī. The Rāṣṭrakūṭas, whose capital was at Mānyakheṭa, patronised both Hindu and Jain art, and their sculpture at Ellora is discussed above.

docs.title: 13.13 Karnataka: The Later Cālukyas and Hoysaḷas
docs.text:
The Hoysaḷa temples of Karnataka (12th–13th century) are built and carved of chloritic schist, a stone that can be worked in great detail (Hardy 1995). Their outer walls are wrapped in horizontal friezes (Figure 13.5, right): elephants, horsemen, scrolls, mythical beasts and narratives from the epics and Purāṇas, above which stand large images of deities under elaborate canopies. Inside, lathe-turned pillars support bracket figures of celestial women (madanikā; Figure 13.5, left), dancing, adorning themselves or playing instruments. The Cennakeśava at Belūr (begun 1117), the Hoysaḷeśvara at Haḷebīḍ (begun about 1121) and the Keśava at Somanāthapura (1268) are the best known. Many Hoysaḷa sculptures are signed by their makers. The later Cālukya temples of the 11th and 12th centuries, such as those at Lakkuṇḍi and Itagi, are carved with similar finesse.

Figure 13.5. Hoysaḷa carving in chloritic schist, 12th century. Left: a bracket figure of a celestial woman (madanikā) from the Cennakeśava temple, Belūr, under a canopy of openwork foliage. Right: horizontal bands of figures and ornament on the outer wall of the Hoysaḷeśvara temple, Haḷebīḍ. Photo: Basavaraj M, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 13.14 Kashmir and the Himalaya
docs.text: Kashmir produced stone and metal sculpture from the 6th to the 12th century, much of it in brass inlaid with silver and copper, for Buddhist and Hindu patrons. Its style, with full, rounded bodies and crisply detailed ornament, drew on Gandhāran and Gupta traditions, and influenced the art of the western Himalaya and Tibet. In Himachal Pradesh, metal images and carved wooden temples survive at sites such as Chamba and Brahmaur. Nepal, especially the Kathmandu valley, has a continuous tradition of metal casting and stone sculpture from the Licchavi period (5th–9th century) to the present (on its temples see Chapter 5, Section 5.7.6).

docs.title: 13.15 Jain Metal Images
docs.text: Jain communities commissioned metal images from an early date. A hoard of bronzes found at Chausa in Bihar includes some of the earliest known Jain metal images, of the early centuries CE. At Akota near Vadodara in Gujarat, a large hoard of Jain bronzes of the 6th to 11th centuries was found in the 1950s, among them standing tīrthaṅkaras, the goddess Ambikā, and images inscribed with the names of monks and lay donors. Metal images, often inlaid with silver and copper and inscribed with the names of donors and dates, continued to be made in great numbers in western India and Karnataka, and many are still worshipped in household and temple shrines.

docs.title: 13.16 Jain Colossi
docs.text: The most famous colossal image in India is the monolithic statue of Bāhubali (Gommaṭeśvara) at Śravaṇabeḷagoḷa in Karnataka, carved from the granite of a hilltop in about 981–983 for Cāmuṇḍarāya, a minister of the Gaṅga kings, and about seventeen metres (57 feet) high. It is the focus of the great mahāmastakābhiṣeka ceremony, in which the image is bathed from above, held about every twelve years. Similar colossi were carved later at Kārkaḷa (1432) and Veṇūr (1604) in coastal Karnataka. In the 15th century, colossal Jinas were carved into the rock faces of Gwalior fort.

docs.title: 13.17.1 Vijayanagara and Nāyaka
docs.text: The temples of Vijayanagara and the Nāyaka kingdoms (14th–18th century) are covered with carving: pillars sculpted as rearing horses and composite beasts (yāḷi), portrait figures of rulers and donors, narrative friezes, and great numbers of painted stucco figures on the gopuras. The life-size portrait sculptures of Kṛṣṇadevarāya and his queens at Tirupati, in bronze, and of the Nāyaka rulers in the halls of Madurai and elsewhere, in stone, show a developed tradition of royal portraiture.

docs.title: 13.17.2 Bengal Terracotta
docs.text:
In Bengal, where stone is scarce, the brick temples built from the 16th to the 19th century are covered with terracotta plaques showing scenes from the Rāmāyaṇa and Mahābhārata, the life of Kṛṣṇa, the incarnations of Viṣṇu, and contemporary life, including European ships and soldiers. The temples of Viṣṇupur, built by the Malla kings, such as the Śyām Rāy (1643), the Jor Bāṅglā (1655) and the Madan Mohan (1694), and the Kāntajī temple at Kantanagar (completed 1752, now in Bangladesh) are the best known (Table 13.2; on the architecture see Chapter 5, Section 5.7.4) (Ghosh 2005).

Table 13.2. Some terracotta temples of Bengal Temple Place Date Śyām Rāy Viṣṇupur 1643 Jor Bāṅglā (Keṣṭa Rāy) Viṣṇupur 1655 Madan Mohan Viṣṇupur 1694 Ananta Vāsudeva Bansberia 1679 Kāntajī Kantanagar, Dinajpur completed 1752

docs.title: 13.17.3 Sculpture in Indo-Islamic Architecture
docs.text: Islamic religious architecture avoids images of living beings, and sculpture in the Sultanate and Mughal periods took the form of carved ornament: calligraphy, arabesques and geometric patterns, pierced stone screens (jālī), relief carving of flowering plants, and inlay of coloured stones. The workmanship of the screens of the Sīdī Saiyyid mosque in Ahmadābād, of Salīm Chishtī’s tomb at Fatehpur Sīkrī and of the Tāj Mahal ranks with the finest carving in India (Chapter 6). Figural sculpture was not entirely absent from secular buildings, as the stone elephants once placed at the gates of the Agra and Delhi forts show.

docs.title: 13.17.4 Modern Sculpture
docs.text: In the 20th century, sculptors trained in art schools developed modern Indian sculpture. Ramkinkar Baij (1906–1980) at Santiniketan made monumental outdoor works in cement and laterite; D. P. Roy Chowdhury, Sankho Chaudhuri, Meera Mukherjee (who learned from the ḍhokrā metal-casters of Bastar) and many others explored modern forms while drawing in different ways on Indian traditions. Alongside them the traditional workshops described in Chapter 11 continue to produce images for worship.

docs.title: 13.18 Sculpture and Dance
docs.text: Indian sculpture is closely related to dance. Many sculptures of deities, celestial women and musicians adopt the stances, gestures and bends of the body described in the Nāṭyaśāstra, and some temples carry systematic series of dance poses, such as the karaṇas carved at Thanjavur and on the gateways of Chidambaram (Chapter 5). The Viṣṇudharmottara makes the understanding of image-making depend on that of dance (Chapter 14, Section 14.3). In the 20th century, dancers and scholars reconstructing classical dance forms such as Bharatanāṭyam and Odissi used temple sculpture as one of their sources, studying the poses carved at Chidambaram, Thanjavur and Konārak; this use of sculpture to recover dance has itself become part of the modern history of both arts.

docs.title: 13.19 Patrons and Makers
docs.text: Inscriptions on sculptures and buildings show who paid for them, and they reveal a wider range of patrons than the dynastic labels suggest. At Sāñcī and Bhārhut, hundreds of donors, many of them women, monks and nuns, paid for individual railing posts and crossbars. At Mathurā, Kuṣāṇa-period Buddhist and Jain images were dedicated by monks, nuns, merchants, goldsmiths and women of the city. Royal women were among the great patrons: the Cālukya queens Lokamahādevī and Trailokyamahādevī at Paṭṭadakal, the Chola queen Sembiyaṉ Mahādevī, who rebuilt many temples in stone and commissioned bronzes, the Caulukya queen to whom the Rāṇī kī Vāv is attributed, and the Mughal and Rajput women who built mosques, tombs, stepwells and gardens. Merchant and ministerial families paid for the Jain temples of western India. The sculptors themselves are often anonymous, but at some sites, especially in Karnataka, they signed their work, and inscriptions sometimes record their titles and rewards (Chapter 11).

docs.title: 13.20 The North-east
docs.text: The sculpture of ancient Kāmarūpa (Assam) is less well known than that of other regions but of considerable interest. A carved stone doorframe at Da-Parbatiya near Tezpur, with river goddesses at its base, shows the reach of the Gupta-period style in the 5th or 6th century; the ruined temple complex of Madan Kāmdev (10th–12th century) has lively carvings of deities, couples and musicians; and the sculpture of the Pāla style spread into the region. Later, under the Ahom kings, temples at Sivasāgar carried bands of brick and stone carving, and the satras (Vaiṣṇava monasteries) founded in the tradition of Śaṅkaradeva developed their own arts of masks, painted manuscripts and wooden carving.

docs.title: 13.21 Material and Style
docs.text:
The materials available to each school shaped its style. Mathurā’s sandstone favoured broad, rounded forms; Gandhāra’s schist took crisp, deep folds; the fine sandstone of Sārnāth allowed smooth, unbroken surfaces; the dark stone of eastern India, polished to a sheen, encouraged precise linear detail; the chloritic schist of Karnataka permitted extraordinary intricacy; granite in Tamil Nadu demanded simplified forms in stone, while the lost-wax process freed Chola bronze-casters to create open, dynamic compositions. Material alone does not explain style, which also depended on patronage, religious function and the inventiveness of individual workshops; but the relation between the two is one of the threads that run through the history of Indian sculpture (Table 13.3).

Sandstone, terracotta, metal Hindu, Buddhist, Jain Pallava and Chola 7th–13th c. Granite, bronze Hindu, Jain Pāla and Sena 8th–12th c. Dark stone, bronze Buddhist, Hindu Hoysaḷa 12th–13th c.
